### Stage Seven — Power and action

This stage asks why every moving thing needs a mover, and whether the chain of movers can continue without end. It examines God's power and the powers of the soul, how the soul differs from the body's physical condition, and why beings free of matter neither die nor seek anything through motion. It then considers what things are made from, why they begin after not existing, and whether the possibility of coming to be is an added feature. It examines possibility and actuality, and the different ways power and action can come before one another. Finally, it looks at how nature and substances change, how bodies, the world, beings free of matter, and time come into existence, what causes time and what it belongs to, and why nothing comes before time except God.

#### Chapter 1 — The meanings of power

The word *power* is used for several different things,[^V03-1] but its earliest meaning seems to be the strength an animal has to carry out strenuous movements.[^V03-2] Its opposite is weakness. In this sense, power is a kind of added strength in the ability to act. It has a source and a sign. Its source is the ability to act: an animal acts when it wills and does not act when it does not will. The opposite of this ability is inability. Its sign is resistance to being affected. Someone carrying out strenuous movements may be affected by the effort, and that can keep them from finishing what they are doing. So resistance to being affected points to strength. The word *power* then came to be used both for its source—the ability to act—and for its sign—the ability to resist being affected.

Power also has a general description and a feature that follows from it. Its general description is a quality that affects something else, considered as something distinct from itself.[^V03-3] The feature that follows is possibility. Someone with power can act, but can also refrain from acting, so whether the action occurs remains open. Since possibility follows from power in this sense, the word *power* also came to mean possibility itself. That is why people say a white garment is “black potentially”: it can become black.

People also call attainment and existence “act,” even when, strictly speaking, these are not actions but states that are received. The original meaning of *power* was tied to action. So once people called possibility “power,” they called what that possibility leads to—attainment and existence—“act.”

Mathematicians noticed that some lines can serve as a side of a particular square, while others cannot. They called the square the “power” of the line, as though the square were something that could potentially come from it.[^V03-4] Some held that the square is formed when one of its sides turns around itself.

Once we understand power, we can identify its opposites: weakness, inability, ease of being affected, necessity, ineffectiveness, and a line's inability to serve as a side of a given square. Each is opposed to power in a different respect. We have already discussed possibility as one meaning of power. But possibility opposed to actuality differs in one respect from possibility opposed to necessary existence or impossibility. This will become clear when we discuss why matter is needed for everything that comes to be or changes. Power as resistance to being affected is one kind of quality. Power as strength or ability seems to be a kind of active quality—a quality that produces an effect.

#### Chapter 2 — Defining power as the source of change

Power can mean the source of change in one thing that brings about change in another, insofar as the other is distinct from it. We add that last qualification because if something acted on itself—as when a doctor treats himself—it would have to differ from itself in some respect or have different parts. Otherwise, the same thing would be both the one acting and the one affected in the very same respect. That is impossible, even for something made of parts, let alone something simple.

A feature may follow necessarily from what a thing is, without the thing first having to become able to receive it. This is the exception: the feature is already fully present, as with features that necessarily belong to what a thing is. Some writers, including the author of *Al-Mulakhkhas*, saw that something can seem to act and be acted on in this different sense. They then began to doubt that one thing cannot be both agent and recipient. But the difference between what is possible and what is actual is clear and certain.

There is no doubt that nothing can be the source of its own change. If a thing were the source of a feature or state in itself, that feature would remain for as long as the thing did. The thing would not be changing. So the source of its change must be something else. This shows that every moving thing has a mover other than itself.

An agent's power may involve awareness and choice, or it may involve neither. Each kind can be divided further. The capacity to be affected may belong to bodies or to souls. A thing may be able to take on a form without keeping it, as water takes the shape of a container but does not hold that shape. Or it may be able both to take on a form and keep it, as wax and earth do.

An affected thing may be able to undergo one kind of change, like a heavenly sphere's rotation; a limited range of changes, like an animal; or any change at all, like basic matter. An agent's power may likewise be limited to one action, like fire's power to burn; it may extend to many but limited actions, as with the choices of those who can choose; or it may extend to everything, as God's power does: He has power over all things.

Here is a rule that applies to both kinds of power: the more fully formed a thing is, the more it can act and the less it is acted upon. The less fully formed it is, the more it is acted upon and the less it acts. God—may His name be exalted—has the fullest and strongest existence. He acts on all things and is the goal toward which all things tend. His power extends without limit. Basic matter, by contrast, is as indeterminate as anything can be. It is like the broadest class of things because it is bare of every form that would make things distinct kinds and give them actual existence. It can receive all things, as the broadest class can include every kind. I do not mean that basic matter is ready for every form at once. Readiness is a specific capacity for one change that is close to taking place, and it arises only through a specific form. Basic matter is not, by itself, ready for every form; a particular form makes it ready for a particular thing.

Let us now divide powers by the actions they produce.[^V03-5] A power may produce one action or several. In either case, it may act with awareness or without it. This gives us four kinds.

The first kind is a power that produces one action without awareness of that action. It may be a form that makes a thing what it is, or a feature that does not. In things such as fire and water it is called a nature. In bodies made from different elements, it is called the form of that kind of body; examples include opium's cooling nature and euphorbium's heating nature. If it is a feature of the second kind, examples include heat and cold.

### The second kind — Power that produces different actions without awareness

This is the set of powers found in plants.

### The third kind — Power that produces one steady action with awareness

This is the soul attributed to the heavenly spheres.

### The fourth kind — Power that produces different actions with awareness

This is the ability found in animals on earth.

These are the four kinds of power. They cannot all be grouped under one general type, because some are forms that make a thing what it is, while others are features a thing can have. We discuss the first kind when we study matter and form, the second and third when we study the soul, and the fourth when we study qualities.[^V03-6]

One more point should be clear. A power to act may be limited to one action, like fire's power to burn, or may extend to several actions, like the power of someone who can choose what to do. When a power can act on any one of many possible individuals of a kind, outside causes determine which particular individual it acts on. Once that individual exists, the power with respect to that specific individual is gone. If it remained, the same result would be both actual and still only possible.[^V03-7] But the power to act on another individual of the same kind does not disappear. The power to act on any individual of that kind remains even when no action is taking place.

It is like the difference between a general idea and an idea tied to one particular person. A general idea does not disappear when one person is gone. But an idea tied to one person in particular ends when that person is gone. As we have explained, necessity stands to possibility as completeness stands to lack. So possibility does not disappear when it becomes necessary, but the power to perform one specific action does disappear once that action is complete.

#### Chapter 3 — Must the ability to act exist when the action happens?

Some thinkers held that the ability to act must exist at the same time as the action. Avicenna rejected this as implausible. In the metaphysics section of *The Healing*, he says:

> On this view, a person sitting down cannot be able to stand. The ability would come only once the person was already standing—so how could they stand? Such a person would also be unable to see or look around several times in a single day. In effect, they would be blind.

It is even more surprising that the author of *Al-Mulakhkhas* tries to defend their view this way:[^V03-8]

> The objection Avicenna raises does not seem justified. If you define power as the source of change, then either all the conditions needed for it to bring about an effect are present, or they are not. If they are all present, the effect must occur at the same time as the power; the power cannot come before the effect. In that sense, we can say the power and action happen together. But if a condition needed to produce the effect is missing, what is present is not the full cause, but only part of it. It is not the full power to act, but only part of that power. The quality called ability clearly exists both before and after the action. But it is not the full power to produce the action; it is only one part. If we can understand their words this way, why accuse them of error and make their view look foolish?

I say that this defender has confused two meanings of power. One is the ability to act while the action is still only possible. The other is the full power that produces the action once all its conditions are in place. He also seems to have forgotten that he already admitted possibility follows from the first kind of power.[^V03-9] He did not see that this possibility is only readiness for an action, not the action itself. It cannot exist together with the completed action. This differs from the way the mind considers what something is apart from whether it exists. The mind can make that distinction even for simple things that do exist in reality.

The word *source* also has two meanings. It can mean what makes something possible, or what makes it actual. The form present in semen is a source of the possibility of a human being, but it cannot by itself bring an actual human being into existence. Otherwise, power as power would already be actual in relation to the very thing it is only able to bring about. Yet the defender also admits that an incomplete cause cannot produce its effect; once complete, it must produce it. A thing cannot be incomplete and complete, or impossible and necessary, in the same respect.

What makes both action and inaction possible cannot, without anything more, be the source of one particular action. The source of ability—the possibility of acting—is one thing. The source that makes the action real and necessary is another. How can anyone, by reason and common sense, claim that the ability to do something exists only when the action is happening? If we think carefully about what we mean by a source of change, we see that, in relation to the change it can bring about, the result must still be possible and not yet real. A source of something that follows from it necessarily should not be called the source of change in another thing. I will make this clearer.

#### Chapter 4 — When must a change happen, and when can it fail to happen?

When a limited power to act meets a limited capacity to be affected, the action must follow. Power to act is also called ability. If it involves awareness and choice, it is an ability whether or not the action always follows without fail.

Theologians say that ability belongs only to someone who can both act and refrain from acting. So they do not call a cause that always acts a capable agent, even if it is fully able to do so. This view is wrong. It is right only if “capable” means that both acting and refraining are possible, and neither is settled on its own. Animal ability works this way: it needs something to tip the balance, such as a motive, before it can act. But if we define a capable agent as one whose action comes with awareness and will, then anyone who acts by will is capable and free. The statement “if it wills, it acts; if it does not will, it does not act” is true whether not willing can actually happen or is impossible. A conditional statement like this does not depend on either part being true on its own, and does not require an alternative to occur.[^V03-10] There are several kinds of capable agent.

One kind is an agent that acts by intention. In itself, it is equally related to two possible outcomes, so it needs something extra to tip the balance. That might be new knowledge, or the presence of something to act on and its readiness to receive the action. A writer, for example, needs a tablet with a smooth surface. The agent may need a tool, such as a pen or a chisel; a helper, as one sawyer needs another; a suitable time, as a leatherworker needs summer; or a motive, as hunger prompts someone to eat. It may also need an obstacle removed: a dyer needs dirt cleared from the cloth, and a washer needs the clouds to pass so the cloth can dry.[^V03-11]

A motive is different from will. An agent acting by will may have an additional motive, or may have none. A motive may also arise after being absent. In all these cases, the agent is still described as acting by will.[^V03-12]

Another kind is an agent[^V03-13] whose action comes from its knowledge. Its knowledge of the order and goodness of the action is the only source and motive for acting; nothing is added to the knowledge itself. This is how the Necessary Being acts, according to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school.

A third kind is an agent whose own self-knowledge is enough to bring about its action. Its knowledge of what it makes is identical with the being of what it makes, just as its knowledge of itself as maker is identical with itself. This is how God acts, according to the Illuminationist philosophers, who regard Him as light. His light[^V03-14]—His knowledge of Himself—is what makes other beings appear in the world. His first creations are the ruling and guiding lights of intellect and soul. Through them come lesser lights and beings with awareness, some constant and some passing, down through all existence from the brightest to the darkest.

These three kinds all act by choice and will, guided by knowledge. The knowledge may be separate from the agent, be an added feature that always belongs to it, or be identical with it.[^V03-15] Every other kind of agent[^V03-16] acts under compulsion, and there are three such kinds.

One kind acts by nature. It acts according to its bodily nature when nothing blocks it. A second kind acts under force: its nature is made to act against its usual direction by an outside force. If left alone, it would act otherwise. A third kind acts under the direction of a higher power. This happens when a stronger power guides a natural power and uses it to produce movements and changes in the body below. For example, the powers of plants and animals serve the soul by drawing things in, pushing them out, changing them, digesting food, growing, and reproducing. These actions are neither simply the body's nature acting on its own, nor actions against its nature. They follow the higher principles that guide these powers and help make them what they are. This kind of action differs from natural action, forced action, and voluntary action as such.

For example, when the soul moves the body by choice, the movement belongs both to the soul and to the body. In relation to the soul, we call it voluntary. In relation to the body or one of its parts, we call it action under direction.

All three kinds are compelled in some way. If we look closely, only God acts by choice in the fullest sense. All others act under His power, whether they choose or are forced. Many are compelled even in their very act of choosing.

Returning to our question, some powers that start movements and actions work with reason and imagination, while others do not. The powers linked to reason and imagination do not act on their own just because something is present for them to act on. Nor does the meeting of a power with something that can be affected make the action inevitable. Just as bodily matter can be equally ready for two opposite forms, these mental powers can be equally ready for opposite possibilities when considered on their own. One power of the intellect can take in both human and nonhuman things; one power in an animal can imagine both pleasure and pain, a thing and its opposite.[^V03-17]

In themselves, these powers can act in either direction. They become able to bring about an action only when joined by a will that grows from belief or thought, or by a desire raised by imagining something pleasant or painful. In short, there must be a motive that gives rise to a firm resolve, one that does not turn away from its aim. This resolve moves the nerves and muscles, and then the action becomes necessary. If these powers alone forced action whenever they were present, they would produce two opposing actions at once, which is impossible.

Powers in beings without reason and imagination may also be able to act without always doing so. But their action becomes necessary when the power is complete, every obstacle is removed, and it meets a capacity to be affected. Likewise, a capacity to be affected must undergo change when it meets a power to act only if that capacity is complete. Like a power to act, it may be complete or incomplete. An incomplete capacity is far from producing the change; a complete one is close. There are different degrees of distance.

Semen has the potential to become a man, and so does a boy. But the potential in semen is more remote: it must meet two powers to act, one that brings it to childhood and another that develops the child into an adult man. A boy needs to meet only one such power to reach adulthood. More remote still is the capacity in an element, and farther away than that is basic matter's capacity to become an intellect fully at work—even an intellect able to understand ideas below it, as we will explain later.

#### Chapter 5 — Another way to divide the power to act

Power to act may be a source of existence or a source of change.[^V03-18] Philosophers who study existence and its causes call an agent the source that gives existence. Those who study nature mean the source of change, in its different forms. The first is more deserving of the name “agent.” A source of change is itself subject to change: it renews a state that was different before. It is like a changing tool. It moves and is moved, acts and is acted upon, and is kept in being while also changing and passing away.

If you ask[^V03-19] who most deserves the name “agent,” the answer is God[^V03-20]. He removes nonexistence completely from things and removes their deficiency and evil. His action is the unbounded giving of good and existence. It is not limited to a period, conditioned by a quality, or confined to one time rather than another. It is eternal and necessary, in measure with what each recipient can bear and each prepared thing can receive.

The powers that directly cause movement do something else. They prepare matter and make it ready. They remove some opposing qualities so matter can receive another form once those qualities are gone, or divide it according to its different levels of readiness. They do not give existence itself.

#### Chapter 6 — Another way to divide causes

When we discuss causes and effects, you will see how something can be a cause only indirectly. Keep this in mind here: most things people call agents do not truly give existence to the things attributed to them. A father, a farmer, or a builder, for example, does not give existence to children, crops, or buildings. They prepare the conditions that allow these things to come about, so they are only indirect causes. God is the one who gives them existence. He points this out when He says:

> Have you considered the seed you emit? Do you create it, or are We the Creator? Have you considered what you sow? Do you make it grow, or are We the One who makes it grow? Have you considered the fire you kindle? Did you make its tree grow, or are We the One who made it grow?

The point is that what most people call an agent only sets things in motion and brings about changes in matter. God is the one who gives things their forms and existence. Exalted is His name.

#### Chapter 7 — Another way to classify abilities to act

Some abilities to act come from nature, some from habit, some from learned skill, and some from chance. To learn a skill, a person deliberately uses materials, tools, and movements. With practice, the soul gains a lasting ability that lets the action come easily. This ability gives the skill its character, much as fire's nature makes it heat and water's nature makes it cool. In our discussion of the next life, we will see that this lasting ability may become part of what the soul is, and that the soul may be raised in that form on the Day of Resurrection.[^V03-21]

Actions done from habit, on the other hand, may start for another reason—desire, anger, or an opinion. Habit then develops as a result; the person did not set out to form it or direct their actions toward it from the start. A habit does not have to mean that the same actions have taken root in the soul. Repeating them may create something else in the soul, something different from the actions themselves. The actions prepare the soul for it, and what prepares something need not be like what it prepares. So a skill learned through practice differs from a habit that grows out of repeated action.

A habit does not have to depend on particular tools or materials. The habit of walking, for example, is very different from the habit of trading. Even so, if we look closely, we see that habits and learned skills both grow from the same basic quality in the soul.[^V03-22] Natural abilities are found in both nonliving and living bodies. We will explain chance, randomness, and aimless action when we discuss what things are for.[^V03-23]

#### Chapter 8 — Does every action have to start after a time when it did not exist?

Not every action has to come after a time when it did not exist, as the theologians claim.[^V03-24] They hold that something needs a cause because it began to exist, not simply because it is possible.[^V03-25] The only exception would be if they use “action” to mean a particular kind of effect that happens while an agent acts on something—for example, heating an object while it is being heated, or darkening it while it is being darkened. But if “an agent’s action” means giving something existence, it does not have to come after a time when it did not exist. An effect needs a cause because it is possible, not because it once did not exist.

Some actions are renewed moment by moment, such as motion and time, and nature as it works through bodies. They need a cause to begin, but not to keep existing, since they do not last from one moment to the next. They also need a cause because they are possible: they come into being and change. We will explain this later.

But the theologians do not mean this. They even say that if God ceased to exist after bringing the world into being, the world would still exist.

Those who have examined this carefully say that a caused thing cannot exist on its own. Its existence depends on the cause that brings it into being and keeps it in being. This dependence does not come from what the thing is, because the cause did not make its nature. It does not come from the time before it existed, because the cause did not make it nonexistent. Nor does it come simply from the fact that it came after not existing. That order is part of the kind of existence it has; it does not need a cause of its own.

Instead, a new thing depends on its cause because its existence cannot stand on its own. It is too weak and incomplete to be whole without something else. Its cause completes it. Dependence ends with God, whose own reality is complete. Through Him, all that is complete is completed, every need is met, and every movement and longing reaches its goal. This prevents the explanation from looping back on itself or going on forever. God is fully complete and more than complete, as we have explained. Everything else depends on Him and needs Him. As we have said, this dependence is part of what holds everything else up.

If things coming into being were fully ready to receive existence, they would always exist. But they become ready through changes that happen one after another. These changes complete their ability to exist. Once that ability is complete, they exist without delay. So an action happens as soon as its cause is fully in place. This is why Aristotle said that an action that happens in time must come from a cause that also exists in time. He explains:

> To find out whether the cause of an action exists in time, look at the action itself. If it takes place in time, so does its cause, because the cause cannot be separated from it.

#### Chapter 9 — Power is not the body's temperament, as some doctors claim

Here is why. As we will explain, bodily temperament is a blend of the basic qualities we feel by touch: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. It is a mix of these four, balanced among them and weaker than each one on its own. Its effects should therefore be like theirs, but weaker. Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness have direct, strong effects; the body's blended temperament has mild, weak effects.

Since the soul's power does not have the same kind of effect as these four qualities, it cannot be the temperament itself. Instead, power is a quality of the soul that depends on the body's temperament. It, in turn, calls for a guiding form that manages and preserves that temperament. This form replaces, little by little, what the body loses as it changes, and repairs what tends to come apart under the opposing effects and shifting conditions of those qualities. So this guiding form, with its ability to direct, repair, and control, belongs to a higher level than the body's temperament. This question fits better in the study of nature.[^V03-26]

#### Chapter 10 — Motion and rest

Motion and rest resemble potentiality and actuality. In the broadest sense, they are features of things simply insofar as they exist;[^V03-27] a thing need not first be classified as a particular natural or mathematical kind for them to apply.[^V03-28] An existing thing is either actual in every respect, so that it cannot change or leave its state; potential in every respect, though this can apply to something that exists only when its potentiality itself has some actuality, as it does in prime matter; or actual in one respect and potential in another. In the last case, it must be made up of two aspects: one actual, the other potential. As actual, it comes before what is potential in it. We will see that actuality comes before potentiality in every sense of “before.”

The first kind—what is actual in every respect and cannot change at all—must be truly simple. Yet, despite its simplicity, it must contain all things and the fullness of all existence, as we will prove. A thing that is actual in one respect and potential in another must be brought from potentiality to actuality by something other than itself, in the respect in which it is potential. Otherwise, it would not be potential.

This transition can happen gradually or all at once. In the broad sense, transition from potentiality to actuality occurs in every category: in each one, something can move from potential to actual. But the established use of the word motion is narrower. It means a transition that does not happen all at once. The absence of such a transition in something capable of receiving it is called rest. Motion can therefore be defined as gradual coming-to-be, gradual arrival, or a step-by-step transition from potentiality to actuality. Each of these phrases can define motion.

You might object that “all at once” means coming to be in an instant; an instant is the boundary of time; and time is the measure of motion. So defining motion by what happens all at once seems to define it through time, which is itself defined through motion. That would make the definition circular. The same problem seems to arise if we say “step by step” or “gradually,” since both are understood through time, which is understood through motion.

We can answer, as some careful thinkers have, that we grasp these ideas—happening all at once, happening gradually, and the like—directly, with help from the senses. Defining them precisely may require their essential parts, such as time and the instant. Those precise definitions, however, are what need proof.[^V03-29] We can define motion using these familiar ideas, then use motion to understand time and the instant: one is its measure, the other the boundary of that measure. Time and the instant are what account for these ideas that we grasp at once. Many things are immediately familiar to us even though their true nature is hard to explain.[^V03-30] There is no circle here. This answer was given by the author of *Discussions* and approved by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in *Eastern Investigations*. Earlier philosophers, however, rejected this definition because they thought it contained a hidden circle.

For a gradual process to count, though, it must be laid out along something extended that comes to be gradually. That is why Avicenna says in *The Healing* that all such definitions involve circular reasoning. Our master in this discipline therefore took another path. Earlier philosophers set these definitions aside and said that motion is a potential arrival. Whatever a thing can arrive at is a completion for that thing. Motion, then, is a completion of what moves. But it differs from other kinds of completion: its whole nature lies in passing toward something else and moving along the way to it. This gives it two features. First, there must be some attainable goal toward which the movement is directed. Second, as long as the movement is still under way, something about it remains potential.[^V03-31] A thing is moving in actuality only while it has not reached its goal. Until then, some part of the goal remains potential for it. Motion therefore depends on some part of it remaining potential, and on the goal not yet being fully actual. Other completions have neither feature. When something that is potentially square becomes square, its squareness does not require it to keep reaching for anything. And once the square shape is present, no part of it remains potential.

Consider a body in one place that could be in another. It has two possibilities: being in that other place, and moving toward it. We have already seen that whatever a thing could attain would be a completion for it. So moving toward the goal is a completion. But it must come before reaching the goal; otherwise, there would be no gradual arrival, which is what we are discussing. Thus, moving toward the goal is the first completion of what is potential.[^V03-32] It is not a completion of the body in every respect. Motion does not complete the body simply as a body; it completes it in the respect in which it was potential.[^V03-33] Motion, then, is the first completion of what is potential, precisely insofar as it is potential. This is the definition given by Aristotle, the greatest philosopher.

Plato, the divine philosopher, defined motion as “leaving equality”: a thing’s state at one instant is no longer the same as it was just before or just after. Pythagoras is reported to have defined motion as “otherness.”[^V03-34] This comes close to Plato’s definition: at every instant, the thing differs in some respect from how it was just before and how it will be just after. We can make both definitions more complete by understanding them to include continuous gradual change.[^V03-35] If a thing’s state at each moment differs from its state at another moment before or after, then its successive states are different, yet form one continuous process. Plato called this “leaving equality”; Pythagoras called it “otherness.” They mean much the same thing.

It would be no objection that “leaving equality” and “otherness” are each simple ideas and do not, by themselves, express extension and continuity. The point is that the definitions can be understood in the fuller sense just described. Avicenna did not take this approach. In *The Healing*, he says that motion has been defined in several confused ways because its nature is itself hard to grasp.[^V03-36] Its stages are never fixed in actuality: as one state passes away, another begins. Some defined it as “otherness,” since motion changes a state and brings about something different from what was there before. But they failed to see that what brings about otherness need not itself be otherness. Not everything that produces something is identical with what it produces. If otherness itself were motion, then everything different would be moving, which is not so.

Some have called motion an unlimited nature. At most, Avicenna says, this could be one of its features, and not a feature unique to motion; infinity and time are unlimited in the same way.[^V03-37] Others defined it as “leaving equality”: a stable state is one that remains the same in relation to every passing time, while in motion the relation between the thing and its states is not the same at different times. A body moving from place to place is in a different place at every instant; something changing in quality has a different quality at every instant. These definitions were attempts to cope with a difficult subject. We do not need to spend a long time rejecting them; a sound mind can see the problem from what we have already said. That is the end of Avicenna’s account.

I say: Avicenna’s criticism of the Pythagorean definition does not quite hold.[^V03-38] Motion is not something that causes otherness; motion is change itself, a thing’s passing from one state to another. It is not whatever makes the thing change. A thing’s leaving one state is itself its being different from that state in reality, even if the two ideas differ in our minds. That is enough for a definition. As for the definition attributed to some thinkers—that motion is an unlimited nature—we will discuss it when we prove that the substance of nature is constantly changing and flowing through every body.[^V03-39] This constant renewal in nature’s own substance is the source of all the changing motions and qualities of earthly things.

#### A Difficulty and Its Solution

In *Eastern Investigations* and his commentary on *The Sources of Wisdom*, Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raises a doubt about the claim that a thing comes from potentiality to actuality gradually, although the philosophers agree on it. When something changes, he says, either something comes to be in it or something leaves it. If neither happens—if nothing absent appears and nothing present disappears—then its state at that instant is the same as before, so it has not changed. But change was assumed. Therefore, when a thing changes, something must come to be in it or leave it.

Suppose something comes to be in it. That thing was absent and then became present, so it must have a beginning. The beginning cannot be divided, or one part would come before the other and would not be the beginning itself. At its beginning, then, the new thing either exists or does not. If it does not exist, it is still absent and has not begun to exist. If it does exist, then either some part of it remains potential or none does. If none remains, the whole thing came to be at once, not gradually. If some part remains potential, that remaining part is either the very same thing that has come to be—which is impossible, since one thing cannot be present and absent at once—or it is something else. In the latter case, what came first came to be all at once, while what has not yet come to be is wholly absent. No one thing has come to be gradually; there are only separate things following one another. The conclusion, al-Razi says, is that a simple, indivisible thing can only come to be all at once. A thing with many parts can be said to come to be gradually only because each part appears after another. Strictly speaking, anything that has come to be has come to be all at once, and whatever has not come to be is wholly absent. That is his argument.

I reply that Bahmanyar records this objection from earlier philosophers and rejects it. It only denies motion as a continuous whole, he says, which does not exist in external things. What exists is motion as “being between” its endpoints: a flowing state, neither something that has yet to begin nor something that has already come to an end. Most later philosophers took this approach, claiming it was the right philosophical view. But our master and teacher—may his standing remain high—explained that even those who deny motion as a continuous whole still imagine this “being between” as a new, gradually unfolding, continuous thing, whose parts arise one after another. If one thing cannot come to be gradually, how can we imagine it doing so, whether in the external world or in the mind? This misleading argument would prove just as much about imagined things as about external ones, even though everyone agrees it fails. How, then, can it be sound here?

We have proved that a body is continuous and cannot be divided into parts that have no size, as we will explain in our discussion of substance.[^V03-40] We also see and feel a body moving from one place to another. That passage is gradual and follows a continuous distance. It is plainly true that a continuous, changing quantity extends along another continuous quantity that remains in place, even if only in the imagination. We should therefore uncover the mistake at the root of the objection. This is not difficult once it is understood: a thing’s being fully present at an instant is different from its existing in time. A thing can exist throughout a stretch of time without its whole self—or any part of it—being present at one instant. Only its endpoint is present then. An endpoint lies outside the thing, because it marks where the thing ends and is absent. The unity of a thing does not rule this out. Motion, time, and similar things have a weak kind of existence: the existence of each part goes with the nonexistence of another.[^V03-41] Coming to be gradually does not prevent one continuous thing from existing throughout the whole span of time, which is itself one continuous whole. It only prevents the thing from existing in its entirety, or even in part, at one instant.

Nor must every event have a first instant at which it, or one of its parts, exists. This mistake comes from using the word “beginning” in two different senses. It can mean the endpoint of a thing; or it can mean an instant at which something that comes to be all at once first exists and then remains. Motion does not come to be all at once and then continue. It has no first instant of coming to be, nor does any part of it have one, since each part of motion is motion. It has an endpoint, and that endpoint coincides with an instant at the edge of the motion.

One definition of motion, given by Avicenna in *The Salvation*, is: “a body’s gradual change in a stable state, as it moves toward something and reaches it, whether that goal exists in potential or in actuality.” Let us explain each part of this definition and what it rules out. “A change in a stable state” excludes a transition from one unstable state to another, such as from one time to another, one action to another, or one experience to another. These are unstable states, and the transition between them is not motion, just as being in them is not rest.[^V03-42] “In a body” excludes changes in the stable states of immaterial souls,[^V03-43] such as universal acts of will and intellectual ideas. It also excludes, according to some, the changing readiness and receptivity of prime matter, though matter does have motion in its readiness and capacity. When we speak of motion in quantity, the matter itself is what moves; by “body,” we mean the body together with its matter.

“Gradually” excludes change that does not occur bit by bit, such as the change of one substantial form into another, which Avicenna and most philosophers say cannot happen gradually. You will see the truth of this question in due course. “As it moves toward something” excludes, for example, a body’s gradual loss of light as it grows dark. Its stable state changes gradually, but this change is not a movement directed toward a goal. The word “toward” also marks an essential connection: the goal must be what the change directly and naturally reaches. This excludes gradual changes in stable states that do not essentially lead to the result that follows them. As we will explain in our study of final causes, a goal can be essential or incidental. This excludes a gradual change from one relation to another or one position to another when neither is an essential or primary goal; such a change follows from a change in something else. The definition includes both motions that have an actual endpoint, such as a straight-line motion that comes to rest, and motions that continue without reaching an actual endpoint, such as circular motion. The latter produces a gradual position that can be divided into positions that are still only potential.[^V03-44]

Another definition, given by a group of Muslim philosophers in agreement with earlier thinkers, is that motion is “leaving a state” or “passing from potentiality to actuality.” In *The Healing*, Avicenna calls this mistaken: “leaving” and “passing” are not a broader kind or anything like one; they are simply other words for motion. Motion and these words were first used for a body’s change of place, then extended to other changes. The closest definition, he says, is: motion is “reaching potential boundaries continuously,” while rest is when this reaching stops. This definition gives us motion as a continuous whole, which we will discuss.[^V03-45]

“Potential boundaries” is important here. A motion’s boundaries are only described as lying between its start and end; this points to what makes motion distinctive. The definition of motion as a continuous whole is then a description of it, rather than the kind of separate existence it has in the outside world.

#### Chapter 11 — What kind of existence does motion have?

In *The Healing*, Avicenna says that motion has two meanings. The first is the continuous course the mind understands a moving thing to follow from its beginning to its end. This course does not exist as a completed thing in the outside world. As long as the moving thing has not reached its destination, the whole motion has not yet happened; when it has arrived, the motion has ended and is gone. So this kind of motion exists only in the mind. The moving thing recalls the place it left and the place it reached. When the image of its being in the first place is present in the imagination, and the image of its being in the second place is formed before the first image disappears, both images are present in the imagination. The mind then takes them together as one thing. Outside the mind, however, there is no independently existing whole motion between the endpoints. The moving thing is not present at either endpoint as it moves; it exists in the state between them.

The second meaning is something that exists outside the mind: the body’s being midway between its starting point and its destination. At every boundary we imagine in that middle stretch, the body is neither before nor beyond it. This is a state that lasts as long as the thing is moving. The state itself does not change, though the body may change its position along the way as an incidental result. The body is moving not because it is at one particular intermediate point—for then it would stop moving as soon as it left that point—but because it is between the endpoints in the way described. This state is the same at every intermediate boundary.[^V03-46] It is present in the moving thing at every instant, since at each instant it can be said to be at an intermediate point.

When people say that every motion takes place in time, they may mean the first kind: the continuous course exists in time in the way past events do, though it differs from them because past events existed at some instant when they were present, while motion as a whole did not. Or they may mean the second kind: the body’s being between the endpoints is in time, not because it matches the whole span of time, but because it is accompanied by a process of covering distance, and that process matches the time. Since this state is present at every instant in that time, it lasts through the time by means of the process that accompanies it. That is Avicenna’s account.

There are several points to examine and clarify. First, each nature has its own way of existing. A thing exists outside the mind when its definition applies to something and its defining limits are realized in it, as Avicenna says when he discusses relations.[^V03-47] To say that something exists outside the mind means that its definition is true of things there. Motion, time, powers, and readiness are all like this. It is surprising that Avicenna holds that continuous time exists outside the mind,[^V03-48] since it is divided into years, months, days, and hours. Motion as a continuous whole corresponds to this kind of time, and for him motion is the subject and cause of time. How can something that does not exist be the subject and cause of something that does?

Second, perhaps Avicenna denies that motion as a continuous whole exists because the body is a stable substance, present at every instant of its existence, while motion itself is not present at any instant. If motion were a feature of the body in that sense, it too would have to be present at every instant that the body is present. He therefore says that the motion that exists is the other kind, since it lasts as long as the body does. But we say that the subject and recipient of motion is not the body considered as a fixed thing. It is the body through its matter, which is affected and changed from instant to instant. The mover, too—whether it acts by nature, force, or will—must undergo some change in its conditions so that, together with those conditions, it can bring motion about in what receives it. Avicenna himself explains this elsewhere: a changing effect must have a changing cause, and a stable effect a stable cause. The same applies to what receives the effect.

Third, it is not right to deny all existence to motion as a continuous whole. Avicenna’s words here do say that, but we should understand him to mean that motion does not exist outside the mind as something complete, stable, and self-contained. His words point to this when he says it cannot exist as a stable, established thing, and that it has no stable existence outside the mind as it does there. In the mind, motion is formed gradually but remains all at once once the mind has formed it. Outside the mind, it comes to be and passes away gradually.[^V03-49]

Fourth, Avicenna’s explicit denial here seems to conflict with what he says elsewhere in *The Healing*. In his discussion of time, he says that arguments claiming time does not exist are based on the fact that it does not exist in an instant. But there is a difference between saying that something does not exist at all and saying that it does not exist as a completed thing in an instant. We can accept the latter: time has no completed existence in an instant, except in the mind or imagination. But time does have existence in a broader sense, outside the mind. If time did not exist, we could truly say that there is no interval in which something could cross a distance at a given speed. But that denial is false: there is such an interval. So time exists, even though it does not exist as a complete thing at any single instant. It does not exist merely because we imagine it: even if no one imagined it, it would still exist in this way.

Avicenna adds that some things have a firm, complete existence, while others have a weaker existence; time seems to have a weaker existence than motion. That is the end of his account.

Avicenna is too great a thinker to contradict himself in one book.[^V03-50] His point is that motion, which has a stronger existence than time, exists outside the mind in some way. Time depends on motion and is its measure, so motion must have external existence all the more. This is what Avicenna meant by denying that motion exists as a completed whole.

Fifth, motion as “being between” does not exist outside the mind, someone might say, because it is universal. Universals, insofar as they are universal—open to many instances and shared by them—do not exist outside the mind. What exists in a particular motion is the body’s being at a particular point, and that is present in an instant. Some have therefore said that motion consists of successive positions along a distance, one after another. This would mean that instants follow one another and that adjacent boundaries touch. That is impossible. And if motion consisted of such separate positions, none would be a first completion of what is potential. Each would be a second completion, since motion is the process of reaching a particular position and seeking it, not the position itself. Seeking something is not the same as possessing it; moving toward a position is not being in it.

We answer that this kind of motion is indeed indeterminate in relation to the positions that the mind considers, whether at instants or over time. Still, it is made particular by the unity of its subject,[^V03-51] the distance, the time, the specific mover,[^V03-52] the starting point, and the destination. Motion is also one of the weak kinds of existence we have discussed. That much determination is enough, even if it includes a degree of sharing. The relation of the successive positions to motion as “being between” is like the relation of individual instances to a universal; their relation to motion as a continuous whole is like the relation of parts and boundaries to a whole.

Sixth, someone might object that motion is either made up of parts that cannot be divided at all, or it is not. The first is false, as we showed in our discussion of bodies and quantities. The second means that motion can always be divided. Its imagined parts cannot all exist at once, since motion is not a stable thing. So they must exist one after another. If each part that exists is indivisible, then, once it ends, another indivisible part begins, and motion is made up of indivisible parts—which is impossible. If each part can be divided, then one part is earlier and another later; the whole part is never present. So what we assumed to be present is never present.

I say that this objection, raised by al-Razi, is close to the earlier one. The mistake comes from forgetting that existence in general is broader than existence at an instant. We choose the second option: each part of motion that exists is potentially divisible into earlier and later parts, and this division can continue as far as the mind can carry it.[^V03-53]

Seventh, one might say that the connection between the past and future parts of motion is a connection between something that exists and something that does not. We answer that motion and time are weak kinds of existence, in which existence is intertwined with nonexistence.[^V03-54] Their actuality goes with potentiality, their coming to be with passing away. Each part calls for the nonexistence of another part; in a sense, it is itself its own passing away. Motion raises many questions, and there are many answers. We will not lengthen the discussion here; let us turn to what matters more.

#### Chapter 12 — Proving the First Mover

You now know the definition of motion: it is the first action or completion[^V03-55] of something that is potential in some respect, precisely insofar as it is potential. The potentiality for motion[^V03-56] is part of what makes a moving thing what it is as a moving thing. Rest stands opposite motion as absence stands opposite presence. We say that motion is an existing, possible feature, so it needs something able to receive it. Since it comes to be, it also needs an agent. The receiver and agent must be different: a thing cannot both bring about and receive the same changing action, since acting and being acted on are different categories; nor can the giver receive what it gives. A moving thing needs a mover; it does not move itself.[^V03-57] A heater does not heat itself; it heats something that is only potentially hot.

The recipient of motion must be potential, not actual. The agent that causes it must be actual[^V03-58] in the respect toward which it moves the thing—that is, actual in the existence or completion brought about by the motion—even if it is not itself actual in motion,[^V03-59] or potential for motion.[^V03-60] Motion is not a completion of something already actual in the very respect in which it is actual. But there is a subtle point to notice.[^V03-61]

In existence there must be something other than motion and the thing that receives it: something that moves by its own nature and renews itself, and so is the source of motion by necessity. It has an agent or mover in the sense of something that brings its own renewing existence into being, not in the sense of a separate maker of its motion. There is no separate act of making between a thing and what belongs to its nature. The direct mover of motion must itself be moving; otherwise the cause would not accompany its effect. If motion did not ultimately depend on something whose own existence is renewed, we would face an infinite regress or a circle.[^V03-62] We will return to this in detail, God willing.

For now, we can say briefly that what receives motion is potential, either in the respect at issue or in every respect. What causes it is actual, either in that respect or in every respect. The different levels of actuality must end in something actual in every respect, so that we avoid circular reasoning or an infinite regress. In the same way, potentiality leads back to something potential in every respect, except that its potentiality itself is already actual. That is what distinguishes it from absolute nothingness.

So existence has two extremes.[^V03-63] At one end is the First Reality, pure existence—may His glory be exalted. At the other is prime matter. The first is pure good. The second has goodness only by accident.[^V03-64] Since it is potential for all existing things, it is good by accident; unlike sheer nonexistence, which is pure evil. This also shows that a body is made up of matter and form. A body has the potential for motion, while its bodily form—the substantial continuity of its dimensions—is actual. So it contains a multiplicity of aspects. This points toward a profound idea: whatever is truly simple must contain all things in actuality. I have found no one on earth who knows this idea.

#### Chapter 13 — Answering objections to the rule that every moving thing has a mover

The philosophers have handed down several arguments for this rule. First: if a thing moved itself, it could never rest, because what belongs to a thing by its own nature remains as long as the thing does. But moving things do rest. So the starting claim is false. Second: if a thing moved itself, all the parts of its motion would exist together as something fixed. Whatever is fixed is known to be fixed; if the motion were fixed, it would not be motion. Third: if a thing moved itself, it would either have a place or state that suited it, or it would not. If it did, it would not seek that place or state, and no direction of motion would be better than another. It would either move in every direction, which is impossible, or not move at all. If it had something that suited it, then once it reached that state it would rest. It would not, then, move itself.

Fourth: if a body moved simply because it is a body, every body would move, since all bodies share bodyhood. That is false. If it moved because it was a particular kind of body, then that particular feature—not bodyhood—would be its mover. Fifth: as we saw in the previous chapter, potentiality and actuality are different respects. If a mover causes motion, it either moves without itself being moved, in which case it is not the moving thing, or it is itself moved. But to say that it is moved means that motion, which was only potential, has become actual in it.[^V03-65] Motion would then be both potential and actual in the same thing, which is impossible. Sixth: as the recipient of motion, the moving thing is related to motion as something possible; as its agent, it is related to motion as something necessary. Possibility and necessity are opposites, so the mover cannot be the thing moved.

In *Eastern Investigations*, al-Razi objects to the first three arguments. Is nature not a mover by itself, he asks, even though it does not move at all times? Do the imagined parts of motion not come and go? Does nature not seek a particular place? Why, then, could a body not move itself without any of the problems you describe? If you answer that nature calls for motion only when the body is in a state that does not suit it, or when it loses a state that does, and that new parts of motion arise as it grows nearer to or farther from the suitable state, then rest occurs once it reaches that state. But if a cause acts only while a condition is present, its effect does not continue once that condition is gone. So why could a body not call for motion only while it is in a state that does not suit it, with motion stopping once that state has passed?

You cannot answer this, he says, without using the fourth argument: if bodyhood itself called for a particular state, all bodies would have it. The first three arguments therefore depend on the fourth. Let us examine that argument.

Every body has a size, a bodily form, and matter. Its size consists of the three dimensions, which are plainly shared by all bodies. But we still need to prove that the bodily form is one and the same in every body.[^V03-66] It cannot mean merely the ability to receive three dimensions. That ability is a relation, while bodyhood belongs to the category of substance. How could bodyhood itself be that relational capacity? Rather, bodily form is a substantial nature that entails the ability to receive dimensions.

Once we establish that bodyhood is something that entails three dimensions, it is possible that this nature differs from one body to another even though all bodies share the ability to receive dimensions. Different things can share one feature that follows from them. Al-Razi then says: even if all bodies share one bodily form, they do not share the same matter. So suppose bodyhood is not the cause of motion. Why could a body’s particular matter not be the cause?

I say that it is self-evident that all bodies share a substance that can receive dimensions.[^V03-67] We do not need a proof of this to establish natural principles and particular movers. Motion, position, and location are all features of this shared substance. Only a three-dimensional body can be in a place. Position is the relation of a thing’s parts to one another and to something outside it. Moving from place to place is also an attribute of the body. The body must therefore be what receives these features and changes. Since the body is their recipient, they must also have an efficient cause beyond it. Philosophers give several arguments for this cause. Some begin from the potentiality of these features in the body: something that follows from a thing’s nature, or from its existence, may have one and the same subject as both recipient and agent. Others begin from the fact that different things have the same feature. If that feature followed from their shared nature, it would be found in them all in the same way. The philosophers also prove elsewhere that bodyhood is a shared kind of nature among the different kinds and classes of bodies.[^V03-68]

As for al-Razi’s claim that different things may share one feature that follows from them, we answer that this is possible only when the source of that feature is what they share, not what makes them different. We know that the ability to receive dimensions belongs to a body precisely as a body, not because bodies differ from one another.[^V03-69] This meaning is shared by all bodies, even if their natures differ. Some of the arguments also show that different kinds of matter in bodies cannot be the source of the many distinct motions and effects special to each kind of body. Matter is only potential and ready to receive; its differences come from differences in natures and forms. That also answers the question why a particular matter cannot cause motion: matter is made particular only by a form that comes before it. We will see that actuality precedes potentiality in every kind of priority.

Al-Razi adds that the heavenly sphere cannot come to be or pass away, so its shape, position, and size must necessarily belong to it. If this necessity comes from its bodyhood, even though not every body has those features, then motion too could belong necessarily to some bodies because of their bodyhood, without belonging to every body. If it comes from something present in bodyhood,[^V03-70] then either that thing belongs to bodyhood or it does not. If it does not, what follows from it cannot belong necessarily to bodyhood. If it does, the same question comes up again. The only way out, he says, is to allow that the sphere’s shape and the other features do not necessarily follow from its bodyhood. Then perhaps the sphere could be broken apart or destroyed. Or perhaps those features necessarily follow from bodyhood in general, either directly or through something that belongs to bodyhood—even though they are not shared by every body. Motion could be the same way.

He then suggests that bodyhood is tied to its matter: because the heavenly spheres have matter unlike other matter, their matter could give them their shapes and dimensions. In that case, why could some bodies not have a particular kind of matter, unlike all others, that by its own nature produces a particular motion? This would not mean that all bodies share that motion.

I say that al-Razi’s argument about the heavenly sphere overlooks how an essence works, how a general kind is joined to the feature that makes it a particular kind, and how matter and form are connected in a compound thing.[^V03-71] The heavenly form—and every particular form in a body—makes the body what it is. Bodyhood does not cause a thing to be heavenly, fiery, or watery, or to have the special features and effects that belong to each kind. We will explain this when we discuss forms. As for the claim that matter produces a particular motion and other special features, the “matter” described this way is really a form. It has the name of matter but not its meaning. The meaning given is exactly what we mean by form: the source of the effects special to a thing. Nature is the source of a thing’s own motion. Once proof has established what something is, we do not need to keep its old name.

Al-Razi concludes that this argument cannot prove natural powers unless we first prove that matter is shared; otherwise, the argument fails. If matter cannot be the source of motion because it is only a recipient, and one thing cannot both receive and cause, we have already shown in our discussion of causes that this principle is false. Even if it were true, though, it would be enough to establish the conclusion. This is the fifth argument. The strongest objection to it, he says, is that essences cause their necessary features and receive them as well, which would disprove the rule that one thing cannot be both recipient and cause.[^V03-72]

I say that we have already explained the difference between acting and being acted on, and between potentiality and actuality—that is, possibility and necessity. The objection based on a thing’s necessary features does not apply. It rests on a misleading use of the word “recipient,” which can mean something that undergoes change, or something that is described as having a feature that necessarily belongs to it.

#### Chapter 14 — Dividing the moving power and proving an intellective mover

Some movers act in themselves; others act through something else, as a carpenter works through an axe.[^V03-73] Some move a thing directly by giving it the quality of motion. Others do not act directly on its motion but give the moving thing itself a principle by which it can move, as we will explain. Some movers act by moving in turn; others act without themselves moving, like the beloved who moves the lover or the teacher who moves the student.

Because there cannot be infinitely many bodies, there cannot be an infinite chain of moving things in which each moves another. We can see this, first, because a moving thing must be a body or depend on a body; an infinite chain of moving things would require infinitely many bodies. Second, causes must also come to an end.[^V03-74] If the last moving thing is moved by a mover, and that mover is itself moved, then it cannot move until another mover has moved it. The middle term has two relations and a distinctive role: it moves and is moved. Whether there is one middle mover or many, and whether they are finite or supposedly infinite, motion cannot occur if every mover is only an intermediate link. There must be a mover that does not act like those in the middle of the chain.

This brings what is potential into actuality. The source that brings something into being must itself be actual. It must exist in itself. So a mover that does not move must move either by giving a moving body the immediate principle by which it moves, or by acting as its goal, its good, or what it loves and knows. Every power in a body that moves also moves incidentally. A mover that does not move cannot therefore be a bodily power. We have shown that when a body produces a particular action or motion—not by accident, chance, or force—there must be an additional power beyond its bodyhood. That power is either a nature or a soul’s will. In either case, it must be connected to the body; it cannot be completely separate from it. If a particular action came from a source wholly separate from bodies and never connected with them, the separate source would be seeking through motion something it lacked. We have already shown this to be false. So if a separate mover contributes to the motion, it does so in one of the two ways just described, as in the motions of the heavenly spheres.

#### Chapter 15 — Why the immediate source of particular actions and motions is not separate from matter

Why can this particular body receive an effect from something separate from matter? There are only three possibilities: because it is a body, because it has a power within it, or because the separate being has a power that produces the effect.[^V03-75] If the reason is simply that it is a body, then every body should receive the same effect, as we have already seen. But that is not what happens. If the reason is a power within this body, that is exactly what we are trying to show. If the reason is a power in the separate being, then either that power produces the effect by itself—in which case the same question about the separate being comes up again—or it acts by choice.

If it acts by choice, then either it selects this body because of some feature in the body, or it affects the body at random. Random action cannot explain the lasting or usual order of the world, especially the order of the heavenly spheres. Chance does not produce results that always happen or happen most of the time. Natural actions, by contrast, do happen always or most of the time. As we will see, they are directed toward general purposes, not produced at random. So the effect must depend on a feature in the body itself. That feature is the body's nature: the power that moves it and through motion leads it toward its further completions, such as its proper place and shape. We will discuss this when we study bodily forms.

This nature also restores a body when something unusual has disturbed it. When water is heated, when earth is forced upward, or when air is compressed, the nature within each returns it to its usual state once the outside cause is gone: water becomes cool again, earth returns downward, and air regains its natural lightness and spread. The same is true of a body that has become ill because one element has taken over. When its guiding nature grows strong enough, it brings the body back to a healthy balance.

This also shows that the soul is not the body's temperament. A temperament that no longer exists cannot restore itself to its former state; what has ceased to exist cannot be brought back by itself.

#### Chapter 16 — Every thing that comes to be is preceded by potentiality and the matter that carries it

Nothing can begin to exist unless there is first a potential for it to exist. Anything that comes into being after not existing must have matter that comes before it. Why?[^V03-76] Before it exists, the thing is possible in itself. If it were impossible,[^V03-77] it could never exist; if it were necessary, it could not have been absent. Its possibility is not the agent's power to bring it about.[^V03-78] The thing is possible in relation to its own existence, not in relation to something outside it. This possibility must therefore be real before the possible thing exists. It is a feature of the world, not merely an idea in the mind[^V03-79] or a way of speaking. It is a relation[^V03-80] to the thing whose existence is possible.[^V03-81] That relation is part of what makes the possibility what it is. Possibility taken in general[^V03-82] is neither a substance nor a settled feature apart from this relation. If possibility were a substance, it would have its own existence, whether or not it was related to what might come to be. It would then be something existing on its own, rather than the ground of another thing's possibility.

Nor can it be a settled feature that exists independently of the relation.[^V03-83] We can see, then,[^V03-84] that possibility in general does not first exist outside the mind and then acquire a relation to something else. What exists are particular possibilities, each related to the existence of a particular thing. This relation is part of the possibility itself, not an additional feature attached to it.[^V03-85] Such possibilities are features of subjects. Because an accidental feature cannot constitute a substance, possibility itself must be an accidental feature existing in a subject.[^V03-86] Let us call it the 'potential to exist'[^V03-87], and call what carries it a subject, matter, or prime matter, depending on the way we consider it. This potentiality is real, even though it involves absence. Like existence in general, it is a shared meaning with many kinds beneath it, each a particular potential to exist in a particular way.

So every thing that comes to be is preceded by matter, and matter is one of the causes of coming to be. Whenever something comes to be or passes away, the matter of the thing that begins and the thing that ends must be one and the same. Otherwise, matter itself would have to come to be. It too would need prior potentiality and prior matter, and this would go on without end.[^V03-88] This is impossible, though we will later explain one way matter can renew itself along with its form.[^V03-89]

The subject that carries potentiality must itself be a beginning with no earlier subject; otherwise, potentiality would need another potentiality before it, and the chain would never end. There is also another point: a potentiality that disappears when something becomes actual has a cause, and so must itself have come to be. It must have been preceded by another potentiality in time, and that earlier one by another, without end.

Every matter, simply as matter, has the potential to become something actual. But the potentiality for a form means that the form can exist; it does not mean that the form itself needs to become actual, since form is already actuality. The possibility of a form is a feature of its matter. Think of the capacity of a basin: it is a feature of the basin. If you picture the basin and the amount of water it can hold, you understand the possibility of water being in it. Or think of the open space in a courtyard: once you picture the courtyard and the number of people it can hold, you understand the possibility of those people being there. This answers the question: how can something that exists be related to something that does not yet exist?[^V03-90] The basin and the courtyard exist; their capacity is a real feature of them, directed toward what could fill them. Someone might say that a basin's capacity and a courtyard's space are positive features, while potentiality is negative.[^V03-91] But these features are positive as features of their subjects and negative only in relation to what is not yet there. Potentiality taken in the broadest sense—the potential to exist at all—is absence in relation to existence.

One point needs clarification. Some things are possible because they can exist in matter, such as bodily forms. Other things are possible only along with matter, not inside it; human souls are of this kind.[^V03-92] Matter tips the balance in favor of a soul's existence rather than its nonexistence. Everything that could exist is equally possible to exist or not, so something must tip the balance. The giver of existence is generous and needs only a slight reason to bring a thing out of the middle ground between being and not being.

This shows how matter causes a soul to come to be, and only in this way. Matter can be needed for two reasons: to help make up the thing that comes from it, or to tip the balance in favor of its existence. A rational soul is not made out of matter, so it needs matter only in the second way. Matter is a cause of things that come to be because it carries the potential for their existence and tips the balance toward their being rather than their not being. This will become clearer when we discuss the soul's life after death.

Purely separate beings do not have real potentiality in the outside world. If they did, they would need something to carry it. Their possibility exists only as an idea in the mind: when we consider their general nature, we see that it is possible for them to exist, as explained earlier.

#### Chapter 17 — Actuality comes before potentiality

The earlier chapters may have made it seem that potentiality always comes before actuality. Most people have held this view: matter before form, a general kind before its distinguishing feature, disorder before order, and the nature of a possible thing before its existence. But this is not so.[^V03-93] In *The Healing*, Avicenna describes several views that place potentiality first. Some say matter existed before form, and that an agent later clothed it in form, either for no reason or because something prompted it. Some ancient thinkers even imagined that a soul accidentally took charge of matter, shaped it badly, and that God then stepped in and shaped it well.[^V03-94]

Others said that things had always been moving by their own nature in an irregular way, until God helped nature bring order out of disorder. Others said that darkness, a void, or a bottomless abyss had always existed in stillness and was later set in motion. Anaxagoras spoke of a mixture of all things.[^V03-95] They based these views on examples such as seeds, semen, and things being made, where potentiality seems to come first.

We answer that in particular examples of things that come to be and pass away, a particular potential may come before its result in time. But time order is not the important question. Potentiality as a whole comes after actuality in every kind of priority. It cannot exist by itself; it needs a substance to carry it, and that substance must already be actual. Something that does not exist at all cannot receive anything. There are also things that are actual and never potential, such as God and the separate intellects.

Potentiality also needs an actual cause to bring it into actuality. That cause cannot itself be a new event that needs another cause, and that cause another, without end. The chain must reach something actual that did not come to be. We have already shown that causes cannot go on without an end. Actuality also comes before potentiality in understanding: we can understand a thing's power only by first understanding what it can do. And actuality comes before potentiality in value and completeness. Actuality is completion; potentiality is lack. Any capacity to act is directed toward the action that completes it.[^V03-96]

Goodness belongs to what is actual. Harm and evil come from what is only potential, because it lacks some completion. Nothing is evil simply because it exists. It is evil because it lacks some good, as ignorance does, or because it brings about a lack in something else, as injustice does. Potentiality itself has a real existence, so its nature depends on existence, which is actual.[^V03-97] We can therefore say that actuality comes before potentiality by cause, by nature, in value, in time, and in reality.[^V03-98]

There is a difficulty. Sometimes a capacity for evil seems better than the evil action itself. It is better to have the capacity to act unjustly than to act unjustly; being bad in actuality is worse than being capable of being bad. I agree, but only in comparison. Potentiality considered just as potentiality is a lack and so is bad. An evil action, such as injustice or illness, is an actual thing and so has existence, but it is bad because it causes a further lack. The capacity for that evil is better than the evil action because it is only a lack for an action that would cause another lack.
