All bodily existences are incomplete: they need time and place, position, amount, and quality. The first source of these things must therefore be separate from them in its being and existence. Time cannot be caused by an earlier time, place by an earlier place, or position by another position, and the same is true of amount and the rest. These things are renewed effects, but their first cause must be a stable, immaterial reality outside the chain of time and place: God in His oneness, or His divine knowledge, His perfect words that never fade, or the realm of His command, where when He says “Be,” it is.[^V03-239]

#### Chapter 31 — Nothing Precedes Time and Motion Except God, Exalted in Glory

You have learned that time and the things connected with it are gradual existences, continually coming to be. Anything that precedes time—whether it is an existence, a nonexistence, or something else—if its “before” cannot coexist with what comes after, must itself be time or something in time.[^V03-240] So before every time there would be another time, and before every motion another motion.

We have also established that a thing's cause must not depend in its own existence on the thing it causes.[^V03-241] Therefore, nothing precedes time except God, His power and command. Different thinkers have called this command God's detailed knowledge, His attributes, the angels, or the divine forms known to the Platonists. People follow different paths according to what they love.

If anything else preceded time and motion through a succession of renewed states, then, when it existed, time and motion would not yet exist. Before they existed, they would have been possible. If they had not been possible, they would have had to be either necessary or impossible, and either would require reality to reverse: what had been absent would become present. That is impossible. But the possibility of motion must belong to something capable of motion, as we have shown. That can only be a body or something bodily. Whenever a thing capable of motion does not move, either its moving cause is absent or some condition of that cause is missing. When motion begins, a moving cause or one of its conditions must have come to be. The same question then arises about the coming-to-be of that cause, and the question continues without end.

A chain of causes arranged in order cannot all exist together, and a chain of causes coming one after another cannot consist of separate, disconnected moments. Both are impossible, as we have shown and as the leading philosophers agree.[^V03-242] If causes existed one by one, each in an instant that immediately followed the last, there would be instants with no time between them. The impossibility of this will be explained when we discuss indivisible atoms and what follows from them. If, instead, each cause existed in a different time, with gaps between those times, then neither the causes nor their times would exist in reality or even in the mind. Things that do not exist in either way cannot stand in an ordered or causal relation to one another. Time exists as one connected individual reality, not as separate pieces. We cannot imagine an infinite number of separate times and temporal things either; such an imagined series would not match what exists.[^V03-243]

If the causes are connected and continuous, each arising after the last, then the reality that is itself connected and renewed is the existence of substantial nature: the form of a body, with the body's capacity as its matter. Its continuity is motion in the sense of a connected path, and the measure of that continuity is time. Its lasting root is always the middle between its limits and parts. In one respect those parts are also parts of the nature itself. The flowing instant corresponds to this lasting middle, just as the middle stage of motion corresponds to the whole connected path.[^V03-244]

Here, then, is one intellectual reality that acts through endlessly many states, as the Qur'an says: “Every day He is at work.” This reality cannot be a body or anything bodily. Anything bodily is subject to time and motion. The source must therefore be a soul, an intellect, or God Himself.[^V03-245] It cannot be a soul insofar as the soul is attached to a body: in that respect, it is like material nature and a changing bodily form. The independent source of time and all the renewed things in time must be God Himself, or His highest command, called the Active Intellect or the Spirit. This is a near angel containing many angels who serve God, as the Qur'an says: “None knows the hosts of your Lord but He.”

The Spirit's relation to God is like the relation of a command to the one who gives it, or of speech to the speaker. God is the source of both command and creation. The created world includes whatever has form, measure, and dimensions: bodies and bodily things. These come to be gradually, their identities following in succession, through God's power and knowledge. The realm of command is different: God has always acted, known, and willed, and He has always issued His command. His command is eternal, while what He creates comes to be. That is why scripture says, “God's command is done,” not “God's creation is done.”[^V03-246]

#### Chapter 32 — How the Changing Is Linked to the Eternal

The minds of theologians and philosophers have long been troubled by the question of how what comes to be can depend on the eternal. The strongest and most reasonable of their answers is this: all changing things depend on a lasting, circular motion. This motion needs no cause that begins in time, because it has no beginning in time. In one respect it is eternal and depends on an eternal cause; in another respect it is always coming to be and is the source of changing things.

If someone asks how its changing aspect can need no changing cause, when we have said as a general rule that every thing that comes to be needs a cause that also comes to be, we answer: the subject of that rule is an essence that has coming-to-be as a feature. Circular motion is different. Its very essence is coming-to-be and renewal.

If that renewal belongs to it by its very nature, it does not need a cause that is itself renewed. When we reflect on the matter, we find that we judge a cause must come to be only when its effect comes to be while the effect's essence is not renewal itself. We do not make that judgment about an effect that is nothing but renewal and change, unless a further change is added to it—for example, a motion that begins after it did not exist. That is different from a continuous motion that never stops. Nor does the cause required by a changing effect need to undergo an additional change; otherwise, changing things could not depend on continuous motion.[^V03-247][^V03-248][^V03-249]

In short, every change ends in something whose very nature is change and passing away. Since it is always coming to be, its cause need not itself begin in time. And since it is change itself, it can be the cause of changing things. This is why some define motion as a state that, by its very nature, cannot remain fixed.

I say: this account does remove many difficulties, but it still contains serious flaws.[^V03-250] First, motion is a relation. In itself it is neither beginningless nor newly begun; it takes on these features through what it is related to. As we have already said, motion means that something moves from potentiality to actuality little by little. Strictly speaking, the thing that changes is what moves from potentiality to actuality; motion is the renewal of what changes, the coming-to-be of what comes to be.[^V03-251][^V03-252]

Second, motion exists only as potentiality. It cannot precede something that has already come to be in actuality.[^V03-253] We are discussing a cause that brings a thing into existence. Such a cause must exist together with what it causes, while being prior to it in the order of nature. A thing that has come to be therefore needs a cause that also comes to be, exists with it in time, comes before it in the order of nature, and has a stronger way of existing than it. But motion is not actual in this way.

Third, the other thinker's argument treats circular motion as eternal in one respect, and says that in that respect it depends on an eternal cause. That is not right. Pure renewal has no lasting existence at all, let alone an eternal one. A universal essence, meanwhile, is not made by a cause; it does not make anything either. Its continuity is no proof.[^V03-254]

Fourth, we have proved that neither the sphere's substantial form, its natural position, nor the celestial bodies and stars remain the same individual through time. The cause and subject of motion is an individual body, which is not eternal. So it is wrong to say that motion has an eternal cause; it is also wrong to say that it needs no cause that comes to be.[^V03-255][^V03-256]

The true view is this: what is renewed in its own being and identity is the existence of bodily nature. It has a reality in God's knowledge and a connected, gradual identity in prime matter, which is pure potentiality and readiness. The nature's essence is not “coming-to-be,” but its way of existing is renewal and coming-to-be. This is like the difference between a substance's essence, which the mind can consider apart from a subject, and its actual existence in the world, where it depends on a subject. Existence can have features that an essence considered apart from existence does not have. As the existence of different things varies in strength and weakness while their essences do not, so some existences are gradual in their identity, not because of a separate feature added to them. Their very way of existing is gradual, though their essence is not.

The existence of bodily nature, which gives form to material bodies, is too limited to remain as one individual forever. It can exist only as a gradual succession.

I do not mean that the essence of a bodily nature requires change and passing away when considered apart from existence. We can think of a bodily nature without thinking of it as changing, just as we can think of it without thinking of it as lasting. How, then, could change be one of its essential or defining features? The mistake lies in confusing the essence of a thing with its existence. Existence itself cannot be pictured in the mind, as we have explained many times. It is made individual through itself, while everything in the mind is open to sharing and generalization. If existence could be represented in the mind, an individual would become general, what is outside the mind would become something mental, and existence would become an essence. All of this is impossible.

#### A Clarifying Note

Many things do not have an intellectual reality that matches the way they appear to the senses or imagination. This is true of time, motion, a circle, and power.[^V03-257] It is also true of quantities and mathematical objects, such as a body considered simply as an extended quantity. Its mode of existence consists in a particular spatial extension, whether it exists in matter and a specific natural body or in the imagination apart from any specific matter and nature. It has no existence in the intellect as an extended thing, because anything understood by the intellect is general; a general idea cannot itself be extended or measured, nor can it exist as something extended and measured. The intellectual idea of quantity is not itself a quantity, nor is it something with quantity, nor can it be treated as quantity in the ordinary way.

Many material things are like this: there is no intellectual counterpart that matches them exactly as they exist. In fact, if you ask me what is true, none of the particular forms of actual bodily things, simple or compound, has an exact match in the intellect. They are individual realities that cannot be shared, while what the intellect grasps is general and can be shared. The same is true of the gradual, changing forms of bodily nature. The specific forms that distinguish bodily kinds and ground their defining features are, in truth, renewed existences. Taken as fleeting instants, they have no essence of their own. The mind does draw general ideas from them and calls these ideas essences. In reality, those ideas follow from the existences, though they are essential to the meanings drawn from them.

We will prove in this book that the specific forms of substances do not fall under the general category of substance, or under any category of qualities. They are individual realities of existence that do not, in their own right, belong to substance, quantity, quality, or any other category or class. They are pure existences flowing from the aspects of the First Reality, effects of its intellectual rays and shadows of its light.

#### Discussion and Clarification

You can put the objection this way:[^V03-258] how can these renewed realities, called specific forms and bodily natures, come from an eternal source? If they come from it without a prepared recipient, then they must be separate forms, and so intellectual rather than material. Besides being impossible, this contradicts what we are trying to explain: renewal is incompatible with a separate, immaterial existence.[^V03-259]

If they come from an eternal source through a prepared recipient,[^V03-260] then if the recipient is itself new, it must depend on another recipient and a prior readiness, and so on without end.[^V03-261] If the recipient is eternal,[^V03-262] either it is sufficient by itself to receive the form or it is sufficient together with something that necessarily follows from it. In either case, the form would also be fixed, not renewed,[^V03-263] even though we assumed it was renewed.

If the recipient is not sufficient by itself, nor with anything that necessarily follows from it, to receive the form, and instead needs later, changing preparations, then you must accept that matter is eternal and that an endless succession of events follows.[^V03-264] But you are trying to prove that the world and everything in it began in time. You would also have to accept that there is one eternal matter for each specific form and kind, so that the number of eternal individuals would match the number of specific forms.[^V03-265] In any case, the argument returns to the coming-to-be of each particular readiness. Potentiality depends on actuality;[^V03-266] each specific readiness comes to be through an actual form that precedes it by nature, though not in time, because that form is its essential cause rather than a mere preparation.[^V03-267]

I reply that what I have said already resolves this problem and similar ones. If the receptive matter is prime matter, its unity is a unity of kind, not a single numerical identity. Prime matter means substance in potentiality; being a substance does not give it a specific form. Potentiality is a lack of actuality, and it becomes actual only through whatever form it receives. If the matter is some other kind of matter, the same account applies insofar as it is matter: its potentiality and incompleteness have one source.[^V03-268][^V03-269]

Any other matter becomes actual through the form paired with it, though it is more actual than prime matter because it has already been made actual once. Each form through which matter becomes actual is prior to that matter in its basic reality. But as an individual form in matter, it is one with that matter; the two are individual together and take on their limits together. I do not mean that the form is one with matter through some prior readiness: that readiness is set against the form and is not one with it. Rather, each readiness of a later individual of a nature may imply an earlier individual, prior to it in time, but the readiness itself is prior in the order of nature. You have already seen how renewed realities that are passing away work this way. In short, nothing here requires any matter to be eternal.[^V03-270]

I have also indicated that every bodily nature has a reality with God, present in His knowledge. In that intellectual reality, it needs no matter, readiness, motion, time, nonexistence, coming-to-be, or potentiality. But it has successive, worldly states of existence connected continuously. Their continuous unity depends on the unity of the nature present in God's knowledge. If you consider these states as many, each appears at a particular time. In that respect, it needs a receptive matter prepared for it earlier in time. As potentiality, that recipient is something lacking in actuality and does not need a specific cause; it needs only some form, whatever form that may be.[^V03-271] It may be the power belonging to a form that is clothed in potentiality, or the potentiality that belongs to a form, or the potentiality for some further perfection.[^V03-272] But the recipient's particular, immediate readiness does require a particular form: that form gives it the capacity for a certain kind of change and a certain form.[^V03-273]

When the recipient leaves one specific, immediate potentiality for the actuality opposed to it, that potentiality disappears. The earlier form gives way to the later form because the two cannot exist together. The form of an embryo, for example, disappears when the form of the animal comes to be; the embryo-form was potentiality and a possibility for the animal-form. Every new form arises with the passing away of the previous one, then passes away in turn as its successor comes to be. This happens continuously through renewal.

Why does each particular form belong to its particular time? Sometimes nothing beyond that form's own individual reality explains the timing. This is so when it has a continuous identity that does not break between what comes before and after; in that case, no further cause is needed to place it at that time. If the individuals of a nature are disconnected from each other, the question does arise. Then some further cause makes each reality belong to its particular time. That cause must exist at the time in question. This continues until the causes reach a particular reality whose own identity makes it belong to that time, without a further cause. The chain cannot continue without end among causes that each require another cause.[^V03-274]

Existence differs in its basic reality from one kind of thing to another. God, an angel, a devil, a human being, fire, and water each have a reality and a rank of their own. They do not share one kind of existence. This is one way existences differ. They can also differ through additional features, even when their underlying kind is the same: the existence of Zayd differs from that of ʿAmr, and individual horses differ in the same way. Shades of blackness or whiteness may also differ in strength while occupying the same level of their quality. So a human being differs from a horse, and black from white, through the basic reality of each; but individuals of the same kind differ through additional, individuating features.[^V03-275]

Sometimes, however, a reality that differs through itself, not because a separate maker has made it different, is made by one simple act into a single identity with many changing states. Those states differ through their own earlier and later order, with no separate before or after added to them. The connected time of the common account is like this: they say time has one identity whose parts differ in earlier and later position. Our account of bodily nature is similar, except that its identity is substantial while time, on their view, is an accident. In truth, the substantial form of nature is what has these features in itself, not time. For them, time is an accident whose existence depends on what it measures. Time is the measure of nature's renewal through its own earlier and later states, just as mathematical body measures nature's three dimensions. Nature therefore has two extensions and two measures: a gradual, temporal extension, divisible in thought into earlier and later times; and a fixed, spatial extension, divisible into earlier and later places. A measure relates to its extension as a definite limit to something indefinite; they are one in existence but distinct in how we consider them.[^V03-276][^V03-277][^V03-278]

Just as mathematical extension in matter cannot be separate from the spatial extension it measures, time cannot be separate from the gradual extension of what renews itself. Time's relation to natural form, which has temporal extension, is like mathematical quantity's relation to bodily form, which has spatial extension. Keep this point in mind: it is more useful than many scattered arguments. A little reflection on time shows that it exists only in the mind as an aspect of what it measures. It does not exist as a separate feature attached to its subject in the way that color or heat does. Time is an analytical feature of what it measures. It exists outside the mind only through the existence of what it measures, because the distinction between time and what it measures is made only in thought.[^V03-279][^V03-280]

Since time exists in the world only through the existence of what it measures, its renewal, passing away, coming-to-be, and continuity depend on that thing's own renewal, passing away, coming-to-be, and continuity. It is surprising that some philosophers still assign time an independently renewed identity. Perhaps they mean that motion is, by nature, the renewal and passing away of something, while time is the quantity of that motion. That is why the author of *Pointers* thought motion, considered as measurable, was the same as time, though motion as motion was different. In the world, motion and time do not differ; they differ only in the mind, when we consider motion without considering its measure.

#### Discussion continued

In *The Healing*, Avicenna says people have held several views about time. Some deny that it exists at all.[^V03-281] Some say it exists only as something imagined, with no real existence.[^V03-282] Others say it is not one thing in itself, but a relation between various events and other events, each of which serves as the time of another. On that view, time is the sum of such occasions.[^V03-283]

Some treat time as one independent substance separate from bodies.[^V03-284] Others say time is a bodily substance, the outermost sphere itself.[^V03-285] Others identify it with motion.[^V03-286] Some say that only the sphere's motion is time, and still others say that time is one full revolution of the sphere.[^V03-287]

These were the views known in earlier times, listed in the study of nature. Abu al-Barakat of Baghdad held that time is the measure of existence.[^V03-288] The Ashʿarite theologians adopted the third view. Some who held the fourth view imagined time to be a separate, self-subsisting existence, even necessary in itself. Some early philosophers also described it as a separate substance, distinct from matter, and ascribed this view to the divine Plato and his followers.

The starting point for both groups was that no change occurs in time's own reality or duration. If no motion or change took place in time, they thought, it would contain only permanence and eternity, though it could still be called earlier or later because of its relation to changing things. If related to beings that last and do not change, time in that respect is called eternity. If related to things that move and change, it is called the everlasting age. If related to changes that occur within it, it is called time.[^V03-289][^V03-290]

In *Eastern Investigations*, after listing the different views and objections, the author admits: “I have not yet reached the true nature of time. Let this book satisfy you by examining what can be said from every side. I will not twist the answers to favor one group over another, especially on this question.”

In his commentary on *ʿUyūn al-Ḥikma*, after setting out the views and objections, he says that defenders of Aristotle's account of time as the measure of motion cannot enter the most difficult questions about time without returning to Plato's view. He himself finds Plato's view most convincing: time exists by itself, independent of other things. He then describes the three relations just mentioned, which are called eternity, the everlasting age, and time.

He adds that Plato's view is closer to sound proof and farther from the darkness of doubt, though perfect knowledge comes only from God. He also argues that common sense says the God of the world existed before today's event, exists with it now, and will remain after it. If earlier, present, and later states implied change in the thing described by them, then the Necessary Being would change, which no reasonable person accepts. If someone answers that God could not be called prior, present, and later without change in the event, he replies that they already allow a thing to be described as prior, present, and later because something else changes. Why, then, could time not be that way too?[^V03-291][^V03-292]

Plato, he says, held that when no motion or change occurs, time contains only permanence and continuity, which is called the everlasting age or eternity. When motion and change occur in it, earlier and later arise—not because time itself changes, but because other things do. That is his account.

I say: you have learned by decisive proof that there is a reality whose very existence is renewed and passing away, with no separate act that first gives it existence and then gives it renewal. By God's grace, when we come to the proper place in this book, the difficulties that made time and motion seem so hard to understand will be resolved. The First Reality is too exalted to be earlier or later than daily events in a temporal sense, or to exist at the same time as them in the ordinary way. His presence with them is a sustaining presence, beyond time, motion, change, and coming-to-be. Perhaps those who deny that time exists at all mean only that it has no existence apart from the existence of what renews itself. Those who deny that time exists outside the mind may mean that it is an analytical feature, added to an essence in thought, not an independently existing feature added to its subject in reality.[^V03-293]

Those who call time a bodily substance and identify it with the outermost sphere may mean the sphere's renewed nature. In that case, they mean by “sphere” its nature itself. This agrees with our view that time measures nature according to its own renewal. We have also indicated that time, like mathematical extension, is not an independently existing feature. The existence of a measure is first the existence of what it measures, and it is an “accident” only by analysis.

Those who describe time as a separate substance may mean the separate intellectual reality of the natural form, whose material existence is measured and extended through renewal, while its existence in God's knowledge is fixed and eternal. And those who say that time is necessary in itself may mean something higher than people understand.

A prophetic saying tells us not to curse time, because time is God. People cursed time when misfortune came, imagining that time brought it about. The saying corrects them: God, not time, brings about events. It may also mean that time is God's effect and the record of His pen; whoever loves a thing loves its traces and its work. Or “time” may mean the realm of the universal intellects, which belongs to the divine order. In that sense, ordinary time is a subtle reflection of a higher reality.[^V03-294]

The sages also say: the relation of the fixed to the fixed is eternity; the relation of the fixed to the changing is the everlasting age; and the relation of the changing to the changing is time. By the first, they mean the relation of God to His names and knowledge. By the second, the relation of His fixed knowledge to its changing objects—the beings of the bodily world—as they exist together. By the third, the temporal relation of those objects to one another.[^V03-295]

#### Chapter 33 — Why Time Has No First or Last Moment

Some say that every event in time is preceded by a nonexistence that does not coexist with its existence.[^V03-296] What makes that nonexistence “before” the event cannot be nonexistence itself, since nonexistence may also come after something. Nor can it be the event's cause: the cause also exists alongside its effect. And nothing that can exist together with the later event is, by its own nature, earlier than it in this particular way.

So for nonexistence to be earlier, that nonexistence must be tied to a time, and the event's existence must begin in a later time. Then, before any moment chosen as the beginning of time, there must be another time, and the same argument applies to an ending. Time as a whole can have no beginning or end. As the Teacher of the Philosophers says, those who say time began have, without realizing it, also said that it has always existed. We have learned that time follows motion, and motion follows nature. Nature exists only in matter and body. God's generosity and giving never cease; His goodness has no end or limit. As scripture says, “If you tried to count God's blessings, you could not number them.” Even so, every particular time and motion, and every body, comes to be in time and is bounded by nonexistence on both sides, as we have explained.[^V03-297] This is a strange conclusion.[^V03-298]

Someone may object that this “before” is only imagined, like the supposed emptiness beyond the world's limits. Just as the world ending in space does not require its nonexistence to occupy another place, time ending need not require its nonexistence to occupy another time. I reply that the mind plainly recognizes an order between a thing's existence and its nonexistence, since they cannot coexist.[^V03-299] That order is not causal, since cause and effect must exist together. It is not natural priority either, since what is prior by nature may exist together with what is later by nature. It is plainly not priority of rank or place. It must therefore be priority in time. In short, this kind of order is what we mean by time. If there is no such order, then you have admitted that time did not come into existence after nonexistence. If there is such an order, then the nonexistence of time must itself be in time.

The comparison with imagined places beyond the world fails. Space can be finite without needing another space beyond it. But for something to begin to exist, it must be preceded by nonexistence.

If someone says this makes God subject to time[^V03-300], and requires another time for time, with an endless regress of times, I reply: the claim that God precedes a particular time also concerns time. Although God is beyond change and beyond time and the things that coexist in time, He is with every thing without physical contact or being mixed with it. He is with the earlier time in a way that does not change Him. We may therefore truly say He exists before a particular time, just as He exists with it and after it.[^V03-301]

The claim that every time is preceded by another time, because the nonexistence of each time occurs in a time, means that before every time there is another time, before every motion another motion, and before every body another body, without beginning. This regress is not impossible. These things have a weak mode of existence in which existence and nonexistence are intertwined: the existence of one particular time entails the nonexistence of another, and the nonexistence of one entails the existence of another. Time's nonexistence occurs only in time.

Someone may object that God's being present with a time requires another time in which God and that time are together. Likewise, if time's nonexistence is present with the preceding or following time, that seems to require another time. I reply: when two things are together in time and neither one is time itself, they need a time that contains them both. But the relation between time and something that exists in time does not require another time, because the time itself is what makes them present together. Each time is distinct through itself. It is one kind of existence that cannot be anything other than this particular time, before or after itself. The same applies to every other time and every part of time. Their existence in the form they have is made necessary by a simple act of creation. Therefore, the presence of a thing with a time does not require yet another time.

When two things that are not themselves times exist together, their being together requires a third thing that makes them simultaneous. The same is true of priority and posteriority. Time has priority and posteriority by its own nature, since these belong to what time is. Each time is earlier than some times, later than others, and present with whatever coincides with it.

This does not mean that time belongs to the category of relation. That confuses the concept of a thing with its existence. The concept of time belongs to quantity: time is a continuous amount that does not remain fixed. What is understood from it may imply another concept, but its actual existence depends on another thing or its nonexistence. Priority and posteriority belong to time's essence because its existence is itself the existence of priority and posteriority.[^V03-302] It is the concepts of priority and posteriority, not their existence as what makes things earlier or later, that belong to the category of relation.

There is another difficulty: the parts of time must differ in essence, even though parts of a continuum must resemble one another. Each part of time has its own place in the order of earlier and later. Thursday cannot be Wednesday, nor can it be a different Thursday that comes before or after it. This seems to bring back the same impossibilities.

The answer is that a continuous whole's parts resemble one another in what makes it continuous. Their differences are required by this very continuity. Each part of one stretch of space has a different position from the others, and the unity and continuity of space require this. The same is true of the hours of time: each has a different state, and the unity and continuity of time require it.[^V03-303]

#### Chapter 34 — Arguments for a Beginning of Time and Replies

Those who say time began offer several arguments. First, past events can increase or decrease in number. Whatever can increase or decrease must have a beginning, so past events must have had one. Second, if past events were infinite in number, the event happening today would depend on an infinite number of earlier events having passed away. It could not then happen. But it plainly does happen, so the past cannot be infinite. Third, if every individual event has a beginning, the whole collection must have a beginning too. Fourth, past events have reached us. If they were infinite, then an infinite series would have come to an end, which is a contradiction. Fifth, either an event occurred in eternity or none did. The first is impossible, since then the event would not be a new event. If no event occurred in eternity, there was a time when no event existed, so all events began after nonexistence.

Sixth, past events have entered into existence. Whatever has entered into existence has thereby been bounded and counted, so past events must be finite.[^V03-304] Seventh, suppose a body had existed eternally and that it contained events with no first event. That body would precede neither their existence nor their nonexistence, which is impossible.[^V03-305]

Eighth, the world is never without events, and whatever is never without events must itself have begun. So the world began.

These arguments are weak when used to show that time and motion themselves began. The first argument is taken from the proof that spatial dimensions are finite.[^V03-306] It can be stated this way: count the revolutions, years, or past souls, then add one more revolution, year, or soul from the future. The two totals differ by a finite amount. Compare them by matching their parts, and one must exceed the other by a finite amount. What exceeds something by a finite amount must itself be finite.

But this reasoning applies to things that can exist together. Past motions, times, and events cannot all exist together. Any proof that depends on their being gathered into one whole cannot establish a limit for them. The past can be infinite precisely because its events are not all present at once. Their continuity depends on each later event coming after an earlier one, and the later existence of one is tied to the earlier nonexistence of another. So how could one make the impossible assumption that they exist all together, then use that assumption to rule out infinity? It uses a contradiction as the basis for its proof.[^V03-307]

The second argument also fails. What cannot depend on an infinite series is something whose existence waits on all the infinitely many things before it, none of which has yet come to be. Such a thing cannot happen. But this is not the situation with the past. There was never a time when an infinite series of past events was still waiting to occur, followed by the present event. If the claim is simply that no event occurs except after an infinite past, that is the very question under debate, not proof against it.

The third argument wrongly transfers what is true of each individual to the whole.[^V03-308] The objectors could make a stronger case by saying that the collection of past rational souls must itself have begun, since each soul in it began. Then, they argue, the collection too must have begun, since it is the result of those individual beginnings. This is a stronger argument than simply giving the whole the same property as each of its members: it tries to infer that an effect begins because its causes began. But it still does not prove their conclusion. The total collection of souls does not cause time and all the events within it. At every moment another collection exists, as more souls leave their bodies. The world as a whole is also renewed at every moment. Neither claim shows that the number of past events is finite.[^V03-309][^V03-310]

The fourth argument proves only that the past has an end on the side that reaches us. An end on one side does not rule out that it has no beginning on the other. The motions of the people of Paradise, for example, have no end, yet they had a beginning.

The fifth argument assumes that eternity is a particular time with a definite state. It is not. Eternity means the absence of a first moment. A temporal event that is preceded by nonexistence cannot occur in eternity,[^V03-311] but this objection can be turned around: was the possibility of events present in eternity or not? If it was present, then an event could have occurred eternally, which is impossible. If it was not present, that possibility must itself have begun, which is also impossible. This argument does not disprove the possibility of events; otherwise it would also disprove God's power to bring events about. The same reply applies here.[^V03-312]

The sixth argument assumes that to be bounded is to have two ends. We agree that past events have an end on the side that reaches us. But an end on one side does not rule out that events can continue without beginning on the other. And we can turn the argument around and ask whether events can begin at all.[^V03-313]

The seventh argument assumes either that one body is described at once by all past events and by their absence, or that at every time it is described by one event and by the absence of another. The first is false: the whole collection of past events does not exist at once, so the body is not described by all of them together. The second is not contradictory. At any given time, the body is described by one event and by the absence of different events; it is not both present and absent in the same respect.[^V03-314]

The eighth argument is close to the earlier arguments and, as usually stated, has flaws in its premises. If “the world” means all bodies, then it is never without motion and other changing features. If it means the world considered as one collection, then, as we have already explained, there is a new collection at each moment; that does not show there are only finitely many events. If “the world” means everything other than God, the premise is false, because some possible beings do not change at all.[^V03-315][^V03-316]

The second premise also has a problem. If “never without events” means that the world is never without any particular event, it is plainly false: the world precedes every particular event. If it means that the world is never without the entire collection of events, there is no such collection of all events for anything to precede. The claim that anything which does not precede all events must itself have begun simply assumes what it is trying to prove. On the opponent's own view, the heavenly bodies are never without motion and never precede it in time. To make their case, the objectors must return to the claim that past events are finite, which we have already answered.[^V03-317][^V03-318]

These are the arguments and replies that have passed between the two sides. With God's help, we have explained how the world began and how every particular body, nature, soul, and accident is preceded by temporal nonexistence. We have also shown that these claims can stand together: the world's substances are never without change, and whatever is never without change has itself begun in time. We have already established some of what is needed for this conclusion; the rest will be discussed in its proper place, God willing.[^V03-319]

Most people find it difficult to state their own view clearly or identify where the disagreement lies. If they say “the world began,” ask what they mean. If they mean that it depends on a Maker, their opponents agree completely. The philosophers say the world depends on a maker both when it begins and as it continues, in its essence and in its features. If they mean that a period of time came before the world, they cannot accept that: they consider everything other than God to be the world, and time is part of the world. How, then, could time come before the world?

If they say “the world is not eternal,” the philosophers agree that it is not eternal in the sense of being necessary in itself. If they mean that it is not lasting, ask what “lasting” means. In everyday speech it can mean that something exists for a long time. In that sense, there is no dispute that the world lasts. If they mean there was a time when the world did not exist, that conflicts with their view, since there was no time before the world—just as there cannot be a time before time. If they say the world is not beginningless, ask what “beginningless” means; the same difficulty returns.

If they say that the number of past motions in the mind is finite, the philosophers agree: any number of motions held in the mind is finite. But that does not mean the world depends for its existence on anything other than God.[^V03-320][^V03-321] Even if we imagine the past events together as one collection, that imagined collection has begun too.[^V03-322] If they say the world was nonexistent and then came to be, then if “was” means “before it in time,” their claim contradicts itself and assumes that time existed before the world. If “was” means priority in the order of nature, the philosophers agree: they say the possible thing is nothing in itself and becomes something through its cause.[^V03-323][^V03-324]

If someone says God preceded the world by a period of time, that is not the religious position. Before the world, they say, there was nothing but God's own being. The philosophers say the same. The real priority is the priority of a cause, the truest kind of priority.[^V03-325][^V03-326] The disagreement is therefore not about time. It is whether the world depends on something other than God, as a partner in its existence, or whether God's own being and attributes are enough to bring it into existence. Once that is clear, we can distinguish belief in one God from treating another as His partner.[^V03-327]

Proving that the world depends on no creatorless force, but on a Maker who brings things into existence without being changed by them or made a subject for them, is one of the most important questions in philosophy. Whoever fails to understand God's oneness in action will not understand His oneness in being, His necessary existence, His power, knowledge, will, wisdom, or any of His other attributes.[^V03-328][^V03-329] Once a person understands this question, and understands the soul, its survival, and its return after death, after learning its origin, maker, and oneness, that person has gained a great deal of knowledge. The remaining questions matter less.

When this question is settled, and we understand the causes of new events and the passing away of things, and how bodies and their natures are renewed from moment to moment—as scripture and reason both indicate, without undermining sound philosophy—we have laid the clearest and firmest path toward intellectual unveiling and direct insight. People are puzzled by how the Necessary Being, who never changes, can bring about new events without taking on a new feature. Until a person is certain about this question and related ones, inquiry cannot rest on a firm foundation. If God could act in an arbitrary way, without reasons, there would be no meaningful account to give and no rational order to discover.

One of the mystics says: “To say that the world is eternal in time is empty talk. Ask what is meant by the world. If it means all bodies, such as the heavens and the elements, or everything besides God, then the statement is still wrong. In the second sense, many things included in the world do not depend on time for their existence. In the first sense, it would mean that bodies have existed for as long as time has existed, implying that time existed before bodies. But bodies exist before time, at least in the order of nature. If the speaker means neither of these, we cannot know what he means. We have answered what we understood; arguing about what we do not understand is for the blind.”[^V03-330][^V03-331]

He continues: “If someone means that bodies have existed for as long as God has existed, that is a grave error. Bodies do not exist where God exists—not now, before, or after. Anyone who says the world exists now alongside God is also gravely mistaken. Where God is, in the oneness of His being, there is no time or place. Yet no time, place, or particle of the world is without Him. He is with every particle, but nothing possible is with Him. His existence precedes the world's, just as it precedes the written form of the words on this page, with no difference between the two. Whoever thinks there is a difference is still caught in doubt and has not freed God from time, any more than ordinary people free Him from place when they imagine Him as a body. Such a person is far from the true faith that a mystic grasps at the beginning of the spiritual path: God is prior to the future just as He is prior to the past. This is certain to the mystic, though many scholars cannot understand it.”[^V03-332]

I say: this mystic's account does not settle the question of whether the world began. Those who say that the heavenly bodies and the basic elements have always existed agree that God relates to the future as He does to the past. They are not unable to understand that bodies do not exist where the First Reality exists, whether now, before, or after. Every effect is like this in relation to its source. Even so, they say that the heavens and other things last forever.[^V03-333]

They can explain the world's eternity by saying that bodies are not preceded by a stretch of time in which they do not exist. So the mystic's account does not answer their position. We must follow what we have established here, which, in this period of Islamic philosophy, we have been the first to prove fully. If earlier Muslim philosophers or scholars had reached this conclusion, it would have been well known, since they had every reason to investigate it.

The closest argument presented here is one attributed to an early Christian thinker: “The world has limited power, and whatever has limited power has a limited duration. So the world cannot have existed forever.” The author of *The Book of Discussions* objects that the world may be limited in its own power to last, while lasting without limit because its cause is eternal and continuously supplies unlimited effects and motions. I say that his reply is ambiguous and misleading. “It does not last forever by itself or by its own power” may mean that its possible essence does not, by itself, give it lasting existence, but that it lasts through existence from the Necessary Being. Perhaps that is not what the argument meant. The argument may instead be that the actual existence of these bodily substances has limited power, not merely that their essences do not give them endless power. Their essences do not exist at all apart from existence, so it makes no sense to say that their essences have unlimited power.[^V03-334]

The reply may also mean that their actual existence, which comes directly from the Maker, has only limited power, but keeps receiving new power and effects from its eternal cause. That can be understood in two ways. First, perhaps each particular bodily existence has only limited power and does not last forever, but it produces unlimited effects through the continuous help of the higher source. This is false: the existence of a body's features and effects depends on the body itself, and the substantial body is stronger in existence than anything that follows from it. Existence reaches those features only through the body on which they depend. If the effects and results are unlimited, the intermediate cause must also be unlimited, whether it is an immediate agent, a receptive power, a tool, or a subject.[^V03-335][^V03-336]

This is not disproved by prime matter, which can receive an unlimited number of effects. It can receive them only through an unlimited succession of preparations and powers. Its lasting unity is an indefinite unity that is renewed each moment as new forms and powers arise.

The second interpretation is that, although the world's existence at each moment has only limited power, the first source gives its matter a new power and a new identity at every moment, different from the one it gave before. But this is exactly the view that the world comes to be and passes away: each individual in it is preceded by temporal nonexistence. That is the very position of the three revealed religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. One could object to the argument by saying that something in the world, such as separate intellects, has unlimited power. That would work only if those separate forms were part of the world in the sense relevant here. You will learn from our account that separate forms, precisely insofar as they are separate, are not part of what is other than God. So the claim that the world and everything in it has limited power and does not last forever as an individual remains sound. It lasts only as a general meaning, not as one individual reality.

#### Chapter 35 — What the “Now” Is, and How It Exists and Passes Away

Know that “now” has two meanings. One depends on time; the other is what gives rise to time by flowing.[^V03-337] In the first sense, the now is a boundary of continuous time. We must ask how it exists and how it ceases to exist. You know that time is a continuous quantity, and anything continuous can be divided without end in principle, though not in fact. Such division happens in one of three ways: by an actual cut, by a change in the aspect under consideration, or by the mind's imagination. An actual cut cannot be made in time, as you have seen.[^V03-338] So time can be divided in either of the two remaining ways: motion may bring something to a point all at once, creating a shared boundary such as sunrise or sunset, or the mind may divide it through its power of imagination.

To explain how the now ceases to exist, first recall a principle Avicenna teaches in *The Healing* and elsewhere: one thing's existence or nonexistence in time can be instantaneous or gradual.[^V03-339] It is instantaneous when the thing comes to exist or ceases to exist all at once, in a single instant. If it continues to exist, that instant is the first instant of its existence.[^V03-340] If it does not continue, as with things that exist only for an instant,[^V03-341] that instant alone is where it occurs. Or a thing may exist gradually: it has one continuous existence that can unfold only across one continuous stretch of time that matches it. We call this gradual existence. It does not mean that many separate things occur in the parts of that time. In its own nature, the thing is one, though it can be divided in principle. Before we divide it, it is one thing extending across one stretch of time. It has no first endpoint at which it exists, since it cannot come to exist at just one end or boundary. It must exist together with the whole stretch of time. Once we divide it, its parts are found one after another in the corresponding parts of time. This kind of gradual existence has no first instant. It exists through time, not at its boundary. A third possibility is that something exists in time without being spread across it. It does not have a continuous existence that matches time part for part, but it exists during that time because there is no instant in it at which the thing is absent.[^V03-342][^V03-343] It has no first instant of existence, either at the beginning of that time or within it. This way of setting out the issue clears up many doubts.

One objection comes from the author of *The Summary*. He says that a thing's full existence or nonexistence must either come about little by little, across a stretch of time that matches it and can be divided along with it, or all at once, in a single instant that must be the first instant of its existence or nonexistence. He asks how there could be a third option: a thing that begins to exist but has no first instant. The answer is that these two options are not direct opposites.[^V03-344] The opposite of “coming about little by little” is simply “not coming about little by little.” That includes both things that begin at a particular instant and things that do not.[^V03-345]

Likewise, the opposite of “beginning at a particular instant” is simply “not beginning at a particular instant.” That, too, includes both things that come about gradually and things that do not. So a third kind is possible: a thing exists throughout a stretch of time and at every part of it, but not by extending across it; and it does not exist at the start of that stretch. The argument and closer examination show that this middle case occurs when things begin to exist. The same applies when things cease to exist, in all three ways, as we will explain. To settle the categories, follow Avicenna's argument in *The Healing*: ask whether the shared instant between two stretches of time can contain one state in the first stretch and a different state in the second. A thing that can be in either of two opposite states cannot be in neither at that instant. Some things occur in an instant and have the same state at every instant in which they exist; they do not need to match a stretch of time. Examples include contact, squareness, and other stable shapes. Such a thing is present at the shared instant.[^V03-346][^V03-347]

Other things exist only in the second stretch of time; the instant between the two cannot contain them. Motion is one example: its state does not stay the same from instant to instant. At each instant, it brings a new degree of closeness to the goal and distance from the starting point. It begins only after the shared instant, throughout the following stretch of time and all its instants. The same is true of things that come about only through motion, such as the absence of contact that follows contact. These things have no first instant of existence. Otherwise, either the new instant would directly follow the shared instant, so that two instants touched, or a stretch of time would lie between them. In the second case, the thing would be neither moving nor at rest, or neither in contact nor out of contact, during that stretch. In short, motion through the middle of a path certainly exists.[^V03-348]

The motion of passage cannot exist at the instant that marks the end of one stretch of time, because that is the last instant of rest. That instant also lies at the end or beginning of the path, so the moving thing cannot be halfway between the path's start and end there.[^V03-349] After that instant, however, motion exists at every instant and in every part of the time it occupies. No second instant can follow the first directly, since that would make the instants touch. So motion exists throughout a stretch of time and at every instant in it, but has no first instant of existence. The same holds for anything whose existence depends on motion but does not require a fixed amount of motion.[^V03-350] It also holds for things that exist only in an instant, such as a particular kind of contact between two cones: the contact occurs at an instant, but its absence has no first instant.[^V03-351]

Once you understand these points, we can ask how the now itself ceases to exist. The now, or anything else that exists only in an instant, cannot cease gradually, because that would divide it and make it last through time. If it ceases all at once, either its instant of nonexistence is the same as its instant of existence, which would make two instants touch, or it comes later. If it comes later, there must either be a stretch of time between the two instants, during which the now continues to exist, or no stretch between them, which again makes two instants touch. Both are impossible. So the now ceases to exist throughout all the time that follows it. This is a third kind of change, and it is a real one.[^V03-352][^V03-353]

You might say: even if the now is absent throughout all the time that follows, we are asking when its absence begins. Surely that beginning does not occupy the whole following stretch of time. So it must happen either gradually or all at once, and the same problem returns. We reply that “beginning” has two meanings.[^V03-354] It can mean the boundary of the time in which something occurs; or it can mean the first instant in which the thing occurs. In the first sense, the absence of the now begins with the now's own existence. In the second sense, its absence has no beginning. As we have seen, not every changing thing must have a first instant in which its change is already under way. Motion has no first instant of motion, and rest has no first instant of rest.[^V03-355]

The first kind—things that occur all at once—includes all things that happen in an instant, such as reaching a point on a path, arriving at the goal of motion, becoming square or hexagonal, taking on other shapes, making contact, and one circle or line meeting another. Each has a first instant and continues to exist for a time.[^V03-356] The second kind—things that exist gradually—includes motion across a path, the amounts of time, and all the states that depend on motion and do not remain fixed, such as sounds.[^V03-357][^V03-358] The third kind includes motion through the middle of a path; things produced by motion, such as an angle formed as one line moves alongside another; a gap that opens between two surfaces or lines; separation after contact; the absence of arrival or contact; and, in general, anything that can come about only through motion without its existence being divided into parts. It also includes the nonexistence of things that occur in an instant, when they cease after the last instant of their existence, and many other cases. These are all cases in which the now that depends on time exists as time's boundary, formed in one of the two ways we have described.[^V03-359][^V03-360]

The other meaning of now is the flowing now that produces continuous time as it flows. To understand it, notice that distance, motion, and time match one another in every respect that concerns their existence. Just as we can imagine a point that, by moving, traces out a distance, so there is something in motion—the moving thing's being between the start and end of its path—that, by flowing, produces motion across the whole path.[^V03-361] If so, time must also have something flowing that produces time as it flows. This is called the flowing now. It matches motion through the middle of the path. The point that draws a line is not the same as the points that mark its ends; likewise, motion through the middle is not the same as instant arrivals or other events that happen all at once.[^V03-362] The source of time is also different from an instant we imagine within it. The flowing now is time's source because it produces time through its motion and flow. Take this to heart.[^V03-363]

#### Chapter 36 — How Motion and Its Effects Can Cease to Exist

There is a problem about how motion across a path, and the time that matches it, cease to exist. Some say that motion and its corresponding time are absent at all times other than the stretch in which they exist. In other words, motion exists only during one stretch of time and is absent at all other times. But this does not answer our question. We are asking how motion passes away—how it begins to be absent after it has existed.[^V03-364]

There is a second problem. Existence and nonexistence are opposites: a thing cannot be neither or both at once. If something exists gradually, little by little, then as each part of it comes to be, the absence of that part ends. The existence of this part does not end the absence of some later part; that absence remains until the later part exists. A gradual thing's existence and nonexistence therefore both unfold little by little.[^V03-365] So if a thing exists gradually, its absence should also be gradual. This seems to create a problem. We need to look more closely.

First, understand that motion and time have a weak kind of existence, mixed with nonexistence. The same is true of something that changes gradually over time, such as a color that deepens or an amount that grows. Its existence over time is weak and mixed with nonexistence. Just as it exists gradually, so it is absent gradually. Its time of existence is also its time of nonexistence.[^V03-366]

Motion, however, can be considered in two ways. First, we can consider it as the gradual change of something else from what it could be into what it is. Here we are looking at that thing's category and its gradual existence. Second, we can consider motion in itself and ask what kind of existence motion has. These are different questions. In the second sense, motion does not exist gradually, and so its absence does not have to be gradual either. In this respect, motion exists all at once: its nature is the gradual change of something else, but it is not itself a gradual change. Motion within motion would be impossible, as we have explained.[^V03-367][^V03-368] Time is similar. It measures something's gradual existence, but it is not a measure of its own nature.

So motion and time, and things like them, each have two kinds of existence and two kinds of nonexistence. One kind is the existence or nonexistence of a thing that unfolds gradually. The other is the existence or nonexistence of the gradual process itself, or of a thing considered together with its gradual nature. The first is gradual; the second is all at once. In this sense, motion exists in the mind. This also explains why someone may say that becoming something and ceasing to be it happen all at once, while someone else may say that they happen gradually. Neither is wrong: each is speaking about a different aspect.

Avicenna says in a passage of this kind that there is no first instant in which something is moving, at rest, coming to be, or passing away, because time can always be divided further. The author of *The Summary* objects: there is no first instant in which something is moving or at rest, but there is a first instant in which something comes to be or passes away, since its form appears or disappears all at once. Avicenna's wording, he says, is therefore not right.[^V03-369]

I reply that coming to be is indeed instantaneous, as the author of *The Summary* reports from Avicenna. But there is no proof that Avicenna says the same of passing away. And anyone who says that forms come to be all at once must also say that they pass away in a way that has no first instant. Our view, however, is that both coming to be and passing away happen gradually. Otherwise matter would be left without a form.[^V03-370] When water becomes air, the airy form cannot appear while the water form is still present; nor can it appear in the last instant of the water form. It must appear in a different instant. Then either two instants touch, which is impossible, or matter is left without either form. Avicenna may have pointed toward the truth here: his words suggest that both forms come to be in a stretch of time that can be divided endlessly.

#### Chapter 37 — How the Instant Measures Time

For geometers, a measure is a part of a length or number that can be taken away again and again until nothing remains. The instant does not measure time in this sense. But “measure” can also mean something that makes a thing ready to be counted in the first sense.[^V03-371] The instant measures time in this second sense: it gives time unity, and repetition gives it plurality. As you know, time is continuous. We can count it only after dividing it, and division requires boundaries. Once boundaries are set, continuous time is split into parts, which can then be counted by one of their own parts. A line, for example, is divided by points. A point makes it possible to count the line's parts, while those parts themselves measure the line in the first sense. So the instant and the parts of time measure time in different ways.

One writer says that the instant both separates and joins time. It separates the past from the future, but it also joins them because it is their shared boundary.[^V03-372] The instant is one thing in itself, but it can be considered in two ways: as the end of the past and as the beginning of the future. As a joining point, it is one in itself and in the way we consider it, because it is the shared point between the two.

#### Chapter 38 — How Motion Divides Time, and Time Measures Motion

We have already seen that the continuity of a path, as a path along which motion occurs, causes time to exist. Motion through each part of the path causes the corresponding part of time to exist. So motion is a measure of time in the sense that it makes time's earlier and later parts exist.[^V03-373][^V03-374] Time, in turn, measures motion by counting it, since time determines the amount of motion. Think of people and numbers: ten people make the number ten exist, while the number ten makes it possible to count them as ten. Ten is ten in itself; people are counted as ten by means of it.[^V03-375]

The same is true of time and things that exist in time, such as motion. Time's existence is its amount, and motion causes it to exist—not because motion causes time to be an amount, since being an amount is part of what time is. Time measures motion in two ways. It makes motion have a certain size,[^V03-376] and it tells us how much motion there is. Motion measures time by showing how much earlier and later there is in it.[^V03-377] There are also two ways to show an amount: a measuring cup can show how much liquid it contains, and the liquid can show how large the cup is. A path can show the amount of motion, as when we say “a journey of two miles”; motion can show the length of a path, as when we say “the distance of a throw.”[^V03-378] But only one of these gives a measure in itself:[^V03-379] it is continuous by its nature, so we call it long or short; and because it can be counted through what comes before and after, we call it great or small in number.

#### Eastern Insight

Distance, motion, and time exist as one thing. They do not exist as three separate things that happen to be connected; the mind separates them and assigns each a different role. Distance is an individual instance of length, size, or another category. Motion is its renewal, its gradual passage from what it could be into what it is. That renewal is an idea the mind draws from the thing. The continuity of motion is the continuity of the path itself, and time gives that continuity a measure and a definite amount. After separating these aspects in thought, we may say that one causes another. The path's continuity gives motion its continuity—but this does not mean that one continuity causes a second, separate continuity. Motion's continuity is the path's continuity considered as motion.[^V03-380]

Someone might imagine motion that is not continuous, as those who believe in indivisible parts do.[^V03-381] But time's continuity is not caused in the same way. Time is, by its nature, a continuous quantity. Its existence still needs a cause, and that cause is not the continuity of the path by itself; it is the path's continuity as carried through motion.

#### Chapter 39 — What Exists in Time

Avicenna says in *The Healing* and elsewhere that something exists in time only if it has an earlier and a later state. These belong directly to motion, and to a moving thing indirectly. He also says that kinds and parts of a thing are in it; the instant is in time as unity is in number; earlier and later are in time as even and odd are in number; hours and days are in time as two and three are in number; motion is in time as the ten categories are in the number ten; and a moving thing is in time as the subject of those categories is in the number ten. Rest is the absence of motion. It is not measured by time in itself, but because it is bounded by two motions, it gains a kind of earlier and later, so we imagine it as existing in time.[^V03-382][^V03-383][^V03-384]

I say that every substance has some kind of change, or is affected by change. We have already shown that nature itself is renewed. So anything at rest in one respect is moving in another, and in that respect it exists in time in itself.[^V03-385] In our account, time follows the ongoing renewal of nature as a whole. It then follows the circular motion, which is the oldest of the motions, especially the motion of the outermost sphere. That motion measures other motions from place to place and changes of position; through those, it measures changes in quality and quantity.[^V03-386] Changes in other categories—such as relation and possession, and even nonexistence and possibility—follow the change of substance and so are motions only indirectly. Their earlier and later order in time is indirect as well.[^V03-387] Things that are neither motions nor involved in motion do not exist in time. Their coexistence with changing things is called timeless duration. Likewise, when changing things coexist with one another not as changing but as stable, that coexistence is timeless duration.[^V03-388]

### Stage Eight — Further Properties and Rules of Motion

#### Chapter 1 — Where Motion Begins and Ends, and When Its Endpoints Oppose Each Other

The starting point and destination may also be opposites, or nearly so.[^V03-389][^V03-390] In quality, motion from black to white joins true opposites. Motion from yellow to indigo joins things that are like opposites: one is closer to white, the other to black. In quantity, motion from an object's larger natural size to its smaller size joins the two extremes. Growth and shrinking that do not reach either extreme lie between opposites.[^V03-391][^V03-392] Places, by themselves, are alike, but they can be opposed by direction. Natural motion from the highest place to the lowest is from one opposite to another, since these are the only two natural directions. If natural motion takes place between them, its endpoints are like opposites.[^V03-393]

For motion that is not natural, its endpoints are opposed in two ways. First, places are like parts of a size: two of them cannot occupy the same point. Second, the starting point and the destination are opposed as beginning and end. In this way, the endpoints become opposites indirectly. In circular motion, however, the beginning and end are not a single point, as some suppose.[^V03-394] Motion is continuous, and each part of it has a beginning and an end that cannot occur together. In a body's change of position, any position can be treated as a beginning or an end, since the body cannot occupy the two positions at the same time.[^V03-395] So what serves as a beginning or an end may exist only as a possibility, or it may exist in fact.

The beginning and end, and their relation to motion, are alike in this respect. Each is related to the motion as a relative term is related to its counterpart: a beginning is the beginning of what begins, and an end is the end of what ends. But they are not necessarily related to each other: understanding a beginning does not always mean understanding its end. A motion could have no beginning or no end, as with the motions of the people of Paradise. Since both beginning and end are positive realities, their opposition is not a matter of presence versus absence, or of a thing and its lack. The only kind of opposition left is contrariety. You may ask: how can opposites exist in one body, when opposites cannot be together?

We reply that opposites can exist together in a subject that is not their immediate subject. The immediate subjects of beginning and end are not the body itself, but its positions and states.

#### Chapter 2 — Why Motion Does Not Occur in the Other Five Categories

We have already given a brief account of this. Here is a fuller explanation. Relation has no independent nature; it depends on something else. If that underlying thing moves, rests, grows, shrinks, strengthens, or weakens, the relation follows its change. It changes through that thing, not by itself.[^V03-396]

As for “when”—the time at which something exists—Avicenna says in *The Deliverance* that time exists for a body through motion. So how could time itself have motion? Every motion occurs in time. If time itself moved, there would have to be another time in which it moved.[^V03-397][^V03-398] In *The Healing*, Avicenna says that moving from one year to another, or one month to another, seems to happen all at once. I have already explained how a gradual process can be considered as a whole and so exist all at once.[^V03-399] Many later thinkers found Avicenna's words troubling and objected to them. I addressed their objections in my commentary on *The Guidance*. Avicenna also says that “when” may be like relation: there is no motion in it; instead, motion occurs first in quality or quantity, and time changes or remains steady as a result.[^V03-400]

But time depends on a changing category in a different way from relation. Time is not a separate, momentary feature of that category. Motion is the category's own renewal, not something that merely follows it.

The same is true of “when” and “having.” Some say motion occurs in the categories of acting and being acted upon. That is wrong unless they mean that one and the same motion can be viewed from the side of the mover or from the side of what is moved.[^V03-401] If they mean a separate motion in those categories, their claim does not hold. When something changes from cooling to heating,[^V03-402] either the cooling continues, which would mean that one thing is moving toward opposites at once, or it ends before the heating begins. In the second case, there must be a pause between them. So there is no single, continuous motion from cooling to heating.

I can state the point more briefly. Motion in a category means that the category comes about little by little, so that it has a different instance at each instant of the motion. Anything that cannot exist in an instant cannot have motion in it. Otherwise the instant would have to last through time.[^V03-403][^V03-404]

Someone may object that a thing can gradually lose its ability to act—not because the thing it acts on becomes less able to receive the effect, but because the agent's own condition changes.

We reply that if the action is natural, the agent's power may weaken little by little; if it acts by choice, its resolve may fade; and if it acts through a tool, the tool may wear out. In every case, the power, resolve, or tool changes first. The agent's ability to act changes as a result, not in itself. So this objection does not apply.[^V03-405]

#### Chapter 3 — What Rest Is, What Kind of Rest Opposes Motion, and How a Body Can Have Neither

When a body is not moving, there are two possible meanings. It may continue to exist in one place, size, quality, or other state. Or it may lack a motion that it is able to undergo. People have agreed to call only the second meaning “rest,” the absence of motion. They give two arguments for this choice.

First, rest is agreed to be the opposite of motion. Opposites must have definitions that are themselves opposed. Motion has been defined as the first completion of something that is able to change, in so far as it is able to change. So the definition of rest must oppose some part of this definition. If rest were a positive state, it would still have to be a kind of completion, since every positive existence is a completion. It would then have to be either a second completion of what is able to change, or a first completion of what is already actual. The first option would mean that every rest must be preceded by motion; the second, that every rest must be followed by motion. Both claims are false. So rest must oppose completion and be something absent: the lack of motion.

If we instead define rest first as a positive state—being in a place—we would have to add that the thing remains there. We could say it stays in the same place for a stretch of time, or for more than an instant, or that it is in the same place before and after. But we know what a stretch of time is only through motion, and we have assumed that motion can be understood only through rest. That would be circular, which is impossible. So motion must be defined first, and rest defined in a way that opposes it. This works only if rest is the absence of motion.[^V03-406][^V03-407]

The second argument is that each kind of motion has something absent that opposes it. Growth is opposed by a halt in growth; change in quality by rest; motion from place to place by the absence of such motion. The rest that opposes growth is not a continuing size, but the absence of change in size. The rest that opposes change in quality is not a continuing quality, but the absence of that change. The same is true of rest that opposes motion from place to place, or any other motion. This is not just a dispute about words, as some have claimed. Some say that the rest opposed to motion is rest at the starting point; others say it is rest at the destination. Each side has arguments.
