The same description applies to the essence of a substance as the mind understands it: it is an essence that, if it existed outside the mind, would not depend on a subject.[^V03-626] In the mind, however, it does not exist in that way. Motion is similar: its nature is to be the completion of something that exists potentially, but motion in the mind is not itself a completion of something in that way.

I say that this answer does not satisfy me. If the arguments for mental existence are sound, they show that things exist in the mind with all their features, relations, and meanings, but in a different way from their fading, material existence. We imagine a human being not only as a kind of substance but also as something that exists on its own, understands itself, and does not depend on a subject. Avicenna’s answer cannot explain this. If we applied it to every feature, broader kind, and distinguishing feature of an essence, nothing of the essence would remain in the mind. If the image of an animal in the mind were not a substance, body, living thing, perceiver, mover, or anything else that belongs to an animal, what would make it an animal? Would it be an animal because it is an actual bodily substance that lives, senses, and moves? No. Or would it be an animal because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be an animal?

What could that last claim mean? If it means that this very mental image, as one individual, could exist outside the mind, that is false. The individual in the mind has become general and can apply to many things; it cannot leave the mind and become that very bodily individual with a particular position and direction. That would confuse different kinds of existence and erase their differences. An individual in the mind can be general and apply to many; an individual outside the mind cannot. If instead the claim is that the essence, as it exists mentally, would be a substance if it existed outside the mind, then the image is an accident of the soul. If it existed outside, it would still be a quality of the soul, not a substance or any other outside category. If the claim is that this essence exists in the mind in such a way that, under an impossible assumption, it could become another essence outside the mind, that claim adds nothing. The same could be said of any essence in any kind of existence. We could say: if a substance were an accident, it would exist in a subject; if a body were an intellect, it would have every perfection; if a possible thing were necessary, it would create the world.

This view also leaves no real difference between mental forms and mere likenesses or shadows. A mental image would be like a picture painted on a wall: it would count as a person, horse, elephant, trees, or rivers only because, if it existed outside the mind, it would be those things. But it could never exist outside that surface. The truth is that the intellectual images of substances outside the mind are the real meanings and realities of those things.[^V03-627] A substance, or a body, has a meaning and a sensible image. Its sensible image is the substance as sensed; its intellectual image is the meaning of substance, understood by the intellect as existing on its own. The intellect understands this without needing another image to be present in the intellect. The same applies to the idea of an animal: it includes the understood meanings of body, life, and sensation. These meanings do not have to be separate existences.[^V03-628]

Nor is the intellectual meaning something that exists in a subject that could do without it. This is a higher, more complete kind of existence. All these meanings can be said of one body as what it is, even though that body exists in a position and direction and none of the intellectual images has a position or direction. It is even more fitting to say that these meanings are one with an intellectual reality. One understood meaning being one with another in intellectual existence is more fitting than an understood meaning being one with something sensed and one with it in sensory existence. Avicenna himself, at the start of the fourth section of *The Pointers*, says that the understood animal exists in the sensed animal.[^V03-629] The animal understood as a general kind clearly has an existence that cannot be pointed to or located in space. Yet it is connected to, and one in meaning with, the animal we sense. This does not mean that the intellectual image is an accident in each individual animal. It is more truly a substance and more independent than these lowly, changing, generated and decaying animals. The same applies to other understood images of substances and other kinds.

People fall into these problems because they think that intellectual images exist in the soul in the same way accidents exist in what contains them. They also reject the claim that the knower and the known can be one. So they cannot escape the problem of how the mind could know a substance without making knowledge both a substance and an accident. Their best answer is that “accident” is an incidental feature when said of a substance, and that substance and accident do not conflict in mental existence, only in outside existence. They say that the nature of a substance remains the same even when it needs the mind as a subject in order to exist there. It can still be called a substance because outside the mind it does not depend on a subject. It would be wrong to say that one thing is both a substance and an accident in the same kind of existence. But, they argue, having the essence of a substance in the mind does not require this.

This answer also fails.[^V03-630] First, being an accident means having the kind of existence that depends on a subject. That is what it means for something to exist in a subject. Existing in a subject is the way qualities such as blackness and heat exist. As we explained earlier, existence does not truly attach itself to an essence as another feature that can come and go. The mind separates them in its analysis. So being an accident is not like an added feature that may change while the essence remains. If a substance such as a human being had the same kind of existence as an accident—that is, if its very being were to exist in a subject—it could not lose that existence and take on another while remaining the same essence. Comparing the way existence belongs to an essence with the way other incidental features belong to it is a comparison without a real likeness. A thing's existence is not truly an added feature. It is the thing's being real, outside the mind or in it.

Even if we allowed that one thing could be a substance in its nature and an accident in the mind, the problem would remain. They agree that knowledge of each category belongs to that category, while they also say that all knowledge is a quality of the soul.[^V03-631] So when we know a substance, knowledge would have to be both a substance and a quality. This is not answered by Avicenna’s reply. Saying that being an accident is not essential to what is beneath it may allow a thing to be a substance outside the mind and an accident inside it. But this does not work for the highest categories, because they are essential to the kinds and individual things beneath them. An essential feature cannot change across different kinds of existence without ceasing to be essential. Then it would no longer be true that the same essence exists in another way in the mind.

A careful thinker asks how one thing could be both a substance and a quality for someone who already rejects its being both a substance and an accident. The conflict between substance and quality seems to come from one existing in a subject and the other not. But not depending on a subject is also true of a substance and a quality, so why does that cause a problem for one and not the other?

Someone might answer that, just as substance means an essence that exists independently outside the mind, quality means an essence that exists as an accident, that is, without parts and without a relation between parts. The same would apply to quantity and the other categories. But this brings back the earlier problem: it would leave no part of the essences or meanings of things that remained the same in mental and outside existence. It also follows from their view that the substantial image of a thing in the mind is an individual image present in one particular mind. Whatever exists in one particular mind must be a particular thing in the outside world. So the intellectual image of the essence of a substance would exist outside the mind as a quality. It would then be both a substance and a quality in outside existence, which is clearly impossible. They have no way out except to say that an essence exists in the mind, but that “outside existence” means an existence in which the features of that essence take effect. Blackness outside the mind makes the eyes contract; heat outside the mind warms things. When these images exist in the mind, those effects do not occur. So they call the first outside existence and the second mental existence.

But the problem remains. We now turn to the view we have already pointed toward and will make the case for it.

#### Chapter 7 — What It Means for the Intellect to Become One with What It Understands

The question of how the soul understands the forms of things is one of the hardest questions in philosophy. No Muslim philosopher, as far as we know, had fully worked it out. We saw how difficult it is to explain how knowing a substance could itself be a substance and an accident. We found no answer in the major books of the leading philosopher, Avicenna—*The Healing*, *The Salvation*, *The Pointers*, or *The Sources of Wisdom*—that could resolve the problem. Avicenna’s followers, including his student Bahmanyār, the distinguished commentator Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, and later thinkers, offered nothing we could rely on either. If even these respected scholars could not settle it, what can we expect from those who trade in guesses, fantasies, and endless disputes?

So we turned to the One who brings all things about, asking for help with this difficult question. We had often seen Him guide those seeking knowledge, reveal divine truths to those who need them, and spread the light of guidance. As I was writing this chapter, He opened a new door of knowledge for me and made a clear way into the matter. That is a gift from God, given to whomever He wills. In gratitude, I will now share it.

Images of things are of two kinds. A material image depends on matter, position, place, and other such conditions. In that material mode of existence, it cannot be an object of thought in act; it cannot even be sensed in that same way except indirectly. The other kind is free of matter, position, and place. If it is wholly free of them, it is an object of thought in act; if it is free only in part, it is imagined or sensed.[^V03-632]

All philosophers agree that an image actually understood has one and the same existence in itself and for the intellect that understands it.[^V03-633] The same is true of something actually sensed: its existence as a sensed thing and its existence for the sensing subject are one in the same respect. If an actually understood image had an existence separate from the intellect, then the two would be distinct beings, like blackness and the body in which it occurs. Each would have to be able to exist without the other. But that is not how an actual object of thought exists.

An actual object of thought has no existence apart from the existence in which it is understood. It is intelligible in itself, not because something else turns it into an object of thought.[^V03-634] If its intellect were separate from it, then, considered on its own, it would not be intelligible. Its existence would not be the intellectual existence of an understood form. But an essence free of matter is intelligible in act, whether or not some outside intellect happens to understand it. This is unlike a body's being in motion: if we set aside what moves it, it is no longer moving in that respect, only a body. It is also unlike a body's being hot: without what heats it, it is no longer hot, because the body's existence is not the same as the existence of heat.

The case of an actual object of thought is different. It cannot exist in act without being intelligible in act. Its very existence is its being understood, whether or not another intellect understands it. So it is an intellect in act as well as an object of thought in act. Otherwise, the intellect and the intelligible would come apart, even though each is in act. As we have already explained, the intellect and what it understands must match one another in existence and in level: if one is actual, the other is actual; if one is only potential, the other is only potential; and if one exists at a certain level, the other exists at that level too.[^V03-635]

The same applies to sensible forms. Something may be sensible only in possibility, or it may be sensed in act. What is sensed in act shares its existence with the sensing substance in act. Sensation does not happen by the sense removing the very same form from its matter, as many philosophers have thought, while imagination removes it still further. A form impressed in matter cannot move with its own identity from one piece of matter to another.

Nor does sensation mean that a sense power moves toward a form of the sensed thing that remains in its matter, as some have said about sight. Nor is sensation merely the soul's relation to those material forms, as the author of *The Book of Lights* says. A spatial relation to a body is not perception, and a knowing relation cannot be formed with things that have position and matter. Sensation occurs when the Giver causes a luminous, perceptive form to appear. Through it, awareness takes place. That form is the sense faculty in act and the sensed thing in act. Before it appears, both exist only in possibility. The form in a particular material thing prepares the way for this new form to flow from the Giver. The account of how one image can be sense, sensing subject, and sensed thing is like the account of how one intellectual image can be intellect, intellecting subject, and intelligible.

The First Teacher says in *The Theology of Aristotle*: “Sight does not reach things outside itself until it becomes, in a way, those things. Then it senses and knows them truly, according to its capacity. The same is true of the intellect: when it looks at intellectual things, it does not reach them until it and they become one. Sight looks at what is outside things, while intellect looks at what is within them. Its union with them takes different forms, and with some it is stronger than the union of the senses with what they sense. The longer ordinary sight looks at a thing, the more it is harmed, until the thing falls outside its sight and it sees nothing. Intellectual sight is the opposite.”

What we have said answers many objections to the claim that forms with different natures are imprinted in the intellect. It also answers objections to the claim that possible things are imprinted in God's being, as many followers of the school of Aristotle hold. If understanding happened by images being imprinted in the knower, then when the soul understood substance, quantity, and other kinds of thing, one and the same thing would belong to two basic categories. And God's being would have to serve as a place for possible things. These and other serious problems are discussed elsewhere.

Some people say that the human soul, which is an intellect only in possibility, meets intellectual forms and understands them. But what enables this receptive power to understand a form? Does it understand the form by its bare self, before any intellectual images are present? How could an unknowing, unlit, ordinary self understand a form that is bright in itself and purely intelligible? A blind eye cannot see. If the soul understands the form through another intellectual image that lights it up, then that image is itself an intellect in act, just as it is an intelligible in act. No further image is needed; otherwise the same question would arise again without end. So the intellect and what it understands are one, without any difference in their existence.[^V03-636]

Someone might reply that this image is only a means by which the soul understands other things, while the soul understands the image itself directly.[^V03-637] But unless the image were first understood, it could not help the soul understand anything else. It does not work like a tool used in physical labor. It is more like light in seeing: we see the light first, and through it we see other things. We have also proved that an intellectual image is intelligible in itself, whether or not anything else understands it. The same is true of something actually sensed: in the existence in which it is sensed, it is sensed in act, even if we set aside everything else.

An image that lets the soul understand does not exist in the soul as a house, wealth, or children exist for their owner.[^V03-638] Those things are connected to a person only by a relation; their presence does not complete or develop that person. A natural bodily form does complete matter and make it an actual thing. Matter is not any definite thing until a form gives it shape. The form does not arrive as a separate being moving into matter; rather, matter rises from a less complete state to a more complete one.[^V03-639] The soul likewise becomes intellect in act after being intellect only in possibility.[^V03-640] An intellectual image does not attach to the soul as a separate thing, like a horse standing beside us, or like an accident added to a substance that could exist without it.[^V03-641] Such connections amount only to relations; they do not complete anything. By contrast, an image that the soul understands completes it more deeply than natural forms complete matter.

#### Chapter 8 — Confirming That the Intellect and What It Understands Become One

Avicenna states in many of his books that the intellect and what it understands cannot become one. He strongly rejects this idea and treats it as absurd. In this chapter I will present his arguments against it and the objections he raises against those who say that intellect and knower become one. Then I will answer them.

In *The Pointers*, Avicenna says that some prominent thinkers believe that when an intellecting substance understands an intellectual form, it becomes that form. Suppose, he says, that an intellecting substance understands A and, as these thinkers claim, becomes the very A it understands. Is it still what it was before it understood A, or has something in it ceased to be what it was? If nothing changed, then it makes no difference whether it understands A. If something in it ceased to be, that change must either be a state added to it while its substance remains, like any other change—and then the claim is false—or it must be its very substance. In that case its substance has disappeared and something else has appeared; it has not become another thing while remaining itself. If you think this through, Avicenna adds, the view also requires a shared matter and a composite change, not a simple one.

He makes the same point in another passage: if the intellect first understands A and then B, does it remain as it was when it understood A, whether or not it understands B? Or does it become something else? Either way, the earlier problem returns. He also mocks the book Porphyry wrote about intellect and intelligible forms. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school praise it, he says, even though neither they nor Porphyry himself understood it. One of Porphyry's contemporaries contradicted him, and Porphyry's reply was even weaker. Avicenna then gives a general argument against any two things becoming one: if both remain, they are two distinct things; if one no longer exists, the thing that existed has disappeared. He calls the idea that one thing could remain itself and yet become another, without changing or combining with something else, poetic and unintelligible.

In *The Healing*, Avicenna repeats the argument. If the soul became the intelligible forms, he says, it would have to give up one form and take on another. Then the first thing would have disappeared, while only its subject or a part of it remained. If that is not what happens, we must explain how it happens. When something becomes something else, is it then present or absent? If it is present and the other thing is also present, there are two things, not one. If it is absent, then the present thing has become something absent, not another existing thing. If the first thing disappeared, it did not become something else; it simply ceased to exist and something else appeared. How, then, could the soul become the forms of things?

Avicenna says that Porphyry's *Isagoge* is the best-known example of this view, but that its language is imaginative and poetic rather than clear. The images of things settle in and adorn the soul, making it a kind of place for them by means of the material intellect. If the soul itself became an actual form, and that form were fully actual with no potentiality to receive anything else,[^V03-642] the soul could not accept another form. Yet we see that it does. If the new form did not differ from the first, the soul would somehow both accept and not accept the same thing. If it did differ, the soul would have become something other than itself. Avicenna concludes that the soul is the knower, while “intellect” means either its power to understand or the forms it understands. Since the forms are understood in the soul, intellect, knower, and intelligible cannot be one in us. He allows that they may be one in another being, a point he says he will discuss later. He adds that if “material intellect” means the soul's general capacity to understand, it remains in us as long as we live in a body; if it means a capacity for one particular thing, that capacity disappears when it becomes actual.

Before answering Avicenna, we must keep two things in mind. First, existence is what makes a thing real and individual, and it is the source of what that thing is. Existence can grow stronger or weaker, become more complete or less complete, while the individual remains itself. A human being passes through many stages, from embryo to child to adult who understands and is understood, while its individual existence continues.

Second, there are three different senses in which things might be said to become one. The first is when two existing things merge so that their two existences become one. Avicenna is right that this is impossible. The second is when one concept or essence becomes identical in meaning with another, so that each can be substituted for the other in a definition. That too is impossible: different meanings cannot become one meaning. The concept of the knower cannot become the concept of the intelligible. But one simple existence can truthfully be called both knower and intelligible, with different meanings that do not divide that existence.

The third sense is this: something develops so that a concept or universal nature that could not previously be said of it can now truly be said of it.[^V03-643] This is not impossible; it happens. A human being contains, in one individual, the meanings found separately in nonliving things, plants, animals, and intellect. Someone might say that these meanings are present in a human because the person has many different powers, not because of one power. I reply that they belong to the person's own form, which includes those powers. All human powers of perception and action flow from one simple source: the soul, the person's true self. Those powers are branches of that one source, which senses through the senses and acts through the limbs.

In the same way, the simple intellect that philosophers speak of is the source of the many distinct things understood by the mind. Later in this book it will become clear that the Active Intellect in us is all existing things in this sense: its own being is what makes it true to say all the universal meanings found in the forms of things in the world. It is not strange for one existence to develop until a meaning that could not earlier be said of it can now be said of it. As the saying goes, it is no wonder that God gathers the whole world into one.

With these points in place, we can answer Avicenna. His general argument in *The Pointers* says that if both things exist, they remain two distinct things. We do not accept that. Many different meanings can exist in one existence. “Animal” and “rational” are different meanings, either of which can be considered apart from the other, yet both exist in one human being.

Avicenna's general argument in *The Healing* says that when one thing becomes another, the first must either exist or not exist. If both exist, they are two; if the first does not, it has disappeared. We reply that both meanings can exist in one existence. There is no contradiction in many different meanings being present in one being. Otherwise, how could the human soul be one simple substance that is knowing, able, active, hearing, seeing, and alive? And how could the one divine being be the source of every perfection and every good name in one simple existence, with no different parts or sides?

Now consider Avicenna's arguments about the knower and the intelligible. In *The Pointers* he asks whether the knower remains what it was before it understood A. We answer: it remains itself, except that what was incomplete or lacking in it is gone. The change is like a child becoming an adult. The child loses nothing substantial or positive; what falls away is only a lack, such as being immature or still only capable of adulthood.

Avicenna himself explains two ways in which one thing can come from another. In the first, the first thing naturally moves toward completion in the second. A child is a child because it is on its way to adulthood. When it becomes an adult, it has not been destroyed; it has been completed. It has lost no essential or accidental feature except what belonged to its earlier weakness and potential. In the second way, a thing is not naturally moving toward the next form, even though the matter that carries it can receive that form. Water becomes air by losing its watery form and taking on an airy form. In the first case, the first thing itself remains in the second and becomes complete. In the second, only part of the first remains; its earlier substance is destroyed. Avicenna's own account therefore allows a thing to become another while remaining itself, when it develops toward its natural completion.

When Avicenna says that the soul would be the same whether or not it understood A, we answer that this would follow only if the soul did not itself become the source of a perfection that it lacked before. It is surprising that he denies this, since he says that the human soul develops from potentiality in every kind of perception, including sensation and imagination, until it becomes intellect in act and understands most—or even all—intelligible things, as the simple intellect does. Yet on his account, nothing that could not be said of a soul at the beginning can later be said of it in itself. That would make the souls of prophets, children, people with severe mental disabilities, and embryos all equal in their essential nature; their only differences would be accidental features attached to existence.[^V03-644]

Of course, these perfections differ in meaning from the human essence. But the difference between existence and essence is a difference in our way of thinking, not a split in reality. Existence is what makes things real; essence follows it. When Avicenna says that if the soul changes, something must have disappeared while the soul remains as a subject, we answer that no part of its nature or existence disappears. Only a lack falls away. The soul was less complete and becomes stronger in its way of existing. This is unlike ordinary changes in which one positive feature gives way to its opposite, as when water becomes air or something cold becomes hot.

Avicenna's further claim—that the soul must disappear and a different thing must appear if its very self changes—is also answered by the difference between existence and meaning. What disappears is only a lack, such as potentiality. A thing can also change gradually in its very substance, without its existence ending and a separate thing taking its place. Consider heat that grows stronger. If each moment of stronger heat were a separate existence, motion would be made of indivisible instants and separate pieces of distance.[^V03-645] We have already shown that this is impossible. The growing heat has one continuous existence, even though it has different degrees of heat at different parts of the duration of its change. These degrees are distinct in meaning but belong to one continuous existence.

So it is not impossible for different meanings to be present in one existence, as they are when they are drawn from many separate things. What is impossible is for one actual heat to become another actual heat as a second separate thing, or for two fully existing beings to become one being. Every actual existence has its own definite identity; one identity cannot become another. Every essence has its own definition and meaning; the meaning of a human being cannot become the meaning of a horse. But reason does not rule out every case in which different meanings belong to one existence. Proof rules out only certain combinations, such as the Necessary and the possible, potentiality and actuality, substance and accident, opposites, and other pairs that cannot share one existence.

When Avicenna says that such a change requires shared matter, we do not deny that a thing changing toward completion may depend in some way on a material substance that is itself in motion.[^V03-646] But if he means that the thing is externally composite in itself, we do not accept that. A form's existence is not made of parts, especially when it is ready to become intellect in act. If he means that a living human being is made up of soul and bodily matter, we accept that, but it does not refute our point.

Avicenna's other argument in *The Healing* concerns how the soul could already be a form and still be able to receive further forms. We answer that when the soul first came to be in the body's matter, it was the form of a bodily thing.[^V03-647] At the beginning, it was like a sensory or imagined form, not yet an intellectual form. A purely intellectual form and bodily matter could not make one bodily kind, such as a human being, without the matter first passing through stages of development and change. The soul at the beginning of life was one form among the beings of this world, but it had the capacity to rise gradually toward the spiritual world. It was first the form of a bodily being, with the potential to receive intellectual forms.

The soul's sensory form is like matter for its imagined form, and the imagined form is like matter for the intellectual forms. First, the earliest intelligible meanings flow into it; then, gradually, the later ones. That is how the soul becomes those forms. Avicenna says that a form itself cannot contain the potential to receive another form. We do not accept this. The capacity to develop is included in the form, as a distinguishing feature is included in a simple kind.[^V03-648]

Avicenna says that the capacity to receive belongs only to what receives the form. We agree, but “receiving” has more than one meaning. It can mean undergoing change when an opposite form appears, as when something continuous becomes separate or water becomes air. Or it can mean having the capacity to develop toward greater completeness. A form can have this second kind of capacity as it becomes more complete.

In short, potentiality may be joined to a thing's absence in the outside world, or to an absence that exists only in thought. The first belongs to receptive matter; the second belongs to a form connected to matter.[^V03-649][^V03-650] A form wholly free of matter in every respect has no further perfection waiting for it.

Avicenna says that if the next form does not differ from the first, then receiving and not receiving are the same. We answer that the next form is not a second actual form added to the first. It is a meaning united with the soul in one existence. By “the form of a thing,” we mean its existence, not a general idea of it. Each thing has one simple form, but that form can make many perfections real. It may have a strong, complete existence or a weak, incomplete one.

As the soul grows stronger, it becomes the source of many meanings. Each meaning, if it existed separately, might be the form of an incomplete bodily kind: an understood horse, tree, or piece of earth. When these meanings exist in bodily matter outside the mind, each is the form of a material kind. When understood in the intellectual world, each is joined to an intellectual substance. It need not be the whole nature of that substance or its intellectual mode of existence. It can be one of the meanings united with it, in a way higher and more complete than its union with lowly bodily forms. Intellectual existence is a higher, nobler existence, in which all intelligible things can be present together in one existence, unlike the numerical unity of bodies.[^V03-651]

When Avicenna says that if the soul differs from the form it has become something other than itself, we answer that it has not become numerically different. It has changed in completeness, or in the meaning we can truly apply to it, while the same existence remains and becomes more noble.

He also says that the soul is the knower, while intellect means either the soul's power to understand or the forms it understands. We have already shown that the first meaning cannot be intellect in act. Whether we mean the soul's capacity or its bare self, before intellectual forms are present, it cannot be exactly the same as intellect in act. Otherwise, the same thing would be potential and actual, ignorant and knowing.[^V03-652][^V03-653] As for the second meaning—that the understood forms are intellect in act while the soul, which is the bodily animal's perfection, understands them—we have shown why this account fails from both sides.

First, from the soul's side: how could a soul bare of intellect understand intellectual forms that are separate from it in their existence? A thing can be truly said to have something only if the thing exists in the same setting where the feature is said of it. If the thing is absent in that setting, no other thing can truly belong to it there. What exists belongs to what exists, not to what is absent. The same rule applies to intellectual existence: a purely intellectual form, free of matter and its ties, can be present to something only if that thing also has intellectual existence. An actual object of thought can belong only to something that is itself an actual intellect. So before the soul becomes an intellect, it cannot have an intellectual image in itself, except potentially, as imagined or sensed forms exist before the light of the Active Intellect shines on them.

Now consider the intellectual forms themselves.[^V03-654] By a proof God inspired in me, I have shown that each form is intelligible in its own being, apart from everything else. Whether or not something exists to understand it, it is intelligible in itself. If it is intelligible apart from the soul, then it is an intellect in itself. The soul must therefore become one with it. That is the very point we are making.

Although Avicenna strongly rejects the union of knower and intelligible in his other books, he sets out this very idea in *The Beginning and the Return*. There he argues that the Necessary Being understands Himself and is intellect and intelligible. I do not know whether he presents this only as another school's view, because of the purpose of that book, or whether it was his own belief after the light of truth appeared to him. Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, in his commentary on *The Pointers*, excuses Avicenna by saying that *The Beginning and the Return* was written to explain the view held by Aristotle’s followers, as Avicenna says at the start. From this we can see that only the earliest philosophers had fully understood this noble teaching. Later scholars of debate and argument did not inherit it—until God granted it to a poor seeker and opened his heart through His power.

#### Chapter 9 — The Earlier Philosophers’ View: The Soul Understands by Joining the Active Intellect

The standard view in many books by philosophers of the Islamic period is that[^V03-655] this account, like the one just discussed, is false. The two views are closely related. Their argument is that the Active Intellect must either be one simple being or a composite made of parts. If it is one simple being, then a soul that joins with it in order to understand one thing would join with it in order to understand every intelligible thing. If the soul joins with only one part of it, not the whole, then the Active Intellect must have a part for every act of understanding a human being can achieve. But human beings can understand endlessly many things, so it would have endlessly many parts of different kinds. Each of these intelligible things could be understood by endlessly many souls. Zayd's understanding of blackness, for example, would be like Amr's understanding of blackness. The Active Intellect would therefore need endlessly many parts of the same kind, repeated endlessly many times.

That is already impossible. There is another problem: parts of the same kind could differ only by their essence or by features that follow from their essence, or else by changeable accidents. But changeable accidents require matter. The Active Intellect is free of matter, so its parts would be even less likely to differ by accidents. They would not be distinct, and so it could not have many parts. It would have to be simple, contrary to the assumption that it is composite. This is the argument later thinkers repeat when they reject this view. Avicenna points to it in *The Pointers*: those who hold the view must either divide the Active Intellect so that one part joins the soul at a time, or say that the soul joins it in one act and thereby becomes complete and able to understand everything.

I say that this view, like the one before it, was held by distinguished earlier philosophers. It must have a subtle and sound meaning, even if it takes careful thought, a clear mind, and God's help to uncover it. We pleaded with Him through our minds, raising our inward hands to Him, not only our passing bodily hands. We laid ourselves before Him and begged Him to reveal this question and others like it, with the persistence of someone driven to seek help and unwilling to give up. Then He lit our minds with His radiant light and lifted some of the veils and obstacles. We have seen the intellectual world as one being, joined to all the beings in our world. They begin from it and return to it. It is the source of intelligible things and all essences, yet it does not divide into parts, lose anything as things flow from it, or gain anything when things join it. The proof of this reality belongs elsewhere in the book. Here I will give three points that may ease people's doubts about the soul joining that world whenever it understands something.

First, as we have already proved, when the soul understands something, it becomes that intellectual form. Second, the intellect is all intelligible things. We have proved this elsewhere. This does not mean that all things come together in one place with all their separate bodily existences.[^V03-656] A horse has an outside existence with size, position, color, and matter. It also has a distinct intellectual existence with intellectual features that belong to that mode of being. Just as individual horses exist in the senses and occupy different places, each kind also has its own intellectual existence. In that mode, the understood horse is one thing and the understood plant another.

Rather, all the essences that exist outside the mind as many separate things can exist in the intellect in one intellectual existence that gathers their meanings while remaining simple and one. Third, the unity of intellects is not numerical unity, like the unity of bodies, blackness, color, or motion. If two bodies of the same size existed, they would be larger together than either one alone. Two black things likewise make more blackness than either by itself. Intellectual unity works differently. If we imagined a thousand intellects like one intellect, the unity of each would be no greater or less than the unity of the thousand together.

Consider the idea of a human being in general. If you added another idea just like it, leaving aside differences of position, size, place, and other accidents, you would not find anything different in the second idea or in the pair that was not already present in the first. The author of *The Book of Lights* says: “Pure existence, which has no greater degree, remains itself when you suppose it a second time, because nothing can distinguish pure existence.”[^V03-657]

With these points clear, we can say that the human soul can understand all realities and become one with them. It can also become an intellectual world containing the form of every intellectual being and the meaning of every bodily being. Suppose, for example, that the intellectual meaning of a horse is present in the soul. We have established that one intellectual meaning, with one definition and kind but no individual features or location, cannot be multiplied in existence unless something is added to its meaning. So the intellectual horse in the Active Intellect and the intellectual horse in a soul that has become intellect in act cannot differ in meaning or essence. They are one and the same meaning; any difference between them must come from something beyond their definition.

We have also shown that the soul becomes one with every intellectual form it understands. It follows that, in that respect, it joins with the Active Intellect, which contains all things. It does not join with what it has not understood. Since all the meanings exist there in one existence without multiplying or dividing it, their appearing as many things in other places does not divide the Active Intellect. In the same way, many souls can join with it through their different perfections without dividing it, and without every soul receiving every perfection. Anyone who finds this difficult is treating intellectual unity as if it were numerical unity.[^V03-658]

For example, a human being is one with the universal meaning “animal,” and so are a horse, an ox, and a lion. Yet they do not become one another. “Animal” is a universal meaning that can be one with different kinds. The intellectual world can likewise hold many meanings together. The First Teacher says in *The Theology of Aristotle* that the higher world is the complete living being that contains all things. It came from the first, perfect Creator and contains every soul and every intellect. Nothing there is poor or needy. Everything there is full of life and richness, as if life were flowing from one spring—not like one single heat or wind, but like one quality that contains every quality and every taste.

He says further that the different kinds of life and intellect in our world come from different movements of life and intellect. That is why there are different animals and intellects, some brighter and nobler than others.[^V03-659] Some intellects are close to the first intellects and so shine more brightly; others are second or third in rank. Here, some are divine, some rational, and some nonrational, because they are farther from the noble intellects. But in the higher world, all things have intellect. So a horse is intellect, and the intellect of a horse is a horse. The intellect that understands a horse is not the intellect that understands a human being; that would be impossible for the first intellects.[^V03-660]

When the First Intellect understands something, it and what it understands are one. It does not understand anything that has no intellect; it understands it through its universal intellect and universal life.[^V03-661] Individual life does not lack universal life, and likewise an individual intellect does not lack universal intellect. The intellect in an animal is not cut off from the First Intellect. Each part of intellect contains all that can be divided from it. The intellect of a thing is potentially all the things it can understand; when it becomes actual, it is particular and complete. When it is fully actual, it is a horse or some other animal. As life descends to lower forms, it becomes weaker and less complete. Some of its powers become hidden, and weaker animals appear. When their life is weak, intellect compensates by giving them strong body parts: some have claws, some horns, and some fangs. That is the end of the First Teacher's words.

These words clarify and support what I have argued, though some of them need explanation so that readers do not misunderstand them. When he speaks of different “movements” of life and intellect, he means different intellectual aspects in the first intellects, such as necessity and possibility, greater and lesser strength, and the differences that come from being nearer to or farther from the first Creator. “Movement” here means a source or outflow, not change. Differences in movement can be differences in kind, such as whether something flows from the aspect of necessity and existence or from the aspect of essence and possibility. They can also be differences in degree, depending on nearness to or distance from the First. What flows from a higher intellect close to the First is nobler than what flows from a lower one.[^V03-662]

When he says that some intellects are close to the first intellects, he means the intellects that exist apart from matter in act. By the “second” and “third,” he means the essences of kinds and their intellectual forms, which have different levels. The first are human intellects, the second animal, and the third plant.[^V03-663] When he says that something cannot be understood by the first intellects, he means the intellects in the lower ranks. When he says that individual life does not lack universal life, by “universal life” he means the nature of animal, and by “universal intellect” its universal intellectual form.[^V03-664]

Each of these, depending on how we consider it, differs from the first actual intellect, while still being one with it in existence. An essence considered in itself can be universal or particular, separate from matter or embodied, and so on. Its intellectual form, however, is shared in act by all its actual or possible individuals. The first actual intellect is the existence and intellectual identity that gathers many particular meanings.

When he says that the intellect in an animal is not cut off from the First Intellect, he means that the animal's intellectual nature is not cut off from it, because that nature is one with it.[^V03-665] When he speaks of parts of intellect, he means meaningful parts that can be intellectual forms of bodily parts: the understood head, hand, and foot of an understood animal. Each one has the same kinds of existence as the whole, such as being understood or sensed.[^V03-666] And when he says that the intellect of a thing is potentially all things, he uses “potential” and “actual” in a special sense, not the usual one. “Potential” means that one existence, in its unity, gathers many essences and meanings that may appear as many existences elsewhere. As when strong blackness is said to be all weaker blackness potentially, he does not mean it can be divided into them or is ready to be affected by them. It is a pure existence, fully actual and without any lack. “Actual” here means that a bodily thing is brought into being with material qualities. The rest of his words are clear once these ideas are understood.

#### Chapter 10 — Refuting a Later View of Knowledge

One later thinker says that knowledge and awareness are relations, and that a relation exists only when both things it connects exist. If what is understood is the knower itself, he says, then that knower cannot exist without understanding itself. No further image needs to be formed in it; its being a knower is simply its relation to itself as the understood thing.[^V03-667] But if the understood thing differs from the knower, the knower cannot understand it while it is absent from the outside world. So an image of that thing must be formed in the knower to create the relation called understanding. This is the rule, he says, that the arguments support. Since an image must be present and knowledge cannot simply be the image itself, a further relation must be added to it. Once all other possibilities have been ruled out, this must be the correct account.

This view and the argument supporting it are very weak. We have already shown by clear proof that knowledge is a form of existence free of matter. Anyone who looks inward will see that knowledge, like power, is a perfection of a living being. A bare relation is not a perfection in itself. The argument is weak too, because it never tells us what kind of relation knowledge is.[^V03-668] Relation is itself a broad category, and it needs further features to become one specific kind. The same argument could be used for nearly every relation-based feature, such as power, will, desire, anger, love, fear, pain, and mercy. We could say that willing is a relation that exists only when both sides exist.

If the one who wills is also what is willed, then it cannot fail to will itself while it exists. No further image needs to be formed; its being a willer is simply its relation to itself as the willed thing. But if what is willed differs from the willer, and is absent from the outside world, then an image must be present in or before the willer for the relation of willing to exist. The same argument would apply to power and to every other such feature.

If someone replies that one thing cannot be both able and subject to power, or that it cannot move itself or be angry with itself, we answer that these facts are not contained in the concept of power alone. To know that the one who has power differs from what it acts on, or that the mover differs from what is moved, we need an argument beyond the meanings of those words. The same is true of father and child, or an angry person and the one they are angry with. Avicenna explains this point in several places in *The Healing*. We will return to it and explain it further.[^V03-669]

#### Chapter 11 — How One Thing Can Be Intellect, Knower, and Known Without Becoming Many

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī says that literal-minded people admired this grand, poetic claim and concluded that a knower must become one with what it understands, whether it understands itself or something else.[^V03-670] But careful thinkers, he says, rejected union and instead claimed that when a thing understands itself, the intellect, the knower, and the intelligible are one.

I thank God, who showed us this path. With His help and light, we have made clear what many philosophers, let alone other scholars, could not see. No one should still doubt it unless they misunderstand the argument or cannot follow it. There is no disagreement among philosophers that an immaterial substance understands itself and is understood by itself, without becoming many things or needing an extra feature beyond its existence.

In the eighth part of *The Healing*, Avicenna says that God is complete, indeed beyond complete, and is pure intellect because being in matter and tied to matter prevents something from being understood and from being an intellect. What is free of matter and exists apart from it is understood by itself. Since it is an intellect in itself, it is also understood in itself. So it is intellect, knower, and intelligible—not three separate things. As a separate identity, it is an intellect. Considered as an identity that is separate for itself, it is intelligible to itself. And considered as an identity that belongs to itself, it is the knower of itself. The knower is something whose nature is separate for something; the intelligible is something whose nature is separate for something. That “something” need not be another thing; it can be the same thing or another. The concept of knower requires an intelligible, but it does not say whether that intelligible is the same thing or something else. The same is true of motion and what causes motion: the concept alone does not tell us whether the mover and what is moved are one or two. We need a separate argument to show that something cannot move itself. The meanings of relations likewise do not by themselves tell us whether their two sides are distinct.

Al-Rāzī objects that the thing understood and the knower may be the same, but the descriptions “knower” and “intelligible” are not the same.[^V03-671] He says that we can judge something to be understood without judging that it understands, and we can judge that it understands without judging that it is understood. So they must be two distinct positive features. Someone may reply that we cannot understand a thing as a knower without also understanding it as intelligible, and vice versa; this would show that they are one.[^V03-672] Al-Rāzī answers that each description has its own meaning. If one referred to the other, whenever we grasped one we would grasp the other, just as “human being” and “person” name one nature. But we can grasp the meaning of knower without grasping the meaning of intelligible, and vice versa. So the two features differ. And if two features differ in one case, he says, they differ in every case. Blackness differs in nature from motion wherever either is found.

We answer that the two descriptions are tied together, but that does not make what is described one and the same meaning. Knowing that someone is a parent goes with knowing that someone is a child, yet parenthood and childhood are different. If something is moving, knowing it is moving goes with knowing there is something that moves it; but “moving” and “mover” do not mean the same thing. So the knower and the intelligible differ in meaning, while the same being can have both descriptions. That it is intellect is an even clearer case of a different meaning from its being a knower or intelligible. That is the end of al-Rāzī's argument.

This scholar has spent much time on argument but has not understood the difference between a thing's meaning and its existence. He assumes that if two meanings differ, then their existences must differ too. But God's essential perfections—knowledge, power, will, life, hearing, and sight—are one being and one existence. His necessity, existence, and unity are also one reality, with no difference in His being, whether we consider Him in the mind, outside it, or by analysis.

The essential features of a thing may have many meanings, while still existing in one way, especially in a simple being. So a difference between meanings in one place does not prove a difference in existence elsewhere. If positive attributes differed in existence, the being described by them would be many and composite. That would make the one divine being composite. Al-Rāzī's view also erases the difference between being a knower and being intelligible, on the one hand, and being a parent and a child, on the other. If one thing can be both knower of itself and intelligible to itself, with the two features different in both meaning and existence, then why could it not also be its own parent and child, or move itself? The philosophers agree that one thing cannot move itself, be its own parent, or teach itself. Yet they accept that one thing can understand itself and be understood by itself. Some accomplished mystics even say that the simple intellect is all intelligible things. This shows that meanings can differ without their existence differing. One simple being, from one simple side, can be the true source for many meanings without losing its unity.

When philosophers say that two features differ in their basis or point of view, as movement and being moved, potentiality and actuality, possibility and necessity, or unity and multiplicity, they do not infer this from the meanings alone. There must be something else, as Avicenna himself says in the passage we quoted. Al-Rāzī also argues that we know for certain that we have a power by which we understand things. Is the power by which we understand that power the same power, so that it understands itself? Or is it another power? If it is another, then we have one power for understanding things and another for understanding that power, and so on without end. This would mean we have an actual infinite number of powers. So the fact that something is understood does not require a different thing to understand it.

Avicenna also says in *The Annotations* that God's understanding Himself and being understood by Himself do not make Him two in His being or in how we consider Him. His being is one, and our way of considering Him is one. The words put the ideas in a different order, but the point is the same.

It is now clear that a form free of matter can, by its very existence and without any added feature, be intellect, knower, and intelligible. These meanings all exist in one being. They are not simply different words that mean the same thing, as some people think philosophers say about God's attributes. Nor is it right to object, as al-Rāzī does, that philosophers cannot say God's existence is the same as His being because existence is easy to understand while God's essence is unknowable. The same objection applies to His other attributes, whose meanings are familiar even though His essence is not fully known. This objection assumes that philosophers claim the meanings are identical in concept, as if they were synonyms. They mean instead that the meanings are one in existence, as when a subject is said to have different features in ordinary predication.

Al-Rāzī then says that understanding must be a relation, because he has proved that it is relational. A relation, he says, must differ from the thing itself. The philosophers think that understanding is just presence, and that another image of the thing cannot be present to itself. So they claim that the thing's own existence is its understanding. But since, as he argues, understanding is relational, it must be a feature separate from the knower. He offers this proof: if knowing something were the same as the thing's own being, then the reality of knowing and the reality of the thing would be identical, and one could not exist without the other. Yet we can understand a thing without understanding that it understands itself, and we can understand that it is a knower without understanding what it understands. So knowing itself must be something added to the thing. This added feature cannot be an image that matches the thing, for a familiar proof rules out two identical things together.[^V03-673] So it must be something different. If this different feature is related to the thing, the thing is known through that relation.[^V03-674] If it is not related to the thing and does not match it in nature, then the thing's reality is neither present nor related to the mind, and it cannot be known. Therefore, he concludes, knowledge is a relation.

I am surprised that this scholar, whom people call “the Imam,” has made such a mistake about knowledge. The very thing that perfects every living being, gives every excellent being its excellence, and lights the way to our beginning and return, is treated by him as one of the weakest and most dependent accidents. Did he not consider the words of God about the blessed: “Their light will run before them and to their right”? Did he not reflect on “Whoever God does not give light to has no light,” or on “Are those who know equal to those who do not know?” Did he not consider the Prophet's saying, “Faith is a light that God casts into the heart of the believer”? How could this and similar things be only a relation, which exists in neither the outside world nor the mind apart from the two things it connects?

The foundation of his argument is again the failure to distinguish a thing's meaning from its existence. We have often explained that one essence can have several kinds of existence, each different in its being. Many essences with different meanings can also have one simple existence, in reality and in how it is considered.

When al-Rāzī says that if knowing oneself is one's very being, then whatever is true of the being must be true of the knowing, and vice versa, we answer: if “reality” means existence, these two statements work in both directions and cause no problem.[^V03-675] It is true to say that whenever the separate substance exists, its awareness of itself exists; and whenever its awareness of itself exists, that very awareness is the separate substance. If he means that the two meanings or essences are identical, then his conclusion does not follow. No philosopher claims that the concept of knowing is the same as the concept of an immaterial being. His mistake comes from mixing up meaning with existence, or essence with individual reality.

Someone who says knowledge is only a relation should ask what gives rise to that relation and why it belongs to some things, not others, and connects some things rather than others. In truth, every relation that exists requires some settled, positive existence in one or both of its sides before the relation can arise.[^V03-676] That existence is the source of the relation. It may be the very being of one side, or a feature added to it. A relation can never stand on its own.[^V03-677]

#### Chapter 12 — Further Questions About Self-Knowledge

It has been asked: whether we say that perception is a relation,[^V03-678] or that it is the perceived form appearing in the one who perceives it, how can a thing know itself? If knowledge is a relation, then a relation must hold between two things. One thing cannot be related to itself, so it cannot know itself. And if knowledge is the appearance of a form, a thing’s form appears to something else. It makes no sense to say that it appears to itself.

The truth, as we have already explained, is that knowledge is a thing’s actual existence for something. More precisely, knowledge is the existence of something immaterial, whether that existence is for itself or for something else. If it exists for another, it is that other thing’s knowledge;[^V03-679] if it does not exist for another, it is knowledge of itself.

Existence works in the same way. A thing may exist for itself, as substances do, or for something else, as accidents exist for the things in which they occur. But the relation between existence and essence is only a way of speaking, since they differ only when the mind analyzes them. A relation distinguishes its two sides within the setting where the relation holds, not necessarily in every other setting.[^V03-680] If the relation exists in the outside world—as with father and child, or writer and what is written—it requires the two sides to be distinct in that world. One person cannot be both the father and the child in the same relation. But when a relation exists only in the mind, the two sides differ only within that relation and in the way the mind considers them. This second kind has two forms.

In the first, the two sides are one in outside existence but have different essences. The difference between them is enough for one to have a feature or role in thought that the other does not. Essence and existence are like this. Though they are one in reality, the mind considers one as something that receives existence and the other as the existence it receives. The relation between them makes them distinct within that analysis, not in the outside world, where there is no such division.

In the second form, the two sides do not differ at all, either outside the mind or in its analysis. This is possible only in something utterly simple, with no composition of any kind, such as God. When we call Him self-existing, self-sustaining, self-knowing, powerful, willing, or living, there is in reality no relation, attribute, connection, or subject bearing an added feature. There is only pure existence, which itself is the reality meant by knowledge, power, will, life, and every other perfection.

The mind speaks of a subject, an attribute, and a relation because it has seen these features occur in created things. In some things, such features are added to what bears them, and that gives rise to a real relation between them. But the proof that none of existence and its perfections is added to God means that His existence, knowledge, power, will, and other attributes all rest in His own being. This relation between God and Himself is something the mind considers by analogy with created things, to show that no additions belong to Him—not to establish a real relation within God.[^V03-681] The relation is figurative: it means that composition and multiplicity are absent from Him. The difference between the two sides is figurative too. The relation of the simple, immaterial self to its own knowledge belongs to this same kind. It does not create multiplicity outside or inside the mind, because the relation itself is only something the mind considers. In our account, knowledge is immaterial existence.[^V03-682] Just as existence exists for itself, it is also intelligible to itself. Neither self-existence nor self-understanding makes the one simple reality two things or gives it two separate aspects. The difference lies only in the meanings we use.

As we have seen, different meanings can belong to one and the same reality. One simple existence, with no trace of composition, can be what many meanings refer to, even though those same meanings may belong to different things elsewhere. An immaterial being, because it is not in a subject, is called a substance. Because it is a form free of matter, it is called an intellect. Because it is a form of itself, it is called intelligible. Because it exists for itself rather than for another, it is called a knower. Because it is existence free of evil and therefore lovable, and because it perceives that goodness, it loves itself. In this way, many relational meanings can apply to one reality without making it multiple or different in itself; the multiplicity is in the meanings.[^V03-683]

Let us return to some objections. The critic says that, according to Avicenna, for a thing to be understood means that its immaterial essence is present to something. This is broader in meaning than saying that its essence is present to something other than itself. Someone might object that this is exactly the problem: being present to something is a relation, and a relation can hold only between two things. If a thing can be said to move itself because “moving” is broader than “moving something else,” why not also say that a thing can create itself because “creating” is broader than “creating something else”?

The answer is that neither self-understanding nor self-motion is proved merely by saying that one meaning is broader than another. Each needs a separate argument. The philosopher is not claiming that the broader meaning alone proves that a thing can understand itself. That would be like arguing that since something can be an animal, it can therefore be human. The broader meaning does not prove the narrower one, though it does not rule it out either.

Avicenna’s point is to remove a supposed contradiction. Someone might think that “a thing knows” necessarily means that the known thing differs from the knower, as with other relations, and so cannot be identical with it even in meaning. Avicenna points out that the concept of a relation itself requires only a difference in meaning between the related sides. It does not, by itself, show that they must differ in existence. In some relations, outside proof establishes that the two sides must be different in existence. For example, “mover” means something that begins a gradual change, but the concept itself does not tell us whether the mover is different from what it moves. We know by other arguments that a mover, creator, or agent must differ in existence and identity from what is moved, created, or acted upon. A thing’s perceiving or existing for itself, by contrast, involves a difference in meaning while knower and known, or existent and existence, are one in identity and existence, as the proof has shown. Likewise, we know by argument, not merely from the concepts, that a thing cannot be both cause and effect of itself. This is how we should understand the following words from one of the scholars:[^V03-684]

> Knowledge is among relational things. If one and the same being is considered under two descriptions, it is as though we were considering two beings. What belongs to it as knower differs from what belongs to it as known. The one being can therefore bear the relation in view of these two distinct aspects.

It is also reported that Avicenna wrote in *The Discussions* that each individual has an essence and an individuality, and that individuality is always additional to essence. If the essence itself determines that individuality, then the kind exists in only that individual; otherwise, there will be many individuals of that kind. The essence, he says, differs from the whole made up of that essence and its individuality. This difference is enough for the essence to be related as knower to the whole, and for the whole to be related as known to the essence.

I have not seen a copy of *The Discussions*, and this passage does not sound like Avicenna.[^V03-685] For knowing and being known in themselves are features of existence, not of essence considered by itself. Individuation is not something added to existence. A thing’s existence comes before its essence and before any relation between its essence and existence. So if an essence is related to an individual that exists only after that essence exists, the essence can be related to that individual only after it has itself become individual. The thing that is related to itself would then be the individual, and the relation would belong to one individual in one and the same respect. The earlier account is better.

Someone might object that individuation is an existent feature, and so its existence must come after the existence of the thing it individuates. We reply that the same issue arises with a defining feature in relation to the broader kind it completes, existence in relation to the essence it makes actual, and form in relation to the matter it completes. As we explained earlier, things are described by such features within the mind’s analysis, not as separate features in existence. In reality, they are one with the things they describe.

#### Chapter 13 — Kinds of Perception

We perceive things in four ways: through our senses, through imagination, through our grasp of meanings tied to particular things, and through reason. Sensation perceives a thing that exists in matter and is present to the perceiver, together with its particular sensible features: where and when it is, its position, quality, quantity, and other features.[^V03-686] Some of these features always belong to the thing in the outside world, while others may vary; but what is directly sensed and present to the perceiver is the thing’s form, not the material thing itself. Before a sensible thing makes an impression on the sense, the sense is no more actually sensing than it was before. Once the impression occurs, it must fit the nature of the sense. Otherwise, it would not be an act of sensing that thing. So the sense receives the thing’s form, separated from its matter, though it does not separate the form completely.

Imagination perceives the same thing with those features, whether its matter is present or absent. Imagination can picture only what has first been sensed. The third kind, often called estimation, grasps a meaning the senses do not directly perceive. It does not grasp that meaning as universal, but as belonging to a particular sensed thing. That tie to one particular thing makes the meaning particular. Understanding through reason grasps a thing in terms of what it is, whether considered on its own or together with other features that can also be understood in this way.

Every act of perception involves some degree of separation. Sensation requires three conditions: the matter must be present to the sense, the thing must be surrounded by particular features, and the thing perceived must be an individual. Imagination is free of the first condition, estimation of the first two, and understanding through reason of all three. Know, however, that the difference between this third kind and understanding through reason does not lie in the act of perceiving itself. It lies in something added to it: whether or not what is perceived is tied to a particular individual.[^V03-687][^V03-688] In reality, then, there are three kinds of perception, just as there are three worlds.[^V03-689] Estimation is like an intellect that has fallen from its proper level.[^V03-690] Every act of perception draws the realities and spirits of things out of the forms of bodies and structures of matter. The sensible form is drawn out only partly, and remains tied to the presence of matter. The imagined form is drawn out to a middle degree, which is why imagination belongs to a world between the worlds of sense and intellect. The intellectual form is drawn out completely.

This is how it works when forms are taken from matter. But something that is itself an intellect needs no such separation in order to be understood. These are the meanings through which the soul is meant to become an ordered intellectual world: from the First Principle, through the intellects who are the angels nearest to God, then the souls that are angels below them, and on through the heavens, the elements, the forms of the whole, and its nature. The soul thus becomes a bright intellectual world, lit by the First Intellect.

Likewise, something that is itself an imaginal form needs no separation in order to be imagined. When the soul connects with such a form, it becomes a world of the hereafter, a vast realm as wide as the heavens and the earth. The worlds are what they are through their forms, not through their matter.

The incidental features from which we must separate a thing in order to understand it are not its essence or meaning. There is no conflict between understanding one thing and also understanding another feature alongside it. The same is true of imagination: the features that must be set aside are not other imaginal forms, since one thing can be imagined together with another. What blocks some kinds of perception is instead a mode of existence that is dark and bound up with absences, concealing things from perception. Existence in matter, with its position and dimensions, can hide a form from perception altogether.

Being in sensation or imagination can also block intellectual perception, because both are dimensional forms of existence, even when they are free of matter. An intelligible does not exist in a dimensional way. It is free of both modes and beyond both worlds. The different modes of existence therefore occupy different levels: some are intellectual, some belong to the soul, and some are dark and beyond perception. Essences follow each level of existence. A human being, for example, can exist as a particular material person, as a human soul, or as a universal intellectual reality that contains all people in one collective unity, without multiplying into separate human beings.

This resolves a familiar problem. A universal intellectual form exists in an individual soul as an attribute exists in the thing it belongs to. Its being in that soul, its particularity, and its relation to the soul’s other features are all particular features that cannot be separated from it. How, then, can the intellect abstract a form from such incidental features?

A common answer is that the shared human nature found in individuals is, in itself, free of such features. Knowledge of it is called universal because its object is universal, not because the act of knowing is universal in itself.[^V03-691] Later thinkers misunderstood this explanation. They assumed it meant that the intellect contains a universal form, then rejected the answer by saying that the humanity in Zayd is not the same as the humanity in ʿAmr.[^V03-692] The shared humanity that applies to both is not identical with the humanity in either one individually, nor is it a thing that exists in both at once.[^V03-693] If it existed in one person, it would be only part of a supposed whole made up of both persons; and the same would apply to three or more individuals. In the outside world, the number of instances of humanity matches the number of individuals.

Still, if we consider the essence of a human without adding any condition, it is simply what it is: neither one nor many, neither universal nor particular. In that respect, it is compatible with each of these descriptions. With an individual, it is particular; with a universal, it is universal; with one, it is one; with many, it is many. The universal humanity shared by many individuals exists only in the intellect. As one form in one intellect, such as Zayd’s intellect, it is an individual form. As it relates to each of the individuals, it is universal. To say that it relates to them means that the nature grasped by this form could occur in many people: if it were present in the matter of any one of them, it would yield that very person; and whichever person an intelligent observer first encountered, the same form could be grasped from them. This is what it means for the form to be shared.[^V03-694]

Its abstraction means that this nature has been drawn from the external material features of individuals, even though, in another respect, it is surrounded by mental features that make it particular. In one respect, it is used to understand something else; in another, it is itself what the mind considers. We, however, see no conflict between an intellectual form being particular in its own mode of existence and being universal or shared among many.[^V03-695] As we have explained, an intellectual form does not inhere in the mind the way an accident inheres in its subject, becoming particular through the mind’s own particularity or the features surrounding the soul.

As long as the soul is confined to these psychic conditions, it cannot become an intellect in act, and its object of thought cannot become intelligible in act. While the soul exists in its natural or psychic mode, it has only the potential to be intellect and intelligible.[^V03-696] When it sheds that mode and enters a new one, its existence and individuality become intellectual and universal.
