The third is the world of sensory souls, the lower spiritual realm, and all the images that are actually perceived through the senses and their organs. These, too, belong to the lower spiritual realm. As long as they remain at this level, their existence is incomplete. They rise beyond it and become free of matter as they follow the human soul's ascent into the world of immaterial images.

The fourth is the world of bodily matter and the forms that flow through it, constantly changing, passing away, and coming to be. These exist somewhere between possibility and actuality, endurance and decay: their endurance is their decay, and their coming together is their separation. Since the purpose of creation is knowledge, those who know can, in principle, be divided into three kinds.

The first are complete by nature, like the separate intellects. The second are self-sufficient but need to be perfected; they do not need an outside source to complete them. These include the souls of the heavenly spheres, and, by nature, the souls of the prophets. Once perfected, the prophets may belong to the first group. The third are incomplete by nature and need help from outside themselves, such as revealed books and messengers.

God created all these kinds, fulfilling every possibility that reason can conceive. The Qur'an points to them in the verses “By those who line up in ranks, then drive forward, then recite the Reminder,” and “By those who glide swiftly, then race ahead, then manage affairs.” The order in the second passage may run in the reverse direction, from effects to causes. Those who glide may be the heavenly spheres, as in “Each floats in its orbit.” Those who race ahead may be their souls. Those who manage affairs may be their intellects, which belong to the realm of Command and exist through God's command, “Be.” Or the words “manage affairs” may refer to the very command that comes from God.[^V03-962]

We might also say that there are two worlds: the world of separate intellectual and spiritual beings, and the world of luminous and dark bodies. Since the world of separate beings is the world of knowledge and life, God created within it, corresponding to everything in the world of bodies, an intellectual or imaginal form that is its life and the mirror in which it is seen.[^V03-963] The Qur'an alludes to these two worlds when it says, “For whoever fears standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.”[^V03-964]

Plato, the noble philosopher, likewise said that there are two worlds: the world of intellect, which contains intellectual forms, and the world of the senses, which contains sensible images. He called the first the world of Being and the second the world of Becoming. It is also reported that he taught in two ways: one through discipline and direct insight into intellectual truths, the other through teaching and learning by reasoning. The first world's “Being” means that it does not appear to the outer senses, just as the “Becoming” of imaginal forms means that they appear to the inner senses. The intellectual world is the source, foundation, cause, and goal of all other existence. We do not see it because it is too fully present, and the distractions of matter veil it from us. The terms may also point to that world's unity and simplicity, in contrast to the many separate individuals in this world.[^V03-965]

The luminous Platonic forms are substances in themselves and in their existence. They are the source of the substances and essences in this world, and the realities of the material things we sense. The proof that supports these forms—and indeed all suspended images—is different from the proof we gave earlier for Platonic forms. It begins from the fact that something sensible exists in the world, such as a human being with its matter and particular features. This is the natural human being. We have also established that a human being exists in imagination with a particular size, shape, and character, even though its matter is not present outside the mind.

The intellect can also understand a human being with all its substance, parts, shapes, and qualities, both essential and incidental. But it understands these in a universal way that can apply to many individuals of the same kind. To understand a thing, the intellect does not have to strip away every feature except its essence.[^V03-966][^V03-967] It must strip away its spatial, bodily way of existing, the way that requires it to occupy a direction in the material world.

So the human being exists in nature as a material thing, though in that mode it is neither understood by intellect nor sensed as a mental image; it exists in the shared inner sense and imagination, where it can be sensed; and it exists in the intellect, where it is actually understood. We have shown by decisive proof that the existence of a sensible thing, precisely as sensible, is the very existence of a perceiver, and that the actual existence of an intelligible thing is the existence of an intellectual substance. The knower and the known become one in existence. Since the knower is an immaterial substance, the thing known is also immaterial.

The sensible forms that exist in imagination are likewise the very power of imagination, which must be a substance. What exists as one with a substance must itself be a substance. So the human being has an essential image that exists on its own in the world of images, and an intellectual form that exists on its own in the world of intellects. The same applies to every natural thing, each of which has three modes of existence: intellectual, imaginal, and material.[^V03-968]

There can be only one intellectual form of each kind, because the kind has one defining nature. It can multiply only through matter or through outside, accidental causes. But the other two kinds of existence may have many individuals of one kind: natural forms multiply through the changes of matter, while images multiply through the soul's active power. If one human form is stripped of material existence and imaginal appearance, and reaches the intellectual realm, then another human form of the same kind that reaches that realm does not add a second intellectual existence. It is the same existence and the same effect, as are all the forms of the same kind, whether they arrive earlier or later. Even a thousand images of one kind would be one there.

This proof shows that every natural kind, whether it has countless individuals or only one, has an intellectual form that exists in its own right in the Divine intellectual realm. This is Plato's view of the Divine Forms. I doubt that anyone over all these centuries, apart from Plato and perhaps one of his followers, has fully grasped his purpose through proof. Only a single humble and obscure seeker seems to have reached it.

#### Closing discussion — Terms with similar meanings

The following terms are close in meaning, but they are not all interchangeable.

**Perception** means reaching or attaining. When the intellect reaches and grasps the nature of something intelligible, that is perception in the sense used here. This matches the word's ordinary meaning.[^V03-969] Bodily contact, by contrast, is not true meeting; bodies touch only at their surfaces. Some mystics call this world the realm beyond separation.

**Awareness** is perception without firm certainty. It is the first, still unsteady stage at which knowledge reaches the intellect. This is why we do not speak of God as “being aware” of something.

**Conception** is when the intellect has fully grasped a meaning. The word comes from “form.” In ordinary speech, a form is the shape of a body; philosophers use it for several things that share one meaning: what makes a thing actually what it is. In the case of knowledge, the forms of things are their realities and essences.

**Retention** is the state in which forms received by the intellect have become firmly established, so that if they fade from awareness the intellect can bring them back. Retention stands to perception as acting stands to receiving. It may reflect either two different powers or two levels of one power; the second account is more fitting, since the soul's powers and qualities return to one reality.

Some say that God's knowledge cannot be called retention because retention suggests something became firm after being weak, or because we need to retain only what might be lost. The author rejects this. The Qur'an itself speaks of God's keeping the heavens and earth and of His preserving the Reminder.

God's knowledge is His power, and the whole world is the form of His perfect knowledge. His essence, which is His knowledge, preserves all things. His detailed knowledge preserves itself because it is active, not something passively received. The claim that retention implies a change from weakness to firmness is not established. Nor does the possibility of a thing's loss prevent God's detailed knowledge, preserved in the Highest Pen and the Preserved Tablet, from being called retention.

**Remembering** begins when an image has disappeared from the intellect and the mind tries to bring it back. Philosophers have said that this requires an intellectual storehouse containing all intelligible forms. They disagree about whether this storehouse is separate from the human soul or connected to it in an intellectual way but hidden from it—either because the soul is occupied with the senses or because its intellect has not yet moved from potential to actual.

Some sharp thinkers, including Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, were troubled by remembering. If the lost image is already known, it is present, and what is present cannot be acquired again. If it is not known, it cannot be brought back, because one cannot seek something one cannot picture. Yet we know that we can look for and recover a memory.

I say that these thinkers were puzzled because they failed to understand existence, the clearest of all things. Al-Razi treated it as an idea formed by the mind. He did not see that one thing can exist in different ways, some fuller than others, or that knowledge itself is a kind of existence, not merely a relation. I admit that the puzzle is harder to solve on our own account, where intellectual understanding occurs as the soul becomes one with the Active Intellect, the form of all things.[^V03-970]

But it can be solved. The soul has several levels: sensation, imagination, and intellect. Souls differ in strength and completeness. The strongest can be present to one level without losing another. Others are less complete, and some are so limited that only sensation is present to them, with only a faint trace of imagination.

When a soul of intermediate strength connects with the intellectual realm, it leaves the sensory level and directs the body through some of its natural powers. When it returns to the senses, it is no longer present at its intellectual level, but a faint trace remains, like a weak image.[^V03-971] With this trace, and with its still-active ability to recover what it has known, the soul can remember the reality of its own being and the fullness of its intellectual nature.

If the image to be recovered had never been pictured in any way, nor had the soul gained even a close readiness to picture it, then it could not be remembered. But that is not the case at issue. If the soul has pictured it in imagination and acquired the ability to return to its storehouse, then it can remember it. Some have made this question difficult because they assumed that no conception can ever be acquired, whether for the first time through thought or later through memory. We have already answered that mistaken argument.

When a vanished image returns and becomes present again, that is also called memory. If the perception was never preceded by disappearance, it is not called memory. Al-Razi returns to his claim that this problem cannot be solved: if you cannot fully understand memory, though it is one of your own powers and you know you can remember, how can you fully understand what you remember, which seems even farther from you? I reply that God is closer to us than anything else, at the very root of our being. We were created and guided so that we might know Him, reach His generosity, behold His presence, and witness His beauty and majesty. The prophets were sent and the books revealed for this purpose, not to leave people lost and confused.

**Recognition** has been explained in several ways. Some say it is knowledge of particulars, while knowledge is of universals.[^V03-972] Others say recognition is conception, while knowledge is assent or judgment.[^V03-973] Those who hold the second view consider recognition a higher degree of knowledge. They say that it is easy to assent to the fact that the things we sense depend on a Necessary Being,[^V03-974] but beyond human power to picture the reality of the Necessary Being.[^V03-975] On this account, everyone who recognizes knows, but not everyone who knows has reached recognition. A person is called a true knower only after traveling deeply through knowledge, from its starting points to its ends, as far as human ability allows.

Others say that recognition occurs when we perceive something, retain its trace in ourselves, then perceive it again and know that it is what we perceived before.[^V03-976] Some people believe that spirits existed from eternity; others say they came before bodies.[^V03-977] They identify them with the primordial particles drawn from Adam, who acknowledged God's divinity and lordship.[^V03-978] They say that the darkness of bodily life made the spirits forget their Lord. Once freed from the body's darkness, they recognize the One they had known before, and this is why such perception is called recognition.

**Understanding** is grasping a meaning from someone's words. **Making something understood** is conveying a meaning through words to a listener. **Grasping the point of someone's speech** is understanding what the speaker intends. The Qur'an says of some people that they scarcely understand a word. The unbelieving Quraysh, consumed by doubts and desires, could not grasp the truths contained in the Qur'an.[^V03-979] That is why God speaks of their failure to understand the purpose for which the Book was revealed.

**Intellect** has many meanings. In ordinary speech it is the ability to recognize what is useful or harmful, and to distinguish good actions from bad. Theologians use it to mean what reason affirms or denies. Philosophers use it in works on proof,[^V03-980] in ethics as practical reason, in discussions of the rational soul and its levels, and in divine science and metaphysics. Some of these meanings have already been explained.

**Wisdom** also has several meanings. It can refer to any sound knowledge or good action, though it is more often used for practical knowledge than theoretical knowledge.[^V03-981] It can also mean doing something well or skillfully. God's wisdom is creating what benefits people and looking after their interests, now and in the future. The same can be said of human wisdom.

Some define wisdom as knowing things. This suggests that knowledge of particulars, which continually change, is not itself a perfection; knowledge of realities and essences is lasting and protected from change. The Qur'an calls this the Mother of the Book. Others define wisdom as doing what will have a good outcome, or as following the Creator's example in governing our lives as far as human ability allows.[^V03-982]

The philosophers say wisdom is becoming like God in knowledge and action, as far as human beings can. A person should work to keep knowledge free of ignorance, action free of injustice, generosity free of both stinginess and waste, desire free of both excess and weakness, anger free of rashness and cowardice, patience free of laziness and reckless boldness, modesty free of shamelessness and withdrawal, and love free of both excess and neglect. In short, a person should stay on God's path, fulfilling both God's rights and the rights of creation.

**Reasoned knowledge** is knowledge reached by a method: setting out premises and thinking them through. The word originally referred to tracking game, and for that reason some say it cannot be applied to God, who does not reason by thought or method.

**The mind** is the soul's ability to acquire knowledge it does not yet have. Mental existence is not the same as the existence of the mind itself.[^V03-983] The mind exists in the outside world; what exists in it as a likeness of something outside is said to have mental existence. That means it exists in the mind without producing the effects it would have outside.[^V03-984]

God created the human spirit with no knowledge already present in it, as the Qur'an says: “God brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing.” But He created it for knowledge and worship: “I did not create jinn and human beings except to worship Me.” If the human spirit had not been created to know the realities of things, it would have begun with one of them already present in act, rather than being empty of all of them—just as prime matter, created to receive all natural forms, begins as pure potentiality with no bodily form.

The human spirit, too, begins as pure potentiality, without intelligible forms. Yet it is made to know all realities and connect with them. Knowing God, His realm, and His signs is the goal; worship is the way to draw near to Him and travel toward Him. Worship is also made possible by knowledge and results from it, as in the verse “Establish prayer in remembrance of Me.” Knowledge is at once the beginning and the end, the starting point and the goal. The soul must therefore be able to acquire these forms of knowledge; that readiness is what we call the mind.[^V03-985]

**Thought** is the soul's movement from ideas and judgments already present in it toward what it does not yet know. There is no reason to limit thought to judgments, as some have done. One of Avicenna's books compares thinking to prayer: both are ways of seeking a gift from God. When the rational power longs for an intellectual form, it naturally turns toward the Giver. If the form comes through direct insight, no further work is needed. Otherwise, the soul turns to other powers that prepare it to receive the form by bringing it into likeness with what is present in the world of intellectual forms. In this way, it may reach through effort what it did not reach through direct insight, as in the verse, “He taught you what you did not know.”

**Direct insight** is the sudden finding of a middle point that connects the two sides of something unknown. Without that middle point, thought cannot complete a proof or give a definition. The soul in its ignorance is like someone in deep darkness: it needs a guide or a window to light the next step. That window is the middle point, found all at once. The soul's readiness to find such a point directly is called insight.

**Intelligence** is the strength and completeness of this direct insight. At its highest it is the sacred power described in the Qur'an: “Its oil would almost shine, even if no fire touched it.” The word also suggests pressing forward and quickly recognizing what is true.

**Alertness** is noticing something someone intended to point out. The word is often used for solving riddles and puzzles. **A thought that comes to mind** is the soul's movement toward a proof. Strictly speaking, it is the idea that comes to mind, but the soul is called the thinker because it is the place where the idea appears.

**Estimation** can mean a belief that is more likely false than true. It can also mean judging particular, non-sensible things about particular bodies, as when a young lamb judges its mother to be a friend and a wolf to be an enemy. The word also names the power that makes such judgments. In our view, this estimating power is not a substance separate from intellect and imagination.[^V03-986] It is the intellect directed toward an imagined or sensed form. Its judgments are intelligible meanings attached to particular sensible or imagined things. When the soul turns to itself, it becomes intellect free of estimation and of any relation to bodies; when imagined meanings are corrected and their attachments removed, they become pure intelligibles. Estimation is simply the intellect's way of turning toward and being affected by a body, and an estimated thing is an intelligible meaning attached to particular matter.

**Opinion** is a belief that is more likely true than false. It has degrees of strength. At the strongest end it may be called knowledge; in turn, knowledge may sometimes be called opinion.[^V03-987] This is how interpreters understand the Qur'anic phrase “they are certain that they will meet their Lord.” They offer two explanations. First, the knowledge of most people in this life is like opinion when compared with the knowledge of people in the next life. Second, true knowledge in this life is reached only by prophets and the truthful, who are described as those “who believe in God and His Messenger and then do not doubt.”

**Knowledge of certainty, vision of certainty, and truth of certainty** are three levels. The first is assent to general truths established by proof, like a blind person's knowledge that the sun exists. The second is seeing the sun with inner sight, as one sees it with the eyes. The third is when the soul becomes one with the separate intellect, which contains all intelligible forms. There is no sensory example for this, because two things cannot become one in bodily existence.

**Immediate knowledge** is the knowledge a soul has from the beginning, shared by all people. **First principles** are also self-evident, but unlike other immediate knowledge, they need no sensation, experience, testimony, or repeated report; they require only an understanding of the terms and their relation.

**Imagination** is an image that remains in the soul after the thing sensed is gone, whether in sleep or waking life. In our view, these images do not exist in the material world and are not imprinted in a bodily power, as philosophers have often claimed of the back part of the brain. Nor are they separate from the soul in an independent imaginal world, as Illuminationist philosophers hold. They exist in the human soul's own world, joined to it and sustained by it for as long as it preserves them. When the soul turns away from them, they disappear; when it recalls them, they appear again.

The power that perceives imagined forms is itself free of this world, its bodies, and its features. It is one level of the soul, between sensation and intellect. Though the soul is one in its essence, it has different levels, each higher than the one below it, and each belongs to its own world.

**Reflection** is knowledge reached after much thought. **Practical intelligence** is the soul's ability to work out what will benefit a person most. This is why the Prophet said: “The wise person is the one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death.” Nothing a person can gain is better than what comes after death. **Experience** is knowledge reached through testing and careful examination.

**Judgment** is turning over premises from which a desired conclusion may follow. The conclusion itself is also sometimes called a judgment. Judgment is to thought as a tool is to a craftsperson. Hence the sayings: “Beware of a hasty opinion,” and “Do not trust an opinion formed in haste.”

**Physiognomy** is drawing conclusions about a person's inner character from outward features. The Qur'an alludes to it when it says, “There are signs for those who can read them,” “You will know them by their mark,” and “You will know them by the tone of their speech.” The word originally referred to a predator snatching its prey; physiognomy is like snatching up knowledge. It has two kinds. One comes to a person as an insight whose cause is unknown. This is a kind of inspiration, even revelation, and is what the Prophet meant when he said that there are people in his community who receive inspired thoughts. He also said, “Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by God's light.” This is called a thought cast into the heart. The other kind is learned: it infers inner character from outward features. Those who know these matters say that in the verse “Is one who stands on clear proof from his Lord, followed by a witness from Him,” the clear proof points to the first kind—the purity of the spirit—while the witness points to the second, reading inner states from outward signs.

This completes Volume Three of the First Book of *The Four Journeys of the Intellect*, in the blessed month of Shawwal, 1384 AH. I ask God to make it beneficial to us and to all who seek knowledge, in this life and the next, through Muhammad, his family, and the righteous, noble, and pure. May He help us bring out the remaining volumes. Praise be to God, first and last.

## Notes

[^V03-1]: Here, the same word is used in distinct senses; there is no one shared feature behind all of them. The power to act and the capacity to be affected have no common feature that defines them both. The same holds for forms that make a thing what it is and qualities a thing can have, as will be explained later. Some powers to act may still share a common class.

[^V03-2]: The Imam gives this account in *Al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya*. It explains how the meanings of power are related, but it may not match how ordinary speakers extend a word from one similar thing to another. The word may first have meant the source of strenuous actions. It was then applied to the source of being affected, when being affected was itself difficult. People may have thought of being affected as a kind of action, and of an effect as coming from a power in its source. The word was later extended to the source of both action and being affected, whether or not either was strenuous: people thought that a stronger effect came from a stronger source, so strong and weak effects seemed to share one kind of source. Then they came to think that every effect is present in its power. Fire, for example, contains heat that it passes on to nearby things. The effect was said to exist in the power in an indistinct, unformed way, and in the act in a distinct, formed way. Finally, *act* came to mean anything that exists in a distinct and definite form, while *power* meant that same thing without distinction or definite form. On this account, power came to mean the possibility of something existing in the source that brings it about.

[^V03-3]: “Quality” here is used as a descriptive term: the feature described may be the subject itself, one of its parts, or something outside it.

[^V03-4]: The point is that a line may be able to form the side of a square, or may not—like a curved line. The square is called something that could potentially come from the line, as when a curved line could form a square's side if straightened. Do not take the author's note on Avicenna's *The Healing* to mean that the line is the potential of the square: there he says that the square is what the line can potentially produce. Here, as in Avicenna's own wording, the square is called the power of the line. This is a separate use of *power*: it does not mean the source of strenuous action, ability, resistance to being affected, or readiness to become something. A square already contains its side in actuality, so the comparison with possibility is only an analogy. The possibility associated with a square is included in its necessary, actual existence, and is present there in a fuller way. That is why the line's actual presence in the square can be called “power” in this geometric sense. Mathematicians also use “in the power of” when one line's square equals the sum of the squares of two other lines. For example, a line 10 units long is in the power of lines 6 and 8 because 10² = 6² + 8². A line does not fit this usage when its square is not equal to the sum of the other two squares. Here, however, the author and Avicenna mean the familiar square figure.

[^V03-5]: This note restarts the classification from a broader point of view. Active power may be wholly dominant over all beings. In that case, it is the First Principle, exalted be His glory, whose power embraces all. Or it may be subject in some way and under God's control. If it is independent of matter both in what it is and in what it does, it belongs among the higher beings that do not depend on matter. If it is not, then it may produce one action, and so on.

[^V03-6]: The wording here is not fully clear. At first it seems to refer to the power to act, but its ending seems to refer to the capacity to be affected, as the phrase “the actual and the possible would be together” suggests. The point holds either way. A particular action comes from outside causes; it does not come from the power alone. Power and action also come in degrees. If this is power to act, it is at a stronger level than the action it produces. If it is the capacity to be affected, the relation is reversed: the actual change is stronger than the capacity to receive it. The note promises to explain this further.

[^V03-7]: You might object that this argument does not work. It discusses the power to act, not the capacity to be affected, and there is no problem with the power to act existing at the same time as the result it produces. The real problem would be for a thing's readiness to remain once what it was ready for had become actual. The reply is that if the power to act on one particular individual remained after that individual came into being, then, on the recipient's side, the capacity to be affected would remain alongside the actual result. The same thing would then be both still only possible and already actual, which is impossible. This confirms the point: power directed at one particular individual ends when that individual exists, while power directed at an unspecified individual of the same kind remains.

[^V03-8]: Even more surprising, many later writers, including al-Fakhrī, accepted this explanation and tried to reconcile the two views. They said that those who required power to be present with the action meant a power with all the conditions needed to produce the effect; those who said power came before the action meant a power still missing some of those conditions. The commentator says this confuses two meanings. An animal's ability is a power that comes with the possibility of acting or not acting. That possibility cannot exist at the same time as its full realization. A power with every condition in place is power in another sense.

[^V03-9]: As Chapter 1 explained, much of the earlier discussion comes from the Imam's *Al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya*. The thinkers meant that power accompanies an action when power means that the action can proceed. But the Imam explained their claim in terms of the complete power to cause the action: the acting cause together with all the other things a complete cause needs. His wording shows this. He therefore shifts between two meanings of power.

[^V03-10]: The conditional “if He wills, He acts” can be made up of two necessary statements. God is necessary in Himself and in every respect, both in what He is and in what He does. These two meanings of power do not imply each other, contrary to what some theologians say. The possibility of acting or not acting does not apply to God's power. But the statement “if He wills, He acts” does. A conditional statement does not always mean that the outcome could be otherwise. It can be true when both parts are necessary, or even when both are impossible.

[^V03-11]: An agent may have no motive at all, like someone who acts at random, according to theologians. Philosophers say that even such a person has some aim. Or an agent may have no added motive, which is the usual meaning of “without a motive.” This is how philosophers describe the Necessary Being.

[^V03-12]: The difference is that a person acting at random acts from an arbitrary will, while someone acting from a motive acts from a considered will. In either case, the will and motive may be part of the agent's own nature or something added to it.

[^V03-13]: In our earlier discussion of cause and effect, we questioned whether there is really a separate kind of agent whose action comes from its knowledge. It may instead belong with the kind whose own self-knowledge is enough to bring about its action. But an agent whose action is a self-disclosure, mentioned later in the discussion of God, may be a separate kind.

[^V03-14]: Here the author criticizes the view held by Aristotle’s followers that God's knowledge consists of forms or images of things, which then cause them to appear. If God is the Light of Lights, and light is what makes things visible, the true light does not need images to know things. Its light itself reveals them and reaches into their depths.

[^V03-15]: This points to another kind of agent: one whose action is a self-disclosure. Earlier notes explain this kind.

[^V03-16]: Our earlier discussion of cause and effect gave a fuller account and showed that the division into “free” and “compelled” is a familiar way of speaking, not a division into two completely separate kinds. The author's use of “free” and “compelled” here depends on what those words mean. An action is free in the fullest sense when it comes from an agent that knows what it is doing and can cause it on its own. It is compelled in this sense when the agent does not know what it is doing, or knows but cannot act on its own. This differs from the other meaning of “free”: that an agent can act if it wills and refrain if it does not. The author calls all created agents subject to God, whether they choose or are forced, because God alone acts entirely on His own. Created agents can be both free and dependent only in the first sense of these words. In the second sense, freedom and compulsion are opposites.

[^V03-17]: Avicenna says that powers linked to reason and imagination can grasp opposite things: one power can know what is human and what is not human, and imagine pleasure and pain. The author changes Avicenna's line of argument because Avicenna treats perception as something received, while he treats it as an activity. He says that sensing and imagining bring their objects about, and that understanding is the mind's own activity. Philosophers also speak of a “simple intellect”: a settled kind of knowledge already present in an intellect fully at work, which does not need to learn anything new.

[^V03-18]: The phrase should be “source of change,” not “source of motion.” This wider wording includes coming into being and passing away, which these philosophers consider instantaneous.

[^V03-19]: We have already explained that causes work within nature, between nature and what lies beyond it, and among higher things. Those who study nature call nature the cause of change in the natural world; those who study existence more broadly use “source of existence” in a wider sense. So Mulla Sadra's claim that God is most deserving of the name “agent” does not mean that nature cannot cause change or that other causes cannot bring particular things into being.

[^V03-20]: God gives existence to matter and to its readiness; He brings them out of nonexistence. A natural cause, by contrast, only changes matter after God has brought it into being and after it is ready. Once it is ready, its forms come from the world beyond matter, from God, who gives forms. This is one meaning of the teaching of “a middle way between two extremes” about God's power over all things: God is the cause of everything because He gives existence without limit. Other things are causes as sources of movement and change, not as sources of existence. Even motion itself lies between pure possibility and complete actuality.

[^V03-21]: The actions and words used in prayer can lead to calm and trust in God, or to worshipping other things alongside Him. Neither outcome is a bodily movement. The note shows three differences between a skill learned through practice and action that comes from habit: skill uses outside materials and tools; the person aims to gain the skill, while a habit may arise as a side effect; and the learned skill gives shape to the actions it produces, which are of the same kind as the skill. Habit differs in all three ways.

[^V03-22]: This does not mean that action from habit and action from skill are the same thing, or that there are no real differences between them. Both come from a lasting quality of the soul; they differ in what they aim at and how they begin.

[^V03-23]: The meaning of chance has already been explained. The author may have written these and similar passages before he put the discussion in its present order. He first planned to discuss power and action before cause and effect, but arranged them the other way around in the final version.

[^V03-24]: The author made this point just before and repeats it here to address two familiar claims based on the idea that a thing needs a cause because it began to exist. That starting idea has no good basis. The two claims are that an effect must have been nonexistent for some time, and that it no longer needs its cause once it exists. These claims make sense only for actions that unfold over time, such as motion, time, or nature working through bodies. Such an action exists as a sequence of parts. Each part comes after a period when it did not exist, and each part can itself be divided further. It does not need a cause to continue, because it does not last as a single thing. Even so, while natural powers and processes bring it about, it is also an act of God, who encompasses all.

[^V03-25]: By nonexistence, the theologians mean that something did not exist at an earlier time. If they meant nonexistence in a broader sense, an eternal action could still exist. This is why they also claimed that time is only imagined or comes from God's own being. They wanted to avoid two problems: time itself would count as an eternal action, or every time would need an earlier time without end. But if time is only imagined, the whole discussion falls apart and their condition makes no sense. If time comes from God's own being, then God Himself would have to change. They may reply that something can come from a source and still differ from it. But that would let ideas differ from the real things they describe, so our ideas would not need to match reality.

[^V03-26]: This also shows that the soul itself is not the body's temperament.

[^V03-27]: “In the broadest sense” includes transition from nonexistence to existence and from possibility to necessity. It also includes both sudden and gradual transitions from potentiality to actuality. One might object that coming from nonexistence to existence, as in the case of intellects, is motion only figuratively, and that a sudden transition, as in coming to be or passing away, requires a thing to belong to a particular natural kind. The reply is that even if such a transition is called motion figuratively, and coming to be or passing away requires a natural kind because it belongs to a natural body, substantial motion—the flow of nature itself—is not an attribute of a body but one of its principles. Since nature is flowing existence, it is prior to the body. Its natural kind follows from bodyhood itself, not from a later classification.

[^V03-28]: “In the broadest sense” is explained below as any transition from potentiality to actuality, sudden or gradual, and the lack of such a transition in something that can undergo one. The author says these apply to things before they are classified as natural or mathematical kinds. But such transitions occur only in things made up of potentiality and actuality, either in themselves or through a subject: bodily substances. That is already a natural classification. Moreover, many of the rules discussed in this and the following stages apply only to motion in the narrower sense, as a feature of natural bodies. Broadening the word to include coming to be, passing away, and other changes does not help. It is better to divide existing things into stable and flowing things, alongside the division into actual and potential. One can then discuss features shared by motion and existing things more generally.

[^V03-29]: That is, the reasoning and learning that depend on basic concepts. A concept is not acquired through a judgment; definitions and proofs share basic concepts.

[^V03-30]: The author points out that our direct awareness that something exists, and our grasp of simple affirmative statements, help us form these ideas immediately. Their precise definitions may still require reasoning. The question here is whether we grasp their nature directly, not whether we immediately know that they exist.

[^V03-31]: Motion is a kind of waiting and striving. Any part of motion is likewise waiting and striving: it is neither pure actuality nor pure potentiality, nor is it complete all at once like a square when the square shape is attained.

[^V03-32]: “With” here means that the potentiality is bound up with actuality. Motion lies between pure potentiality and complete actuality. It does not mean the pure potentiality that precedes every actuality; otherwise, every event preceded by potentiality would count as motion, even if the potentiality were not itself actual in any way.

[^V03-33]: A completion removes some lack. Motion removes a particular potentiality, so it completes a thing only in the respect in which it was potential. It does not complete the body simply as a body. The body’s first completion as a body is its specific form. It is mistaken to say that this definition is harder to understand than motion itself. We may know that something has come to be before we understand its nature; what is hard to grasp is that its coming-to-be is continuous, from one stable state to another, without a pause.

[^V03-34]: The note suggests that “otherness” may not have been intended as a strict definition, but as a change of wording, like explaining a natural kind as a universal concept or as a particular determination. If the definition may use a broader term, “striving” or “desire” would be more fitting than “otherness.” Out of respect for his teachers, however, Pythagoras may have chosen the latter. Another possible reading is that motion is what makes the natural world different from the divine realm: the latter has no waiting or change. Motion is what makes these two domains distinct.

[^V03-35]: The two expressions may have had a special technical sense among those philosophers, referring to continuous change rather than their ordinary or general meanings.

[^V03-36]: Motion itself is a source of many apparent contradictions, like a difficult passage of scripture. If we say it exists, we are right; if we say it does not, we are also right, because it is potentiality and potentiality is not a thing, even though it is actual in one respect. If we call motion one, we are right, because its continuous unity makes it one thing. If we call it many, we are right, because it can be divided without limit. It is both changing and, in the sense of being between its endpoints, stable.

[^V03-37]: This challenges the claim that motion is unlimited. It is one continuous, particular thing. It is unlimited only in the imagined divisions of its magnitude, which is time or something that matches time. Straight-line motion is unlimited only in thought.

[^V03-38]: I say: granted that motion is change, it is not the same as otherness or difference.

[^V03-39]: “Nature” here means the source of a thing’s own motion and rest. The word can also mean a general essence.

[^V03-40]: Gradual change occurs in the external world even in motion understood as “being between,” as the phrase “even in the imagination” suggests. Being at one point in the middle is simple. If a distance were made of indivisible points, passing through each one would not be gradual. But measured against the continuous boundaries of the distance, the body’s being between points is gradual. Though simple, it flows like a moving instant.

[^V03-41]: This is essential to the answer: motion can be said to exist, but its existence is intertwined with nonexistence, because it has no indivisible part. Matter is actual only as potentiality; the two are intertwined there too.

[^V03-42]: Instability belongs to the meanings of these three categories—when, action, and being acted on—quite apart from whether they exist.

[^V03-43]: “Immaterial souls” means souls considered apart from the body. Their stable states include universal acts of will and intellectual ideas in themselves. These are not motions. If thought is called motion, as when people speak of reasoning from a question to first principles and back to a conclusion, then “motion” is being used broadly for transition. Imaginative souls also undergo changes in particular acts of will and perception. These changes are tied to the body, since such souls depend strongly on it; Avicenna holds that particular powers are embedded in the subtle bodily spirit.

[^V03-44]: Motion is also a completion and actuality, while leaving a state is removal or absence. The idea of continuous gradual change may be understood in “passing” or “leaving a state.” The phrase may also derive from “engaging in” or “practising,” in which case the objection to the definition would not apply.

[^V03-45]: “Reaching” means reaching essentially, not merely encountering things that happen to lie along the way. The moving thing is left unspecified so that the definition includes both bodies and matter, as in substantial motion, as well as motion in quantity. “Gradual” is already implied by calling the boundaries potential: each boundary is a state of waiting that leads to another. “Continuously” is not redundant. A movement could proceed through separate intervals divided by rests; both the potential boundaries and their continuity are needed. This definition makes continuous gradual change clearer than the alternatives.

[^V03-46]: Imagining boundaries, or saying that a body lies between the starting point and the destination, is only a way of indicating the particular state involved in motion. But introducing those boundaries also allows us to divide motion into parts. Divisibility belongs to motion as a continuous course, not to the simple state of being between its endpoints.

[^V03-47]: Existing things fall into two groups: things whose own existence is what we point to, and things that exist because something real gives the mind grounds to derive them. Relations and motion as a continuous whole belong to the second group. If a relation existed in itself, it would have to be an accident, like whiteness, and itself have a relation of inherence to its subject. That would lead to an endless chain. Nor is it merely imaginary, since it exists as long as its real basis exists.

[^V03-48]: Time, like motion, has two senses. Time that matches motion as a continuous whole exists only in the mind. Time that matches motion as “being between” is the flowing instant, and exists along with that motion. Avicenna’s claim that time exists outside the mind refers to the second sense. The past and future do not exist, whether they are long stretches or what we ordinarily call the present. Only the flowing state and the flowing instant—the core of time—exist. Time as the measure of a continuous whole exists through its real basis, which lets us divide it into hours and days. What we sense and imagine is often confused with what exists outside us.

[^V03-49]: On this account, motion can be considered as arising all at once: this is motion as “being between.” Or it can be considered as arising gradually: this is motion as a continuous whole. In the second case, if its gradual arising and passing away are both considered, it exists outside the mind; if its continuing existence is considered as complete all at once, it exists only in the mind.

[^V03-50]: There is no contradiction. Time as the flowing instant exists, so motion as “being between,” which it contains, also exists. Time as the measure of the continuous whole and motion as a continuous whole exist only through their real basis.

[^V03-51]: The objection accepts that “being between” is vague and tries to offset that vagueness with particular features. One could say these pull in opposite directions and cancel out. Better to say that the vagueness is a mistake caused by confusing what is in the mind with what exists outside it. Universality belongs to the general idea in the mind. What exists outside the mind is an expansive, particular motion, not a universal concept or a randomly chosen instance. It is like the “some form” that makes matter receptive to a bodily form: what is meant is not the general idea or a single instance, but a broad reality that applies to a continuous series of particular forms.

[^V03-52]: For these philosophers, motion is not made particular by the unity of one specific mover. It remains one even when several things successively draw or push it along, as with motion in place, or several sources of heat, as with change in quality.

[^V03-53]: Strictly speaking, the answer accepts a connection between what exists and what does not exist—but this kind of nonexistence is not sheer nothingness. Motion is actual in one respect: its subject is at the starting point. In another respect, the continuous passage toward the destination is still potential, because motion is always passing away. In these weak kinds of existence, it is possible for actuality and this kind of nonexistence to be connected. The same holds for time, which measures motion.

[^V03-54]: A thing’s state can be divided into parts, some actual in relation to others and still potential in relation to what comes later. If we imagine a quality divided into three parts, for instance, the second is actual relative to the first and potential relative to the third. Further division does not change this. The parts exist only potentially, so existence is intertwined with nonexistence, actuality with potentiality, and coming to be with passing away. Each part requires the passing away of another; it is itself the passing away of what came before. The actuality of a later part begins only when the potentiality for it gives way.

[^V03-55]: Calling motion an “action” seems to prepare for the first argument below: motion is an action in relation to its mover and something undergone in relation to what is moved. If mover and moved were the same, acting and being acted on would be one category, which is impossible. But it is not clear that this distinction follows from the definition of motion already given. Motion is not itself in one of the categories, and neither are moving and being moved, which are ways of relating to motion. This point is sound for heating and being heated, which are action and undergoing, while heat belongs to the category of quality.

[^V03-56]: Motion is made up of potentiality intertwined with actuality, just as prime matter is pure potentiality and is what makes a body a substance that is only potentially actual.

[^V03-57]: Manuscripts differ here. Some read “the mover,” and in the example “the heater,” where the intended reading is “the moving thing” and “the thing being heated.” That version is poor in meaning: the point is that a moving thing needs a mover, not that a mover must itself have something moved by it. The grammar also supports the standard reading. In the next clause, the pronoun refers to what is being heated, not the heater.

[^V03-58]: Nature contains, in an integrated way, the effects that gradually appear in matter. The nature of fire, for example, contains the different instances of heat that flow from it. Likewise, the rational soul’s active power gathers the different kinds of knowledge and will that come from it. In its own self-subsisting existence, the soul is knowledge and will.

[^V03-59]: In their account, substance is stable.

[^V03-60]: In their account, the mover is not itself subject to the possibility of motion. Some copies read “in itself,” meaning its essence, which is possible; on that reading, “not potential” means it is not like an essence or prime matter. The claim that motion is not a completion of what is already actual explains the previous point.

[^V03-61]: This point is clear if we accept that a direct mover is not actual in motion itself, as do those who deny substantial motion. But for us, natures flow and change. Here “motion” means the accidental motion in the four categories; “something other than motion” means nature, and “by necessity” means that this motion follows from it.

[^V03-62]: If each motion were caused by another motion in an accidental category, the chain would have to end in motion belonging to something substantial. A merely conceptual change, such as growing nearer to a natural place, is not enough. The details will follow.

[^V03-63]: It has also been established that motion always lies between two endpoints: one free from the potentiality and possibility involved in motion, the other potential in relation to all the actual states along the way. It has also been established that a body whose substance moves is made of matter and form, joined as one.

[^V03-64]: Prime matter also has goodness in itself, since it exists, and everything that exists is either purely good or has more good than evil. The potentiality for existence is also a kind of existence, and a shadow is a kind of light when compared with darkness. The author explicitly distinguishes matter from absolute nonexistence. The point is clearer still if matter and form are understood as joined together.

[^V03-65]: The argument is that the subject of motion disappears. Motion is defined as a completion that follows potentiality. If a body moved itself, and what belongs to it by nature could never be absent from it, there would be no prior potentiality for motion in it. Motion would be actual in the body, even though motion is a first completion and must raise some potentiality.

[^V03-66]: There is another possibility: bodily form may mean a substance that can receive dimensions. On that meaning, it is the feature that divides substance into kinds and makes bodyhood what it is. It is still one and the same nature, and bodyhood is one kind.

[^V03-67]: “Self-evident” does not mean that the claim needs no explanation for anyone. The comparison with self-evident truths is not inconsistent with the philosophers proving it elsewhere. Some minds need a reminder; the point itself takes reasoning to establish. They mean by bodyhood a thing that can receive three dimensions—three lines crossing at right angles. What makes it receptive is extension. If that feature differed by kind, the difference would have to be between heavenly, elemental, fiery, or airy bodies, but such differences do not explain what makes all of them receptive to dimensions. A difference in the essence of what receives them is also impossible if they all share that capacity. No feature other than extension—even a single indivisible substance or a collection of them—can explain that capacity. As Avicenna says, a body is continuous by its very nature; if it were divided, it would not cease to be able to receive dimensions. Al-Razi’s objection is therefore unsound.

[^V03-68]: The same answer applies to the fifth and sixth arguments. The same point also applies to some arguments against treating different kinds of matter as sources of different motions.

[^V03-69]: That is, they differ as heavenly bodies or as bodies made of the elements, and elemental bodies differ from one another accordingly. The same applies to the claim that bodies have different natures.

[^V03-70]: “A feature present in bodyhood” could mean nature, or some other feature.

[^V03-71]: The objection treats the general kind in a mental combination and matter—the extended prime matter—in a physical compound as if each existed independently, with form added later. It then asks what makes the body acquire its special effects, whether bodyhood or something else. But the general kind and matter are not independent things in the external world that receive their form or special effects afterward. Form and the feature that makes a kind particular are what make the general kind and matter actual. The former are indeterminate; form and species make them determinate. Bodyhood is a general feature of particular natures, not the other way around. See the discussion of how a defining feature makes a general kind a particular kind.

[^V03-72]: Once al-Razi grants that one thing cannot be both agent and recipient, his claim that essences produce and receive their necessary features contradicts that admission. One might interpret his “strongest objection” as a counterargument rather than an objection from within his own argument, and read “disproves” in the looser sense of “challenges.” Even then, the problem remains.

[^V03-73]: “By itself” is the opposite of “incidentally.” Avicenna’s discussion in the last part of *The Healing* divides movers into those that move incidentally and those that move in themselves. A mover may move incidentally in itself—for example, any power in a body moves along with the body—or incidentally through something else, as wind moves a person sitting in a boat when it moves the boat. A mover that acts in itself may act directly, or through one or more intermediaries. An intermediary connected to the mover, such as a hand, is called an instrument; one separate from it, such as an axe, is called a tool. Some authors do not distinguish these terms.

[^V03-74]: This proof is based on Avicenna’s argument from the middle term and the endpoints, which he uses to show that a causal chain cannot continue without end. It establishes that motions must ultimately come from an intellective mover that does not itself move by its own nature.

[^V03-75]: The alternatives include the three intellectual powers of the theoretical mind, the acquired intellect, and the particular powers of the animal soul. If the separate being's power is a particular power that perceives, it still does not explain why it affects this body rather than another; its relation to all bodies would be the same. There is another possibility: the separate being acts by its own nature. The author does not discuss it here, perhaps because it is plainly unable to act directly on a particular body. The phrase “particular motions” points to this: how could a separate being directly bring about a specific motion if its relation to all bodies were equal?

[^V03-76]: The argument is adapted from Avicenna, with a small change in how it is stated.

[^V03-77]: One might object that denying that a thing is impossible or already necessary gives us only its possibility in itself. Its nature could carry this possibility, so matter would not be needed. The reply is that matter is needed because this thing comes after another thing in time, not merely because it is neither impossible nor necessary. A nature does not exist earlier in time than the thing itself.

[^V03-78]: Otherwise, the thing would have to come before itself. An agent's ability to bring something about depends on the possibility of its effect, since no one can bring about what is impossible. This argument tries to avoid the need for prior matter by saying that the effect only needs an agent, not a subject. The reply is that possibility belongs to the thing affected, while ability belongs to the agent. It is like defining God's ability by saying that He can do what is possible: the possibility is on the side of what is made, not a feature that defines the agent.

[^V03-79]: Unlike possibility in itself, which consists of two negations and is purely negative, readiness is a real feature of a subject. It is not an abstract idea of a thing's nature.

[^V03-80]: Readiness can be stronger or weaker as a possible thing comes closer to or farther from being actual. Such degrees belong to realities outside the mind, not to abstract ideas.

[^V03-81]: “What is ready” is the particular thing it is ready to become. In this sense, readiness is a possibility for a specific result. Considered as a feature of the matter or subject itself, it is called a disposition or capacity, rather than possibility.

[^V03-82]: “Existence in general” means existence as a simple fact, as in “something exists.” “Limited existence” means existence with a feature, as in “Zayd is writing.”

[^V03-83]: If readiness were a settled quality, then it would itself be something that could exist or fail to exist; it would be possible, rather than possibility. The comparison with a self-standing thing is not meant to say that it exists without a subject. The point is that readiness is a relation, not a separate settled feature. Readiness is the basis for the possibility of something that can follow it, not the same thing as the readiness itself. It is a real relation to what may come to be, and so a relation in the full sense. A settled quality is called an “accident” in the traditional classification; a relation is not a settled quality in that sense.

[^V03-84]: The possibility of becoming something is the relation itself, distinct from the underlying readiness. “In general” includes the soul, qualities, and forms.

[^V03-85]: This note clarifies the grammar: “rather” refers to the phrase immediately before it.

[^V03-86]: Readiness is a state in a subject that connects it to a possible thing. When the mind considers it, it sees a relation with two sides: the subject's potential to become that thing, and the thing's potential to exist in that subject.

[^V03-87]: Calling this readiness “potential existence,” as opposed to actual existence, is a way of speaking. The division of existence into actual and potential means that something either exists independently, without being related to another thing, or is a real capacity for something that can exist in a subject. The latter is still a kind of existence.

[^V03-88]: Matter must also remain through changes. It lets us say that what comes to be is the same thing that passed away, since one form does not turn into another and the forms are different. If matter did not remain, we could not call the new thing a change of the old one. One might reply that an endless series of matters is not impossible if each is only earlier in time than the next. But readiness for existence exists in the same subject as the thing that is coming to be.

[^V03-89]: This points ahead to substantial motion: matter and form are joined as one, and matter follows the form as both are renewed.

[^V03-90]: The problem is not simply that a relation is repeated in the mind. The deeper question is how a real relation can connect something that exists with something that does not yet exist, since a relation itself must exist and needs both sides to be present in the same realm. The answer is that the readiness for a coming form is a real feature of a subject, but the subject is not the first form that will pass away. It is an underlying substance that continues through the change. The new form is not yet present with all its effects, but it has a weaker kind of existence in the subject as the form that is about to come to be. Once it becomes fully actual, its readiness ends—not because one thing vanished and another unrelated thing appeared, but because the same underlying matter took on the new form.

    The same is true of all changes in time: something changes into something else, whether a form or a quality, as when air becomes fire or water, or a body takes on a new quality or size. The matter holds the readiness for what can come next. Because the matter remains, the earlier thing and the later thing are connected. It can hold the potentiality for all forms, and the forms appear one after another in continuous change. Each form is actual in its own time and potential before that. The earlier form and its potentiality for the next one belong to one continuous, changing existence. Matter is joined to form, not simply added beside it.

    This is substantial motion: matter itself moves through forms. What exists in potential is a real, weaker level of existence, without all the effects of what exists fully in actuality. This explains how we can divide all existence into what is actual and what is potential, and how matter and form are joined as one. Many further results follow, which the author will explain where they belong.

[^V03-91]: The point of the condition is that two positive, existing things can still be potentiality. The thing that can come to be is particular, such as water. Pure potentiality means the capacity for existence in general, as in an essence considered apart from whether it exists.

[^V03-92]: The earlier argument applies to human souls that are connected to matter as something they govern, even if they are not embedded in it like bodily forms. This follows the view held by Aristotle’s followers that the human soul is separate from matter from its first moment. On Mulla Sadra's view that the soul begins bodily and later becomes spiritual, the point is clearer still. The argument also applies to nonhuman souls, whether one thinks they are material or separate, and to bodily qualities.

[^V03-93]: Matter does not come before a general kind in time. Nor does a general kind, simply as a body, cause particular motions. It is the particular body and its particular nature that cause them.

[^V03-94]: If these thinkers meant that matter came first in time—whether they called it matter, darkness, an abyss, or an empty space—their view is false. It assumes matter existed without any form, as though God had stopped giving existence. It also implies that light came after darkness, and leads to other problems. If they meant that matter comes first in the order of being, that too is backwards: a general kind becomes a particular kind through its form, and matter becomes actual through form. If they meant a place in the order of ideas, there is no problem, provided prime matter is treated as the lowest starting point in a rise through more complete forms, toward the greatest light. Some old accounts describe the world as first dark and empty, then filled with plants and animals, then with spirits and human beings. This can be understood as a sequence of increasing order and completeness.

[^V03-95]: The author mentions this view here even though its usual form seems to deny potentiality and change: everything is said to exist already, with some things hidden and others appearing as order comes about.

[^V03-96]: Taken literally, this supports the view that potentiality is a weaker level of actuality, which does not yet have all the effects of full actuality. Otherwise, it makes no sense to say that a substantial form completes a readiness in matter if that readiness disappears as soon as the new form arrives.

[^V03-97]: The wording should be “and existence,” with “and” understood. The point is that potentiality is not nothing; it has a kind of existence. Existence comes before an essence in reality, and potentiality is one such essence whose existence is actual.

[^V03-98]: This follows from the meaning of Avicenna's words. In a particular case, one capacity may come before a particular act in time, but another act comes before that capacity. More broadly, actuality comes before potentiality. The claim that actuality comes first in time is part of the general point; the later arguments explain the other kinds of priority.

[^V03-99]: One might say that matter is the subject of substantial motion, or even of motion in quantity. The reply is that the previous argument follows the philosophers' view that matter with a particular form is the subject of a particular change. In the same way, matter with a particular size moves through changes in quantity.

[^V03-100]: The body does exist outside the mind, but in particular kinds; it does not exist as an undefined body on a level with those kinds. The second argument is that if motion were a form that divided bodies into kinds, it would have to complete an undefined body. But no such body exists outside the mind. So a particular body must already exist before motion affects it.

[^V03-101]: This repeats the first point: an accident cannot make a substance into a particular kind. The third argument also rests on the principle that what is merely potential cannot give a kind to something already actual.

[^V03-102]: This argument assumes that motion as a continuous whole exists outside the mind. If we deny that, we could object that what exists outside is motion as “being between,” which is stable enough to belong to a stable subject. This resembles arguments about how a changing thing can be connected to an eternal cause.

[^V03-103]: The renewal of nature's existence is an essential feature, not a later addition. This is what the author means by saying that the immediate mover's existence includes motion. The pronoun in “its immediate mover” refers to accidental motion, which is a later feature of its subject; the wording shifts between these senses. Substantial motion belongs to nature itself and is not separately caused. The author says no act of making comes between nature's existence and this necessary feature.

[^V03-104]: “The nature remains the same” means that change does not occur at the level of its general nature. It does not mean that there is a separate level at which nature is either fixed or changing.

[^V03-105]: The earlier claim that motion does not make a bodily substance into a particular kind applies to accidental motion, not substantial motion. In simple bodies, the specific form has substantial motion as part of its existence. So substantial motion can distinguish one kind from another.

[^V03-106]: This and later remarks suggest that all categories undergo change through substantial motion. The accidental motions in place, position, quantity, and quality depend on the body's deeper change. This view has many further results: what these motions aim at, how one motion can occur within another, how essential motions serve as the goals of accidental motions, and how all material things move toward being free of matter. The author will explain some of these points later.

[^V03-107]: “Stable” here means stable in relation to its accidental features. A body moving in place or changing in quality does not change in the same way as the body's place or quality. Fire's heat, for example, is stable when compared with the gradual heating of water.

[^V03-108]: “Subject” means the thing described as moving. “Composite” means the subject together with its motion. For Mulla Sadra, no body is wholly stable in its existence; what remains is the body through the continuous unity of its motion.

[^V03-109]: That is, the feature through which the body is potentially moving.

[^V03-110]: This applies to substantial motion and the changing nature of things. “Joined as one” means that the body, as the receiver of motion, is enough; no separate cause is needed for a feature that belongs to its nature.

[^V03-111]: The two “new forms” are different in kind: form is what changes. The two “new matters” differ only in their readiness for form. Matter in the elements is shared and remains through changes, since motion needs a subject that continues.

[^V03-112]: The result is one continuing, flowing existence. From its imagined boundaries, the mind draws out general kinds such as human, animal, and plant.

[^V03-113]: Mulla Sadra also says that the soul is the source of all our actions and perceptions because it begins through the body but survives it. The soul has different levels. The thinkers mentioned here deny that there are real powers and natures within things; Mulla Sadra does not.

[^V03-114]: This rules out inclination as the first source, since inclination is only a secondary source.

[^V03-115]: The earlier argument treated the body's changing nearness to its goal as the cause of each stage of motion. Here the two sequences are said to cause one another in different ways. The commentator on Avicenna's *Pointers* defended this view by treating inclination as a middle step between fixed nature and motion. Mulla Sadra's reply still applies: the changing inclination also depends on nature.

[^V03-116]: “Renewal” here means change in substance. Accidental motion is itself an effect, so it cannot cause itself. One might say that renewal is essential to a sphere's motion, and so does not need a cause, just as Mulla Sadra says of nature. But what is only an accidental feature must ultimately depend on something substantial. Accidental features, including accidental motion, depend on substances; substantial forms are the sources of their effects. Philosophers define nature as the first source of a thing's own motion and rest. If renewal were essential to accidental motion, and nature caused its existence, then nature would be a divine cause of existence, which is impossible. For these philosophers, God gives existence to the moving thing, while nature is the direct physical source of its motion.

[^V03-117]: This means the link between renewed nature and the unchanging Source. The Arabic phrase refers back to the nature just discussed. The general question of how change connects to what does not change was already explained in detail.

[^V03-118]: “In” can mean several things. “Motion in quality” may mean that quality contains motion, as ivory contains whiteness, or that a kind falls under a wider kind, as human falls under animal. The word can also describe being in a place, in time, or in a moving thing; each relation is different. The same applies to existence and essence, or to God being in the heavens and on earth.

[^V03-119]: This is correct in the following sense: at each imagined instant, the changing thing can be understood as having another kind or class within the category in which it changes. In accidental motion, the substance receives a new kind at each instant. In substantial motion, the moving thing and its motion are one, because motion in substance exists through itself. It is itself the moving substance, so no separate subject is needed. In short, motion in substance means that a different kind of substance can be drawn from the thing at each instant.

[^V03-120]: If the original blackness and every added feature were all blackness, then two like qualities would exist in one subject. It would also make an outwardly simple quality into a compound.

[^V03-121]: In that case, the original amount would not remain; adding or separating an amount destroys it. So the subject is not the amount but what carries it—matter—unless we mean a general extension that remains through the change.

[^V03-122]: Razi means that “blackness” is a wide general kind containing many shades. As a thing grows blacker, it moves from one kind of blackness to another, but all are still black. His account also reverses the direction of change: growing blacker means moving toward blackness, not away from it. If pure black is the limit farthest from white, then change moves from a different kind into the black kind, not the other way around.

[^V03-123]: All the stages are black, and flowing blackness has no actual first or final point. Any part imagined as the final part can be divided into smaller parts. Choosing one as the true endpoint would be arbitrary.

[^V03-124]: Razi's objection is specific to his own approach. There are several replies. Motion is between pure potentiality and full actuality, so the kinds within it are potential but not wholly unreal. They are potential because the motion is continuous and its limits follow one another; each limit points to the next. The motion is also actual as one whole, even though it can be divided in thought. The changing quality may be understood both as a flowing state that does not fit neatly into time, and as one continuous span that does. The momentary kinds are potential measures of change, as are the imagined parts between any two instants. These distinctions explain how one changing reality can be actual without its stages being separate actual things. They also fit the principle that existence comes before the kinds the mind draws from it.

[^V03-125]: Razi added a short period of time between successive states so that the states would not follow one another at separate instants. But then the quality would remain unchanged during each short period, and its transition to the next state would happen all at once between them. That would rule out motion, which must be gradual and continuous.

[^V03-126]: If each position lasted for a time, then the moving thing would leave one position and reach the next in an instant. The continuous place has infinitely many positions between them, so the thing would have to jump over them. It cannot do so; it must pass through them over time.

[^V03-127]: The objection assumes that motion is an added feature that exists after its subject is already complete. The reply is that motion and the flowing quality exist together as one. The difference between them is in how we describe them, not in separate things outside the mind. The quality's existence is the motion itself.

[^V03-128]: This refers to those who say that a category has both settled and flowing kinds, such as settled and flowing quality or size.

[^V03-129]: The first argument does not work because whiteness can be part of what it is to be white without being the feature that makes white different in kind from black. That does not challenge the point made here: flow is a feature the mind draws from a flowing reality.

[^V03-130]: The change may also be described as movement from one individual of a kind or class to another.

[^V03-131]: “Beginning” may mean a state different from the thing that follows it, like a point to a line, rest to motion, or an instant to time. It may also mean the first part of a thing. Continuous things, whether settled or flowing, have no actual first part in this second sense. Here, “beginning,” “end,” “from,” and “toward” mean the first and last limits of what changes—for example, warmth and the strongest heat in a change of quality. They do not mean the periods of rest before and after motion. The motion's limits follow from its definition. A limit can be both a “from” and a “toward,” depending on the direction considered, especially in the endless motion of the celestial spheres. Each imagined part can in turn be divided without end.

[^V03-132]: The positions may be alike in kind and nature, but “the same” here means one and the same individual. A position that has ceased to exist does not return as that exact same individual. Otherwise, the same reasoning would apply to every position between the two daily positions, which would mean an endless number of positions repeating in the sphere's motion. Common sense rules this out.

[^V03-133]: “Point” is used loosely. Each position at an instant is simple, like a flowing point.

[^V03-134]: On this view, each category is related to motion in its own way. It resembles the view that knowledge belongs to the category of the thing known.

[^V03-135]: Another view says that motion belongs to the categories of acting and being acted on: motion as being moved belongs to one, and motion as moving something belongs to the other. Mulla Sadra instead sees motion as a way of existing, and the whole natural world as flowing.
