What he says here does not conflict with that view: being moved and moving are not motion itself, just as heating and being heated are not heat.

[^V03-136]: The highest categories do not change according to how we look at them. So it is unclear how motion could count as being acted on when viewed from the receiver, and as acting when viewed from the agent. Nor does motion become place, position, quality, size, or substance simply by being considered on its own. The point may instead be that motion in one of these five categories gives the agent and receiver the relative features of acting and being acted on.

[^V03-137]: The argument is that motion in a category requires the subject to have a different individual of that category at each instant. So the categories of acting and being acted on would need momentary individuals that exist only potentially. Motion is the subject's passage from one such individual to another. But acting and being acted on are themselves gradual states. If motion occurred within them, the subject would be moving further into a state it had not yet reached, rather than leaving one settled state for another. Leaving one gradual state for another would itself have to be gradual, which would start another motion and lead to an endless chain. The same problem arises if these categories are identified with motion itself: they are not separate, momentary individuals, but a continuing process. The deeper point is that if substantial motion occurs, the body's accidental features also move with it, since they are levels or appearances of the body's existence. Mulla Sadra recognized this result and argued for it elsewhere, though he did not fully work through all its consequences here. On this view, a body has a motion in its own substance and, through it, a motion in its place, position, size, and quality. These motions may be nested: the body's place can change because its substance changes, and it may also move from one place to another. The same applies to the other categories.

[^V03-138]: Each gradual state has infinitely many parts. If motion occurred within such a state, the subject could not leave it in a single instant. It would have to remain in each part for some time, which would make it at rest.

[^V03-139]: There is a further problem. If motion occurred in acting, then the subject would have to move from one kind of heating to another. But it cannot leave one kind of heating while still heating, or stop heating all at once and begin cooling in the next instant. Both results conflict with what motion means.

[^V03-140]: This depends on how rest is defined. If rest means that a thing stays in one place, it is the opposite of motion. If it means the absence of motion in something that can move, it is the absence of a capacity, not the opposite. Avicenna discusses this in *The Healing*.

[^V03-141]: The philosophers say that the outermost sphere has a position relative to the other bodies, even though it has no place around it. Mulla Sadra says that it does have a place, since place is a kind of dimension.

[^V03-142]: A moving thing moves toward a goal that completes it. Each stage of motion is a first completion compared with the stage before it, but only potential compared with the stage after it. Motion therefore has degrees of completion. This also shows that a thing cannot move naturally from greater strength to lesser strength: motion is a gradual passage from potentiality to actuality. When something seems to weaken, such as a bitter liquid gradually cooling, another feature may be replacing its heat. The body's changing features are part of its changing existence, so this need not be strange.

[^V03-143]: This makes clear that Mulla Sadra does not regard any kind of motion as lacking degrees. It also rules out motion from one equal stage to another, where no stage is more or less complete.

[^V03-144]: The earlier discussion showed that blackness itself cannot be the subject of change. Here the point is how change in quality works. A flowing blackness has a weak unity when compared with settled blackness: it lies between pure potentiality and complete actuality. Taken without that comparison, it has a broad unity that includes all the shades of black. It resembles the continuous motion considered between its limits.

[^V03-145]: This explanation keeps us from treating the lasting blackness and the added degrees as two separate things outside the mind. The distinction is made by the mind.

[^V03-146]: In a change of quality, there can be something like a lasting base and added features, but the distinction between them exists only in thought. The difference here is that those particular features pass away while the base remains. In the present account, the apparent branches pass away within the lasting base.

[^V03-147]: If what a thing is were the basic reality, then all the different kinds would exist separately in actuality, and the changes between them would contain infinitely many actual divisions. But if existence is primary, it is like a thread that holds them together; the different kinds are distinctions the mind draws from it. Even the view held by Aristotle’s followers that existence is primary but made up of entirely distinct simple realities would still support the argument, since the multiplicity would be in actual existence. Here, however, there is one continuous, flowing existence. Mulla Sadra does not accept that other view, which is why he interprets its wording in another way.

[^V03-148]: A person’s own existence has stages corresponding to the seven inner dimensions of human life. Notice these stages in yourselves, then turn toward the simple reality that encompasses all existence. The three results drawn here are, first, that existence is what is real; second, that a thing can change in its very being; and third, that many things are united in one reality. The author’s expression of wonder is fitting: if the unity of a changing quality is astonishing, how much more astonishing is the soul, the great sign of God and one of His greatest wonders! Lord, deepen my wonder at You.

[^V03-149]: This raises two problems: how can one thing belong to many kinds, and how can one thing be bodily in its origin but later exist without a body, as Mulla Sadra says of the soul? There is also the problem of what remains the subject through change. The following discussion addresses these points.

[^V03-150]: In *The Divine Witnesses*, Mulla Sadra says that change and nonpersistence belong to existence, while permanence belongs to what a thing is. The two claims can be reconciled by noticing that the present discussion treats different stages as forms of one continuous individual existence. The mind draws different kinds from those stages. In the other work, he looks at differences in existence and at the shared meanings in our concepts. General words can apply to very different realities: “animal,” for example, can refer to a bodily animal, an imaginal being, or a spiritual one; “rational” can mean capable of reason or actually reasoning, as with an intellect that has become actual or the Active Intellect.

[^V03-151]: The earlier reply—that motion itself is one continuous individual, with its different kinds existing only potentially—would already explain the unity of motion without requiring a stable subject. A stable subject alone cannot make separate, unrelated features one motion. A subject must remain in accidental motion because accidents exist in a subject and take their identity from it. Substance exists in itself, so it needs no further subject to remain one. In substantial motion, the material substance is both the moving thing and the motion: its own existence is renewed. A thing made of heat, if heat were a substance, would be both hot and heating. A fixed subject is needed only for accidental motion. But since accidental features also change with the motion of substance, the unity of the substance supports the unity of those motions too.

[^V03-152]: One might ask how matter can become individual before it is individual, or exist before it exists. The true cause of matter and its individual identity is a single separate being. The general form—some form or other—works together with it as a lesser cause. That is enough for matter, which is pure potentiality. A general cause can also account for what is absent, since absence is a light burden for a cause. “Some form” may also mean an eternal, all-embracing form, whose generality means that it contains all particular forms. It relates to particular forms as continuous motion relates to the separate positions we imagine within it, or as a flowing instant relates to the parts of time. The author means a real bodily kind, not a mere idea or a general kind that disappears into different defining features.

[^V03-153]: In the usual account of coming to be and passing away, each form takes matter's place after the prior form has ended. On the view of substantial motion, the forms follow one another as parts of one continuous existence. This continuous form keeps matter actual. The different forms are boundaries the mind draws within it, just as different places are boundaries within motion from place to place. The full account will come in the discussion of matter and form.

[^V03-154]: The phrase “so this should be possible too” is a parenthetical point. “Body” here means a particular kind of body that acts as matter, not the general kind that can be said of different kinds of body. A general kind cannot make matter actual or give it one continuing identity.

[^V03-155]: This is even more likely for particular forms, since they are more fully defined than bodily form, and matter formed as a body is closer to being one and lasting.

[^V03-156]: Nature exists through particular examples, so we can prove substantial motion by saying that the formed matter remains while the changing specific form flows through it. Not every substance flows: intellects, and souls considered in themselves, are not material and do not change in their own nature.

[^V03-157]: An amount cannot remain unchanged when another amount is added to it or separated from it. That is why philosophers say that quantity can be divided in thought, but not broken apart into separate quantities. Prime matter can be broken apart because it is not itself a fixed amount and can receive separation or connection. If we say that the two amounts after division are the same as the first, this refers to the subject that remains, not to the quantities themselves, which are simple outside the mind.

[^V03-158]: According to these philosophers, animal powers are not separate from the body; they are present in the subtle bodily spirit. Nothing in this account remains unchanged. Change is even more obvious in plants, which have no sensation or voluntary motion—powers that point toward a level beyond matter.

[^V03-159]: If we consider the plant through its motion, the stages are potential; if we ask what stays as its original basis, they are actual, as Avicenna says. No one part of its duration is more important than another. A continuous existence is one personal identity, just as a length remains one even though it can be divided without end in thought.

[^V03-160]: Avicenna first says that one form needs one matter, so how could it take on many matters through nourishment? He then suggests that the near matter may be many while the first matter is one. He rejects this too: if a form exists throughout the matter it shapes, how could one form be one while its immediate subjects are many? “Form” here means the specific form.

[^V03-161]: The earlier and later powers are alike in that both exist throughout their subjects. Neither is a separate feature laid over the subject, as relations can be. Neither power exists apart from the subject, even in an imaginal form. So when the later power disappears, the earlier one disappears too.

[^V03-162]: The connection between the parts is only by relation. If it were a true continuous connection, the parts would not be separate individuals. Avicenna does not refute this option here because the earlier points already show why it fails: it would make the instants follow one another with no duration between them.

[^V03-163]: “Flows from” means that the later form comes from God through the original source.

[^V03-164]: Animals have some original parts formed from the bodies of their parents, such as bones, nerves, and ligaments. Other parts, such as flesh and fat, are formed from blood. If the original parts disappear, the other parts also disappear, but not the other way around. It is not clear whether this applies to plants and to some animals.

[^V03-165]: This refers to the “lords of the species,” the separate patterns for kinds of things proposed by the Illuminationist school. In *The Journey of the Soul*, Mulla Sadra says this is the right view, though Avicenna mentions it without settling the question.

[^V03-166]: This is an exception to the claim that plants cannot have original and secondary parts. Parts that look alike may differ in reality: some may be foundational, others added later. The same distinction is clear in animals.

[^V03-167]: “First matter” here means matter considered in the upward development of things. It cannot be the stable subject because it has weak existence and unity, and the different forms that arise in it divide it. But matter has two kinds of unity. One comes from the form and disappears when a single connected form is divided. The other belongs to matter itself and remains whether the forms are connected or come in succession. Separation does not destroy this second unity. Mulla Sadra later says that prime matter is the subject of expansion and contraction; he has already said that it is the subject of nature's flow.

[^V03-168]: This follows from the argument about division and connection that establishes matter. The specific forms stand above bodily form not only in the order of definitions but also in the order of existence: bodily form exists, and specific form exists at a higher level. No bodily form exists without some specific form, whether celestial, elemental, simple, or compound.

[^V03-169]: Another reply: the claim that one amount destroys another applies to settled amounts, not to amounts that are parts of a gradual motion.

[^V03-170]: Compared with real existence, all these general kinds and defining features are necessary features of a thing. They count as parts only when the mind considers what the thing is. They can change without destroying the thing if its final defining feature remains, since that feature gathers the earlier forms and their completions. For Mulla Sadra, the true defining feature is real existence, which gives a thing its unity and simplicity.

[^V03-171]: Matter's persistence is easier to see in expansion and contraction because it remains through the change and is not tied to one particular amount. The body is harder to see as the subject because changing amounts reveal that the measured body also changes. Its general kind remains only as a universal nature or an eternal reality, which is hard for the imagination and the limited intellect to accept. The distinction between original and later parts in plants and animals may also show why matter can be the subject in both kinds of motion.

[^V03-172]: The final defining feature of a complete human being is actual reason, or the Active Intellect. The old definition of a human as a “mortal rational animal” uses “mortal” in the sense of voluntary death. In a complete human being, this final feature gathers all the changing and passing forms: the defining features of lower kinds become general kinds in relation to it, and their forms become like its matter. It is the form of forms and the feature that gathers what is scattered.

[^V03-173]: The stages on the way to the final human form are changes that bring greater completion, not forms that are simply put on and taken off. There is no loss followed by gain, but gain followed by gain, and finding followed by finding, without end.

[^V03-174]: Another reason a subject remains through substantial motion is that bodily natures are delicate traces of higher realities. Their stable aspect comes from their connection to the separate patterns of their kinds.

[^V03-175]: These intellectual forms do not exist separately for themselves; they are relations to the rational soul. One might ask how an intellectual idea can be an image if, as Mulla Sadra says, knowing a general kind means seeing its separate pattern. An image seen from far away can represent what we later see at close range after returning often to the world of intellect. “Image” is a broad term: it includes things sensed outwardly or inwardly, and things understood by the intellect.

[^V03-176]: This gives another account of what remains through motion. Some features mentioned above belong to the agent, some to the receiver, some to what is received, and some to the category in which change occurs. Each helps preserve the body's unity. If natural form itself is flowing, it may seem unable to provide that unity. The reply is that form has a continuous individual through time, both as the middle stage of motion and as the whole connected process. Matter, then, has what gives it multiplicity and what gives it unity. Its unity does not come only from one separate being; it is supported by these other relations too.

[^V03-177]: The four accidental motions are like a body whose soul is substantial motion, the renewal of nature. Time is like a body whose soul is timeless order. Timeless order is in turn like a body whose soul is eternity. The containers relate to one another as their contents do. What is eternal surrounds what is timeless, and both surround what belongs to time. Timeless order, in all its parts, relates to time as a day relates to its hours, minutes, and seconds—or as the flowing instant relates to time. The point is that changing motions and times are stable in relation to separate beings and to the source of both separate and bodily beings.

[^V03-178]: Nature that comes from the soul is a lower level of the soul and exists through it as its effect. The other nature belongs to the elements and exists within them. The first is naturally ready to obey the soul; the second is made to obey. Fatigue comes from the second, not the first. Physicians and natural philosophers use “nature” for the power that manages the body, preserves its health, and pushes illness away. Plato uses it for the divine power that acts in the body by God's permission—the first kind.

[^V03-179]: This alludes to the Qur'anic account in which God tells heaven and earth to come willingly or unwillingly, and they answer that they come willingly. This applies to nature that comes from the soul, which obeys willingly, and the nature of the elements, which obeys under compulsion. The speech is by God through the soul, which is a divine mystery and a command from the Lord. As Rumi says, every voice comes from the King, even when it comes through a servant's throat. God spoke this way to the heavens and earth of the visible world. His word is complete and the Pen has dried in relation to God's eternal reality, though the world remains in a state of renewal for beings confined by place and time. The earth and its like answer willingly when they see their own beauty as a display of God's names and qualities. Their journey toward God is a source of great joy. If they did not make that journey, they would remain in the pit of matter and the unjust town of ignorance, and suffer a deep loss. At first they resist being moved from their familiar places because they do not understand. Ignorance is the root of evil; knowledge is the root of good.

[^V03-180]: A clearer distinction would be between two types of helpers: those that belong to the soul and obey it by their nature, such as senses that follow it into the imaginal world and the afterlife; and those that belong to the body and obey it only indirectly. Mulla Sadra identifies the two kinds here with the sources of motion in quality and quantity, and with those in place and position. One might object that both are the same nature that was just discussed. The distinction may be that “nature” earlier means the body's elements, while the powers here come from the soul; or that the earlier term means the lasting root shared by bodily and plant-like powers, while these are its separate levels and branches. This resembles the debate over whether the animal soul is the sum of all its powers or the ruling power of estimation. The better view is that the animal soul is the shared root of those powers, existing in each at its own level.

[^V03-181]: “Willingly” and “under force” describe how the imagination and thought experience these powers. In themselves, both kinds are natural: both the powers that attract and push, and the powers that move the body. Even walking depends on a nature that is ready to obey the soul, and this nature remains with the soul in the afterlife. Mulla Sadra's contrast is between what is naturally ready to obey and what is made to obey.

[^V03-182]: These powers serve the intellect only when their actions are directed toward rational ends. Otherwise, the outward and inward powers of perception belong to the animal soul, like the powers that move the body. The note's qualification matters because imagination and estimation do not, by themselves, submit to reason.

[^V03-183]: This obedient nature belongs to the imaginal body, just as the power spread through the muscles belongs to the physical body. The powers that come from the soul are its domain and the place where its light appears. This answers those who deny bodily resurrection and accept only spiritual survival. They argue that particular bodily perceptions need particular bodily organs, which disappear when the body falls apart. But the soul has its own sight, hearing, and other senses, as well as a body in the afterlife.

[^V03-184]: My first objection is that this leaves natural powers unable to act, which is as unacceptable as denying them altogether. Some theologians who reject natural causes avoid the problem by saying that powers act only on things outside their own subjects, or that existence flows through nature. Second, why should a spatial relation be required to connect cause and effect? What relation could be closer than the union between a power and its subject? Sadra and many other philosophers say that an agent acts through its very being. In *The Journey of the Soul*, Sadra compares spatial relation in bodily action with the spiritual nearness through which immaterial beings receive the flow of existence. In *Origin and Return*, he says that a cause and what it affects do not always need to be separate, as when form acts on matter. So why require position when a power acts on something outside its own matter? For action within its own matter, the author may be applying the rule “consider the outcomes, not the starting points.” Third, even if we accept the argument, it may show only that action is bodily because the matter that receives the power has a position. This is all the proof establishes: if a thing exists through matter, its action depends on matter, and matter exists positionally. This argument also appears in *The Divine Witnesses*. It fits the Illuminationist view that separate forms for kinds—horizontal intellects—produce all the effects in our world.

[^V03-185]: This argument works only if there is a gradual change that necessarily belongs to a natural kind and is directly intended by its nature, rather than occurring as a side effect. The commentator denies both claims about natural kinds and says the fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

[^V03-186]: If motion were not an effect of nature, it would not come after nature; it would exist together with it, in the same primary mode of existence, rather than as a secondary feature that follows from it.

[^V03-187]: Calling form and matter “co-causes” means that form is not a cause in the usual sense. Existence flows first through form and then through matter. There is no shared causal action between them: a bodily cause acts only through position, and form and matter are united rather than positioned apart from each other. Still, causation does not always require separation. Sadra says in *Origin and Return* that form causes matter, and philosophers also say that a defining feature causes the general kind, though they are united in what the statement describes.

[^V03-188]: The examples show that we name the subject by a feature that follows from it. Strictly speaking, a logical defining feature is a feature of the thing: a general idea given in answer to the question “What is it, in its substance?”

[^V03-189]: There is a subtle point here. Taken as features that belong to the individual, these accidents are signs of individuality, since an individuating feature must apply to the individual. In that respect they are one with their subject, though they are a second level of its existence and an outward appearance of it. We must preserve both levels without losing the unity of the subject. These necessary features are not like unity or individuality, which do not follow existence as later features; they are more like mathematical body and natural body, which, in the experts' view, differ only in how they are considered. This is the way to understand the argument without erasing the nine categories of accidents.

[^V03-190]: Matter, attachment to matter, the possibility of becoming something else, and motion are what make a thing distinct from the higher reality. Where the marks of possibility, especially readiness to become something else, prevail, a thing exists because God brings it into being and continues because God sustains it. But where these marks disappear, so that nothing remains to be attained and even the thing’s possibility is hidden in the light of eternity, it exists through God’s own existence and lasts through His lasting existence. Some of the author’s contemporaries missed this distinction and criticised him in their writings. I have discussed it in my notes on the section concerning divine things in this book; anyone who wishes can consult them.

[^V03-191]: Worship joined with reflection, free from seeing anything besides the One worshipped, leads to complete servanthood. And servanthood is, in its very essence, lordship. It is as though you are being told to become pure intellect, so that you may know the intellect that endures through God’s enduring existence—not through a separate act of preservation or through its own independent being. It has no existence of its own, just as the meaning of a connecting word does not stand alone. Or “those who worship” may refer to the powers and natures whose very substance is constantly renewed; their worship is expressed in their being. This message then announces their arrival at their goals.

[^V03-192]: “Then another form must take its place” and the preceding argument are also refuted by motion in quality and other kinds of motion.

[^V03-193]: This refers to the argument that instants would have to follow one another.

[^V03-194]: Matter is also brought into being as an individual.

[^V03-195]: Here, “form” means the form that underlies a thing's actual motion, like the middle stage of motion, not the general idea of form.

[^V03-196]: This answers the claim that the kind either remains through change or not.

[^V03-197]: “Opposite” may mean any opposite, including intermediate opposites, or it may mean only a strict opposite. Avicenna's argument is also refuted by kinds of motion, such as motion in amount, that do not involve opposites.

[^V03-198]: Avicenna's view is clear: time measures motion, and a measure follows what it measures in either flowing or remaining fixed. The majority view is that a motion considered as one whole from beginning to end is stable and has no parts that pass away; only the path of motion has parts, and they exist only in imagination. If motion itself cannot have parts that pass away, time alone must be inherently unstable. The commentator says their further account of how time's measure remains is another matter. A more precise explanation is that division depends on first treating something as a measure. Without a measure, there is no whole or part, small or large. Philosophers treat division as an essential feature of quantity; division in a physical body is only secondary. On this view, time's parts pass away in themselves, while motion's parts do so only by extension.

[^V03-199]: Motion means the renewal of a thing; but renewal, considered by itself, is not a separate thing. This resembles the claim that a thing's existence is its being real: that reality cannot itself be another thing, or it would need yet another reality to make it real. Motion, then, is like a grammatical particle that makes sense only in relation to a noun. It is not a separate moving thing or a separate measure. The claim that motion and time are themselves unstable therefore misses the point: they are the renewal of something, its measure, and the thing renewed.

[^V03-200]: Philosophers and theologians agree that coming into being is not the same as the thing that comes into being, or the process through which it comes to be. Philosophers say coming into being exists in the mind, with only its source in the thing itself. The theologian Abu Hashim says it is a state that is neither existent nor nonexistent: it is not nonexistent because a real thing can be described as coming into being, but it cannot itself be a separate existent, since then it would either be eternal or need to come into being in turn, leading to an endless chain.

[^V03-201]: A possible thing has both a nature and existence: existence drives nonexistence away, and “existent” describes the relation between the thing's nature and its existence.

[^V03-202]: The verse may refer to mountains changing as one form after another comes to be through substantial motion. Or it may point to the human being's gradual ascent toward fuller existence: through motion in place and in substance, life develops through plant and animal stages toward the fully actual human being. This ascent continues through successive cycles because God's outpouring of existence never ends.

[^V03-203]: This refers to repeated renewal and to the gradual ascent through stages, from human society and plant life toward actual humanity. On the view that the Day of Resurrection includes all the timeless and temporal days, the transformation of the physical earth into an imaginal and afterlife earth takes place in the intermediate world. Reason and scripture agree that this is the first resurrection, though reason calls the earlier stages resurrection too. The heavens undergo similar transformations. These stages do not destroy the identity of what changes, because the process is continuous and its lasting basis is the face of God. Individual identity comes from existence.

[^V03-204]: God wills and brings about this change because the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect. God's will is necessary, not a possibility that might or might not be fulfilled. What is possible for creatures occurs within God's will under necessity.

[^V03-205]: The wording is inverted: the point is that a thing whose causes of preservation are also its causes of destruction must have an existence interwoven with passing away—that is, an existence in motion. Coming into being includes passing away at every stage. Another reading gives no proof of substantial motion: the same powers that preserve a thing can also destroy it. Sight may find something desirable, and desire may consume it. Bodily powers can also bring about illness through excess or restraint. Natural philosophers likewise said that the body's innate heat is both a cause of life and a cause of death.

[^V03-206]: Souls, as rays of the intellects, are what give bodies their stability and light. Bodies themselves are dark and unstable because of their distance in space, separation in time, and dependence on matter. Their lasting and luminous aspect comes from the holy intellects. The commentator adds a short verse: “The mill wheel turns the water over and over; the moon's reflection and the stars remain.”

[^V03-207]: The “and” here describes a condition: matter would then have no form capable of acting as a cause. It would lack the stable side through which existence can be given. As we have seen, form is the channel through which existence reaches matter, so this does not rule out a form that passes away. The form meant here is what makes a thing actual. If all coming-to-be were undone and things flowed back toward matter, that would be a return toward potentiality. Just as a soul can become like an active intellect by drawing close to it, a body can be said to return toward matter by approaching that limit.

[^V03-208]: The “veil” is the imagined division between one stage of change and another, which philosophers call the subject of motion. Mystics speak of these divisions as divine self-disclosures. They exist in thought, not as separate breaks in reality, because motion is one continuous process. The stages are so close together that the dividing line nearly disappears.

[^V03-209]: The Qur'anic verse about the people of Paradise receiving fruits that resemble one another comes from a passage about the forms of the afterlife. Ibn Arabi applies it here to the similar forms that appear successively during a person's ascent. Seen by God's light, these stages resemble heavenly forms. As a person's love and insight grow, manifestations of God's acts give way to manifestations of His attributes and then His essence.

[^V03-210]: “In length and breadth” refers to the world and the afterlife: the afterlife lies within the world, as its inner dimension.

[^V03-211]: The manuscript may properly include the conjunction “and.” Even without it, the point is clear: since coming into being depends on a being that brings things about, God continually turns toward creation.

[^V03-212]: The shorter version of this proof relies only on the difference between speed and slowness: speed covers a longer distance in a shorter time, and slowness the reverse.

[^V03-213]: This is Avicenna's natural-philosophy proof for time, given in *The Physics* of *The Book of Healing*. It shows that each individual motion has its own individual time, distinct from the time of other motions, just as each body has its own measure. Each time can serve as a unit by which other motions are measured. The common time measured by the daily motion is a human convention because it is regular and familiar. Mulla Sadra also holds that a natural time, involved in the existence of events, is the measure of the whole bodily nature's substantial motion.

[^V03-214]: This is one of the proofs for substantial motion.

[^V03-215]: The author points to his view that nature is renewed. Other philosophers say that time measures the changing position of the heavenly sphere; Sadra says that it measures the renewal of celestial nature, since other natures do not change with the same regularity. In this account, nature has quantity as an inseparable feature, just as existence is inseparable from what exists. Or the meaning may be that time is the connected, nonlasting quantity of nature itself—the account previously attributed to other philosophers.

[^V03-216]: The wording is unclear, because if time is a quantity, it cannot be a substance.

[^V03-217]: This is a division of the whole into its parts. The options about whether time measures a material substance or its renewal depend on whether we view time and motion as the same in existence or distinct in concept. Sadra later reconciles the different views of time. Their relation resembles that of mathematical body to natural body: the measured extension is the same, but it is considered in two different ways. If time and nature are one in existence, time is the measure of a substance. If they are distinct in concept and in how they appear to thought, time is the measure of nature's renewal and motion, or of what belongs to a body.

[^V03-218]: Because its changing states include renewed stages of before and after, it would need another motion and another time, and another agent to bring that about.

[^V03-219]: The five or six features listed for the body that time measures come from the old idea of an outermost sphere: a round body surrounding the physical universe whose daily motion marks common time. It has since become clear that the celestial bodies imagined in that account do not exist. These features can instead apply to the universal bodily nature, whose substantial motion marks a common, substantial time. The everyday time we use is a convention based on the Earth's daily rotation.

[^V03-220]: If the body that time measures were removed, its replacement would also have to come before or after it in time, since matter that is formed from it or changed into it would itself be earlier or later.

[^V03-221]: This means that it must come before other bodies in both time and place. Its priority in place would be lost if it moved, or if something else moved toward it, since changes in amount and quality also depend on motion in place. Its priority in time would be lost if another body or another motion came before it. It would also fail to endure if it could change in amount, expand, contract, heat up, or cool down; each of these changes requires matter that can come to be and pass away. This follows if the author's wording is read as it stands. If “its breaking apart” refers to time, the point is even clearer.

[^V03-222]: The note means conceptions of goals. A conception of an end can itself move an agent to act, as the idea of sitting moves someone to make a bed. The reference is not to conceptions of positions or motions, or to features that follow from motion as incidental results; the word “proper” excludes those.

[^V03-223]: This is the immediate goal; the more remote goal is likeness to the higher principles. One objection is that motion is itself an action, so it cannot be the goal of its own action; another is that motion is a seeking, not something sought. The commentator replies that Avicenna may mean the goal of the sphere's existence, nature, and circular tendency. Avicenna says “the goal in motion,” not “the goal of motion.”

[^V03-224]: The individual produced by a particular nature is only an incidental goal in this example. The example concerns particularity: the proper goal of a particular nature is its own completion, including the completion of its matter. Everything aims at itself and at its own perfection.

[^V03-225]: The conceptions agree or differ because of the positions they represent. Positions encountered during one revolution are different in kind; positions repeated in later revolutions resemble earlier ones in kind, but are not the same individual position. A person turning in place encounters many different positions before returning to the starting point; the repeated positions are like the earlier ones. The contrast also applies to different celestial configurations, such as triangular and six-sided arrangements, conjunctions and oppositions. Here “conceptions” means perceptions of positions, not ideas of goals.

[^V03-226]: The conceptions would have to resemble each other in every respect. Still, “resembling” is loose wording, since two things can resemble each other without being identical.

[^V03-227]: The phrase includes the elemental substances whose positions necessarily follow from them. Knowing a thing also means knowing what necessarily follows from it. These forms arrive gradually and continuously: they have one connected existence, yet many kinds or individuals, as colors appear in succession on fruit during a change of quality.

[^V03-228]: Mathematical extension, which can be divided in thought, is one of the features that follow from a natural body without being affected by it. Position—the arrangement of parts in relation to one another—is part of the body's existence and identity. A body's existence cannot be without position or arrangement. Change in position is therefore the very change in the body's substantial existence. “Inseparable” here means not later than the body in existence. Even if positions are later features, their renewal shows that the body's nature is renewed too, since a changing effect points to a changing immediate cause.

[^V03-229]: The sphere's different places are counted through its positions or times. In itself, the sphere has one natural place and no motion from place to place.

[^V03-230]: This develops substantial motion from principles accepted by Avicenna and his followers. Since the sphere's natural place and position do not change into something unnatural, its nature must itself be renewed: each degree of position and place corresponds to a degree of nature. In one view, both nature and its effect are one when considered as continuing; when considered as divided into stages, each has connected parts. Another possibility is that the sphere changes position by its own will. Since each position is wanted and then left, the sphere's motion may be voluntary, even if nature is what acts directly. Avicenna elsewhere calls it natural.

[^V03-231]: This proposal aims to connect the many renewed positions to one stable nature. It also avoids the objection that renewed accidents show their source is renewed, and avoids making the natural place and position multiple. The commentator compares it to the common sense: the shared sense receives many different images, but is one power.

[^V03-232]: The two objections share one basis. One uses the rule that a universal nature has no existence by itself: the individual exists, and the universal exists only through its individual instance. The other uses the primacy of existence over essence. The commentator notes that each school has its own starting point.

[^V03-233]: Sadra is identifying the cause of time. The words “as one individual” point out that time itself makes the sphere an individual, or is inseparable from its individuality. So how could the sphere cause time? Calling it an “unrestricted cause” leaves open the possibility that it is an incomplete cause, such as a receptive subject, but the author denies that it is time's agent. A cause cannot itself be qualified by its effect. Since every body is in time, and substantial motion makes a body flow and pass away in its existence, the sphere cannot be an eternal cause of time.

[^V03-234]: “Shape” is added after the more specific features as a general example.

[^V03-235]: One might object that motion occurs only in some accidents. The reply is that all the world's accidents are unstable, but in different ways: the four named categories are directly flowing in existence; time, acting, and being acted upon are flowing in their meaning; and relations are flowing only because they depend on other things.

[^V03-236]: That is, time is renewed through the celestial body's renewal.

[^V03-237]: The phrase refers back to the claim that the body itself is the source and cause of directions and places, as the same argument shows explicitly.

[^V03-238]: “Precede by nature” is used in the broad sense of priority, including causal priority, rather than only the narrow sense of an incomplete cause.

[^V03-239]: If separate intellects and souls are the surest paths to God, then a cause that acts through position cannot be the source of their existence. Their cause must be immaterial and ultimately be the Necessary Being. The note also points out that time and place are renewed effects, not causes that exist before one another.

[^V03-240]: If the earlier and later cannot coexist by their own nature, they are times. If they cannot coexist only because of an incidental feature, they are things that exist in time.

[^V03-241]: This note connects the phrase “only God” to the earlier proof that a cause cannot depend in its existence on what it causes.

[^V03-242]: A sequence of causes can be allowed if its parts follow one another continuously. But a sequence of separate instants or disconnected times cannot be allowed. The commentator also gives a simpler proof: if circular motion began with an eternal God, its beginning would require a prior condition, and that condition another, without end.

[^V03-243]: Assuming that causes are connected and successive has led to the very things we were assuming did not yet exist: time and motion. The connected reality that changes is bodily nature; its continuous extension is motion, and time measures that extension. The stable middle that runs from beginning to end is motion considered as continuing, and the flowing instant is the setting in which this continuity is present.

[^V03-244]: “Intellectual” here means a real substance that exists in actuality, not merely an essence in the mind. On this reading it could include God.

[^V03-245]: One might ask how the sphere's highest soul can be the cause of time if the argument excludes the soul. The reply is that the soul causes time through its intellectual, unified side; the side attached to the body is its changing nature. The excluded cause is an independent bodily cause.

[^V03-246]: Creation, considered as creation, is new because it is renewal and change; these are forms of incompleteness and do not come from God as a separate thing. What God brings about is the existence in which this renewal occurs. The Qur'an says that God's command is done, not that God's created world is done.

[^V03-247]: The question has already been discussed, but here Sadra reviews the argument, tests it, and states his own position more fully.

[^V03-248]: What belongs to a thing essentially is not explained by a further cause; what belongs to it accidentally needs a cause. The original argument treats renewal as essential to motion.

[^V03-249]: A separate act of “coming-to-be” cannot be added as another cause. Otherwise, it too would need to come to be, and the chain could not connect changing things to continuous motion.

[^V03-250]: The commentator allows that the earlier philosophers may have meant that motion's existence is renewed, rather than that renewal is part of its essence; this would answer Sadra's first objection. The second objection applies to both sides, and they answer it by appealing to the stable, middle motion that maintains circular motion as one whole. The remaining disagreement is whether this perpetual circular motion really exists.

[^V03-251]: The commentator strongly defends the earlier philosopher's argument. The philosopher may mean “a renewed position,” rather than “renewal of position.” Sadra's disagreement is about the renewal of the celestial nature itself. Apart from that point, the earlier argument can be defended; some of the disagreement is about wording.

[^V03-252]: This recalls the familiar point that coming-to-be is not a separate thing: it is the coming-to-be of a thing. Otherwise, that new “coming-to-be” would itself need a further beginning, leading to an endless chain. The same is true of motion. On Sadra's account, motion is the existence of the natural world.

[^V03-253]: Motion cannot come before an actual event in the order of nature while occurring at the same time as it. Each part of motion is itself passing away, so it cannot remain alongside its effect. Motion is potential, while the event that has come to be is actual. Only something free of potentiality can give actuality. The true source is separate and stronger than the bodily effect; motion is instead the condition that determines when the event occurs. The cause is eternal—God or the Active Intellect—and the later condition is a segment of the sphere's circular motion.

[^V03-254]: The lasting feature of movement cannot mean merely that new positions keep replacing one another. That succession has no separate existence over and above its parts, so it cannot by itself provide the enduring link to an eternal cause. The earlier critic therefore took the claim to require a stable basis within motion and objected that a purely changing process cannot have one.

    But the lasting basis intended here is *motion considered as a passage between its beginning and end*. In this sense, the movement is one continuous reality, even while its changing positions come and go. This is what the author meant earlier by saying that the continuous and enduring aspect of movement is its passage between the two limits.

    Many philosophers use this distinction to explain how things that begin can depend on an eternal cause. Circular motion, considered as one ongoing passage, is related to the lasting cause; considered through its endlessly changing positions and relationships, it is connected with changing events. What changes is thus linked through what changes, and what endures through what endures.

[^V03-255]: First, the earlier philosopher means that the remote agent—the First Cause or an eternal intellect—is beginningless. The nearby cause and subject of celestial motion are not.

[^V03-256]: Sadra may be answering that essential renewal needs no separate cause, since what is essential is not caused. But he is also distinguishing the renewal itself from the existence that is renewed: although renewal is not separately caused, the existence in which it occurs is brought about by a cause.

[^V03-257]: The point applies broadly, but time, motion, circles, and powers are especially useful examples. Their intellectual forms are very different from their sensory or imagined forms. A gradual, particular existence is unlike the general, unified reality the intellect grasps; prime matter is pure potentiality, while its intellectual concept is an abstract universal. Water, fire, and separate intellects are more readily understood in both general and particular forms.

[^V03-258]: This is the same problem raised earlier about how a changing thing can depend on an eternal source, now stated in a simpler form.

[^V03-259]: An unstated premise is that anything produced without a prepared receiver must be a separate, immaterial form. Prime matter does not count as such a receiver because it has no actual form of its own.

[^V03-260]: If the receiver itself came to be, there would be a break at the beginning of the supposedly continuous renewal of nature. The account would then need to explain what came before that break.

[^V03-261]: The regress is not merely a succession of causes, which some philosophers allow. The receiver in question is the actual bearer of a form, not the earlier bearer of its potentiality. It exists together with the form it receives, so the argument would produce an endless chain of causes existing together.

[^V03-262]: If the receiver is assumed to be eternal, the argument must still distinguish the case where it is sufficient to receive the form from the case where it is not. The question cannot be answered merely by assuming the receiver's eternity.

[^V03-263]: An eternal receiver that is sufficient for the form would make that form fixed, not renewed. If the receiver and giver are present throughout, every stage of the form would be present together. Also, the question assumes no succession of preparations in matter; without such succession, there can be no succession of levels in the form. The original argument divides the cases into four: no receiver, a new receiver, an eternal receiver with no changing readiness, and an eternal receiver with changing readiness.

[^V03-264]: The claim that matter is eternal is rejected by anyone trying to show that the whole world began. It would also imply an eternal matter for each kind, and possibly for each individual form.

[^V03-265]: The challenge can be repeated for each specific form of each kind, and then for each particular form, leading to as many eternal matters as there are forms.

[^V03-266]: Every specific readiness needs something that makes it ready. Matter has a general, distant potentiality; a particular form gives it the specific, immediate potentiality for one kind of change.

[^V03-267]: The upshot of this account is that bodily nature changes in its very being. It remains constant in being changeable, so it can depend on a cause that does not change. These bodily natures are not separate existences: in their flowing reality they are one continuous, substantial nature. To say that this flowing nature is given to matter means that its existence includes a side of lack and nonexistence. Matter is not something separate from it that is already fully actual; that would be a contradiction.

    On this understanding, the distinctions between bodily forms—fire, water, and the others—are like the distinctions between the parts of a motion. We divide and name them in thought; they are not cut apart in existence. Their effects nevertheless differ, as earlier differs from later and stronger from weaker. Each stage of this flowing nature has its particular degree and place through what it is. Just as one part of a journey comes before another because of its own position in the journey, no extra cause is required to give each stage its order.

    That is how bodily natures stand when considered in their continuously changing existence. When we instead consider the kinds that the mind distinguishes, fire differs from air and a human being from a horse, each with its own features and effects. Each particular form requires matter prepared to receive it. A previous form, together with other preparing conditions, gives matter the readiness for the next; the previous form ceases when the next appears. Each new event is thereby connected with its eternal cause through conditions that themselves arise. Those different conditions follow from successive parts of one uninterrupted motion. Together with the corresponding stretch of time and the eternal cause, a particular stage of that motion makes up a complete cause for the new effect.

[^V03-268]: Prime matter is not one numerically distinct receiver that must be either wholly new or wholly eternal. Its unity is generic, as a kind is shared through its forms. We can say it is new in the sense that its substantial existence is renewed with the forms united to it, not in the sense that it was once absent and then appeared as one event. Or we can call it eternal in the sense that this renewal never stops—not in the sense that it remains fixed or has no cause. Its unity is one identity with many levels, not one fixed state. This is especially clear if matter and form are understood as united in existence: pure potentiality has no fixed actuality that would prevent it from receiving any form.

[^V03-269]: All readiness, nonexistence, and deficiency belong to matter, which is one reality because pure potentiality has no distinctions within itself. This keeps deficiencies from being attributed to God. Every actuality, existence, and perfection comes from the source of actuality and good; evil does not come from it.

[^V03-270]: This suggests that we may choose the first answer if we consider specific forms as absorbed in their separate intellectual forms, or focus on the lasting root within them, like the middle motion within a complete path or the flowing instant within time. In this respect, the forms are creative acts, not dependent on earlier matter, readiness, time, or nonexistence. The natural world as a whole is brought from nothing into being; material and temporal things, by contrast, are considered together with their matter and time.

[^V03-271]: Because prime matter is pure potentiality and has no specific readiness of its own, any general form is enough to make it actual.

[^V03-272]: “For it” means the potentiality belonging to a form that is itself clothed in potentiality, such as a form's subject. “On it” means the potentiality belonging to the form that matter can receive. The final option is potentiality for a further perfection. These are alternatives, not mutually exclusive examples.

[^V03-273]: Although matter is what can receive forms, it is equally open to every form. A specific form is therefore needed to give it the particular readiness for one particular form.

[^V03-274]: As noted earlier, existences may differ in their basic reality, and sometimes the feature that distinguishes them is the same feature they share.

[^V03-275]: This comparison concerns kinds as essences and the additional features that distinguish individuals within a kind. Looked at as actual existences, individual things also differ by degrees of existence; Sadra has already used such differences to argue for substantial motion.

[^V03-276]: A connected whole is one individual reality because its continuity gives it one identity. It has no separate parts until the mind inserts a boundary. Any point we choose can divide it, and there is no final smallest division. A line of any length—even one imagined as endless—is one individual while its continuity remains unbroken.

[^V03-277]: This makes bodily nature four-dimensional: it has length, width, depth, and time.

[^V03-278]: An unbounded spatial extension considered without a particular limit is a natural body. When it is considered with a definite limit, it is mathematical extension, the body's measured size. Similarly, when bodily nature's renewal is considered without a particular time limit, it is motion; when measured by a year, month, or hour, it is time.

[^V03-279]: This reflects the view of Avicenna and Sadra. Some philosophers distinguish two kinds of continuity in a body: substantial continuity, which makes it a body able to receive three dimensions, and accidental continuity, which makes quantity divisible into parts sharing boundaries.

[^V03-280]: Time belongs to motion as a feature considered in thought, and motion belongs to nature in the same way. They are features of nature that are not later than it in existence. This resembles individuality as a feature of existence: existence, unity, and individuality are all present through one reality.

[^V03-281]: The argument against time is that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the indivisible present cannot itself be time. The everyday present is part of the past or future. If the time in the mind is fixed, it is not time; if it flows, it is only the present. The reply is that time exists as a flowing reality, like the continuous middle of motion, which cannot be divided into past and future. A connected path of motion and its measure, time, also exist because their source exists; “existence” includes both a thing and what is real through it.

[^V03-282]: This may refer to the theologians' “imagined time,” which they say exists only as a mental measure before the world, with God's eternal existence as its source. Or it may refer to time that is merely imagined and has no source in reality. Both views are false: eternal, changeless existence cannot be the source of an extension that does not remain fixed.

[^V03-283]: This view does not give a single, consistent measure of time. One event can be called the time of another—sunrise for someone's arrival, a person's arrival for someone's death—and the reverse could be said too. A familiar or prominent event may serve as a sign for a time, but the event itself is not time. It is the period in which two events occur together, and their being together is itself temporal.

[^V03-284]: This view treats time as the spiritual, eternal age, or as the shared reality of separate intellects, which are beyond matter. Their qualities are their very existence, though not their essences. Some who call time necessary in itself may be thinking of that higher, luminous aspect of existence.

[^V03-285]: Avicenna rejects the claim that time is the outermost sphere by pointing out that the argument's middle term shifts: bodies are “in” time, but the sphere is not “in” itself in the same sense. The commentator notes that the intended syllogism may be different, but it still has a weak form.

[^V03-286]: Avicenna rejects the claim that time is motion because some things contain a past and a future without being time, such as a flood or the Resurrection. The commentator adds that motion, like a natural body, is an extension; time, like mathematical body, is its measure. Only when motion is measured can it be divided into past and future. Their claim that we notice time only when we sense motion is weak: failing to notice motion also makes us fail to notice many other things, but that does not make time identical to them.

[^V03-287]: Avicenna argues that one revolution cannot be time, since each part of time is itself time, while part of a revolution is not another revolution.

[^V03-288]: The commentator objects to the claim that time is the measure of existence. Existence is too exalted and broad to be measured by body or motion, since it includes immaterial beings that precede place, time, and direction. If “existence” means one particular thing that exists, then its measure is simply motion. The note criticizes the view as an imprecise use of philosophical language.

[^V03-289]: Here “everlasting age” is used in the ordinary, broad sense of the whole temporal series being present to God at once. In that sense, the technical everlasting age is already included in the first relation described.

[^V03-290]: This means considering each changing thing as present together with each stage of another changing thing.

[^V03-291]: The commentator says Plato and Aristotle need not disagree: time is plainly the measure of celestial motion. Calling time an independent, lasting reality may mean that the reality behind time is the everlasting age, and behind that, eternity. Time is the measure of changing things; the everlasting age is the sphere of stable, separate realities; eternity is the “container,” so to speak, of God's existence and attributes. Each level must remain distinct.

[^V03-292]: If past and future belong to changing things only incidentally, there must be something that has priority and posteriority in its own right. That thing is time.

[^V03-293]: God is not described as earlier or later in time, though He may be called prior in the sense of eternity, causation, or sustaining existence. Causation is one way His presence with things is understood.

[^V03-294]: People used to curse time when misfortune came, thinking time had brought it about. The saying answers that God, not time, brings events about. It may also mean that one should honor time because it is God's effect and the record of His creative act. Or it may refer to the universal intellects, whose existence belongs to God's realm; ordinary time is then a subtle reflection of that higher reality.

[^V03-295]: By the “fixed” the sages mean the universal intellects, filled with God's light and existing through Him. The relation of God to His names and knowledge is eternity; the relation of fixed knowledge to its changing objects is the everlasting age; and the relation among those changing objects is time. The commentator notes that some accounts reverse which side of the relation is being described.

[^V03-296]: Each motion has its own time: its amount measured by its speed. The familiar day is simply the standard people use to compare other motions. Some motions begin or end, but the argument applies to the universal motion that encompasses the bodily world—the substantial motion of bodily nature. The close reading shows that no motion can be preceded by a stretch of its own time. Universal motion therefore has no prior time.

[^V03-297]: Do not mistake this for saying that the world exists eternally in the same way God does. God and what belongs to His own realm are eternal and deserve the names of perfection; the things that receive existence are temporal and pass away. God is always giving, while what receives His gift is renewed and then passes on to another. Each moment He is at work; there is no repetition in the act of giving.

[^V03-298]: The surprising claim is that this natural world has no first time or last time, even though each particular body and motion comes to be in time and is surrounded by nonexistence. The reason is that bodily nature itself renews through substantial motion; it does not need some separate thing outside itself to mark its temporal beginning.

[^V03-299]: This is especially directed at those who imagine the world to have been preceded by a stretch of empty time, with nonexistence placed alongside existence. Once that temporal order is accepted, the conclusion follows.

[^V03-300]: Both problems arise from finding an order in these cases: between nonexistence and existence, and between God and each event. In both, the earlier and later cannot exist together in the relevant respect, so the order is temporal. The comparison with places outside the world does not work: a place can be finite without another place beyond it, but a newly existing thing must be preceded by nonexistence.

[^V03-301]: This is a second way to state the objection that every time needs a prior time. It also risks making all times exist together as container and contained, and thereby making time's parts fixed. Sadra replies that the priority is either essential, in which case the ordered items are parts of time and need no further time, or incidental, in which case they are things in time. The regress is successive, not a simultaneous chain.

[^V03-302]: “By its own nature” refers to time's existence, which relates it to what comes before and after. The first reply is that time would be a relation only if this relation belonged to its concept; it belongs instead to its existence. The second reply distinguishes the concept of priority, which belongs to the category of relation, from the actual existence that makes something prior or later. That existence is not itself a relation.

[^V03-303]: What a continuum's parts cannot differ in is their essence as parts of a continuous whole. They can still differ in their individual identities and positions in the whole.

[^V03-304]: The objector's argument reverses the point. “Finite” here means having a limit in the sense of a boundary, not the opposite of infinity as a number. The past has a boundary on the side that reaches us, but that does not make it finite without qualification. Existence is not a container that counts and confines all that enters it; an infinite series can exist, and there can be more than one infinite series.

[^V03-305]: Suppose a body has existed forever and has always undergone events with no first event, such as a heavenly sphere passing through an endless series of positions. On the argument being examined, the body cannot be earlier than the whole series of events, since there is no first one. Nor can it be earlier than their absence, since that absence is also said to be eternal. Some manuscripts repeat the words 'and is earlier' at this point.

    A contradiction then threatens. The body is *not* earlier than the events, by the assumption just made. Yet it also seems that it *is* earlier: it exists together with the supposed eternal absence of the events, and what exists with something earlier should itself be earlier. Or the body is earlier than every particular event; the whole series has no existence beyond those particular events, so it should be earlier than the series too.

    Another problem appears. The body is said not to precede the events, yet it must precede the eternal absence that is earlier than each event. Whatever has truly existed eternally cannot at the same time have been absent; the supposed eternal absence comes to an end when an event begins. This is another way to state the difficulty.

    The reasoning may also be put like this: although the body is not prior to the collection of events considered together, it is prior to each event. Since the collection has no separate existence apart from its members, that difference is hard to maintain. The same point will become clearer in the reply to the eighth objection, where something that always accompanies changing events is said to precede their individual occurrences.

    The wording needs care. 'Of these things' may explain what is meant by 'each one.' The repeated phrase in some copies is probably a copying error. The final claim that such priority is impossible may be intended to support the denial that the body precedes the eternal absence: if the body does not precede the events that come *after* that absence, how could it precede the absence itself?

[^V03-306]: The first argument resembles the proof that spatial dimensions are finite: compare the number of past cycles, years, or souls with the same number plus one from the future. The comparison assumes that all these things can be gathered together. But past events do not coexist as one collection; only the imagination gathers them. Bodily powers are finite, and the intellect, which is immaterial, cannot be measured by this comparison.

[^V03-307]: The first part of the argument repeats the second: if prior nonexistence is in time, it already assumes the conclusion. The other reading—that an earlier existence entails later nonexistence—is the converse of the same point.

[^V03-308]: A better argument would say that the whole collection begins because each event in it begins. But the whole has no existence separate from its members. This is not always a fallacy: it works for a connected continuum, where the whole and its parts are connected. Sadra himself argues that every bodily event is renewed and surrounded by nonexistence, and therefore the whole natural world is renewed too. Without this point, that conclusion would be unsupported.

[^V03-309]: Most philosophers say that the collection exists as one whole. Sadra denies that it has a separate existence of its own.

[^V03-310]: At every moment there is a new collection of departed rational souls, as more people die and leave their bodies. The world as a whole is also renewed continually. This may refer to substantial motion, as Sadra holds, or to the idea that the whole world changes because some of its parts pass away at every moment. The first reading better fits his account; the second fits the immediate example.

[^V03-311]: That is, the event cannot be described as having no beginning. Yet an endless series of events need have neither a last event nor a first event. There was no particular time empty of events: to say that something is beginningless is, in this use, to deny a first moment, not to name a time. This answer is closest to the opponent’s own way of thinking.

    A stronger answer distinguishes the senses in which we speak of eternity. Sometimes we mean the indefinitely distant past. That is still time: a continuous extent whose parts pass away. It would be unworthy of God to say that His existence, attributes or action belong to such a past. Sometimes we mean something like the setting for an existence beyond all completeness, from which the descending order of beings begins. What corresponds to it at the end of the ascending order is called everlastingness. Both belong to the order flowing from God. In a still fuller sense, eternity refers to existence before all particular forms and limitations, without viewing it merely as the beginning of beginnings or the end of ends. True oneness sets aside these relations.

    In the last two senses, eternity is no bounded time. It embraces all such settings of existence, including past and future times, as necessary existence encompasses the essences of things. Scripture and those who speak on God’s behalf use it in these senses when referring to His existence, attributes, and power to act. The same distinctions apply to everlastingness.

[^V03-312]: The objector's argument about the possibility of events is meant to imply that God's power must have a beginning. For theologians, the possibility of the world and its being created are tied to divine power. The commentator says this makes the objection too long and weak: possibility belongs to the created world, while power belongs to God. A sharper reply is that possibility is the same as potentiality, and it cannot itself have a beginning.

[^V03-313]: The objector means that existence has bounded past events on the side that reaches the present. The reply is that this does not prove a beginning on the other side. The argument can also be turned against the claim that events can begin.

[^V03-314]: The seventh argument may mean that the body is described both by all past events and by their nonexistence, which would be contradictory. But the whole collection of past events does not exist at once. Or it may mean that the body is described at each moment by one event and by the absence of another. That is not contradictory: the event present at that time is not the event absent from it.

[^V03-315]: This notes a hidden individual case, as opposed to the obvious case of any one event. If “the world” is a collection, each moment has a new collection of events; if it means every individual event, none of those individuals is absent from the world as a whole in the same sense.

[^V03-316]: This objection answers those who define “the world” as everything other than God, and who accept separate intellects. It does not apply to those who mean only the bodily world by “the world.”

[^V03-317]: This wording points toward Sadra's own argument: if the world had not begun, it would precede and be separate from its events, contrary to what is assumed.

[^V03-318]: The point is that a subject that never lacks events would, if those events were finite, have to precede the earliest event. If the events are infinite, however, any event the subject precedes is itself preceded by another event, and so on without end.

[^V03-319]: Sadra accepts the eighth argument, but gives it a different meaning. The world is always accompanied by changing events, and what is never without change has itself begun in time. This means that each bodily substance, nature, soul, and accident is preceded by temporal nonexistence; it does not mean that there was one first time after which the world began all at once.

[^V03-320]: “What is in the mind” means the existence of the world as represented in the mind—in other words, the world as known by someone who knows it.

[^V03-321]: This anticipates the conclusion: the opponent's position would make the world's existence depend on something other than God. It also does not follow that the world's actual existence is finite; the past may be an endless succession, though not one collection that exists all at once.

[^V03-322]: The “whole collection” is either an imagined collection of events or a collection that exists outside the mind. If it is imagined, it began as a mental picture. If it is taken to exist in the world, it is finite because past events no longer exist and future ones do not yet exist; the infinite series is successive, not one whole.

[^V03-323]: The past-tense word “was” implies both existence and time. If it means only “was nonexistent, then came to exist,” the claim still assumes succession and contradicts the view that time itself belongs to the world.

[^V03-324]: Priority in the order of nature is essential: a possible thing is nothing by itself and exists only through its cause. What belongs to a thing by itself is prior to what it has through another.

[^V03-325]: The same issue appears in Jamal al-Din al-Khwansari's claim that the religious view requires a gap between God and the world. This would make God's existence new or limited, and would place pure, all-encompassing existence alongside the world.

[^V03-326]: The philosophers say priority has several degrees, and causal priority is the clearest and most deserving of being called priority.

[^V03-327]: The parties may also disagree about whether God's giving is unending and His words never pass away, while what receives existence is temporary and limited. One side says that what belongs to God is eternal and what comes from Him is new; the other reverses this. Then the difference between belief in a creator and denying one becomes clear. It also distinguishes belief in God's oneness from imagining Him as a body: power, when treated as a bodily capacity, depends on matter. The note connects this issue to the Qur'anic image of God's hands being tied, and argues that the best account of creation preserves both God's perfect names and attributes and the world's renewal.

[^V03-328]: This can mean, first, that denying God's oneness in action makes Him one among several agents: some new event or will would share the work of bringing the world into being. That added agent would itself have to be necessary in existence, or the world would not be new. Second, the phrase can mean that denying oneness in what is produced does not imply that God's own essence is multiple; philosophers hold that one source gives rise to one thing.

[^V03-329]: A second agent would also conflict with God's will being one in its relation to all things, His knowledge being active, His will effective, and His existence necessary in every respect. It would also make Him seem to withhold the goodness and generosity that follow from wisdom and fullness, or to fall silent instead of endlessly speaking and giving.

[^V03-330]: The mystic's criticism assumes that “the world is eternal in time” means that the world has existed only since time existed. If “world” means everything other than God, the phrase may be using “time” broadly to include the everlasting age; if it means pure intellects, “with time” can mean that they coexist with their cause. In either case, it need not mean that all things are measured by ordinary time.

[^V03-331]: The idea that time existed before bodies is a weak interpretation and has no place in a serious account.

[^V03-332]: The Persian couplet means: “Where You are, there is no me; / no one can enter this mystery.” The point is that beings are related to God, while God is not dependent on them.

[^V03-333]: The mystic's words do not prove that the world began. Those who say that the heavens and basic elements last forever can accept that God is beyond time and that effects do not exist in the same way as their cause.

[^V03-334]: A bodily power is limited both in its own capacity and in what it can do or undergo. Since it is spread through a body, its strength changes with the body's size and cannot exceed the body's limits. The note says the question of its power to act and be affected will be discussed later.

[^V03-335]: This is the first of two ways to understand the opponent's reply. The world, as one individual existence, may have only limited power and may not last forever by itself, yet its effects may be continually supplied by a higher source. The note reads this as a view that denies substantial motion and treats the world's existence as numerically fixed.

[^V03-336]: This answer rules out the first interpretation, so the text can turn to the second.

[^V03-337]: This is the flowing now, which traces or produces time as it flows, just as motion through the middle of a path traces the motion considered as a whole.

[^V03-338]: Cutting time apart would also cut the celestial motion that measures it, and that would make the celestial body stop. The note also says that cutting time in principle means a break in the flow of existence.
