[^V03-339]: “In time” is broader than “at the boundary of time.” Something that occurs at an instant is still temporal, since an instant is the boundary of time. So instantaneous things and things spread across time can both be called temporal.

[^V03-340]: For example, contact that lasts for a while.

[^V03-341]: For example, reaching a point along a path while moving.

[^V03-342]: A fuller account of where things exist distinguishes the eternal realm, where God exists; higher and lower levels of the timeless realm, where intellects and universal souls exist; higher and lower levels of the realm of suspended forms and universal natural principles; existence in an instant; and two ways of existing in time—with something spread across it or without being spread across it. The book gives examples of these kinds.

[^V03-343]: You might object that if something can occur in an instant, it must exist only in an instant. Here, however, “now” means the flowing now, which produces time rather than contradicting it. The author later says that a moving thing is never without motion or rest at any instant of its motion. Motion itself cannot occur in a single instant, and rest is not actual motion. Yet at each instant the moving thing is still described as moving. Not having a specific kind of motion does not mean it has no motion at all.

[^V03-344]: The first either-or asks whether a thing occurs all at once or not all at once. The second asks whether its coming to be has a first instant or has none. These are not the same question.

[^V03-345]: “Gradually” here means strictly spread across time, not the broader sense of moving from potential to actual. That broader meaning also includes motion through the middle of a path, which exists in time without matching it part for part.

[^V03-346]: The phrase “and it does not exist at the start of that time” means that it is not present at the first instant, which would make it instantaneous. Something spread across time has an extension and parts corresponding to parts of time. Something that exists in time without being spread across it has no parts or extension; motion through the middle of a path is simple but flowing, as are the absence of an instant and other cases discussed later. The first kind is present throughout its time; the second occurs in time without extending across it.

[^V03-347]: Avicenna's wording in *The Healing* is: “It is proper to ask whether the shared instant between two stretches of time can be free of both states, or whether one state must be present there.” In the present text, some words needed to introduce the question seem to be missing. Perhaps the author is shortening Avicenna's passage, or using “whether” as in the question “Does it exist?”

[^V03-348]: You might say that motion begins at the shared instant, so there are not two instants. The reply is that the shared instant belongs to rest; the moving thing has not yet begun moving. Its first instant of motion must come after the shared instant.

[^V03-349]: Motion through the middle of a path is simple but not at rest, so it cannot exist at a single fixed instant. The flowing now is what suits it. As Avicenna says, it is a renewed state of the moving thing, a changing nearness or distance. Since its state is never the same, Plato called motion “a departure from equality.”

[^V03-350]: For example, an angle formed as one line moves alongside another, discussed later.

[^V03-351]: For example, the contact of a moving cone with a stationary cone at their tips. Their contact occurs in an instant, but its absence unfolds through time without matching time part for part. The same is true when one sphere moves away from another after they touch.

[^V03-352]: One might say that absence of contact is temporal, not instantaneous, so this does not divide the contact itself. The answer is that “gradual” here has the strict meaning of being spread across time. It does not mean every kind of change from potential to actual, which includes both motion through the middle of a path and motion considered as a whole. Strictly speaking, motion through the middle is the real gradual process.

[^V03-353]: That is, an interval of time between the two instants. The word “between” makes clear that it is a real interval, not another instant.

[^V03-354]: A thing can have two kinds of beginning. One is a boundary of a different kind, such as a point for a line, rest for motion, or an instant for time. The other is its first part, which is of the same kind as the thing itself. A gradual process has no first part of that second kind. No indivisible part can begin a line or stretch of time; even the smallest part that can be imagined can still be divided, and every part has the same nature as the whole.

[^V03-355]: You may think rest is instantaneous, since it is the absence of motion. But rest is not instantaneous. Motion itself is measured by the moving thing's being between the start and end of its path: at any point on the path, it has not yet reached that point before the instant of arrival, and after arrival it is no longer moving toward it. Rest is measured by two states of the thing in which motion is possible, so it lasts through time. Also, the absence of a gradual process is gradual, as we will see.

[^V03-356]: Motion in a category requires the thing to have, at every instant, a state in that category different from its state at the instant before and the instant after. That is the test for motion in a category.

[^V03-357]: That is, gradual in the strict sense of extending across time. The reference is to motion considered as a whole, not to motion through the middle of a path.

[^V03-358]: The passage names sounds as examples of states that do not remain fixed in themselves but follow from motion. Here the reference is to motion along a straight path and its measures. An angle formed by two crossing lines occurs in an instant; an angle formed by a moving line has no first instant in the same sense as motion itself.

[^V03-359]: That is, instantaneous things that remain after the first instant in which they exist.

[^V03-360]: The boundary may come from dividing time in thought or from the different events that occur within it. As explained earlier, time has no boundary in either of the two senses discussed there.

[^V03-361]: The moving thing is between the start and end of its path in such a way that it has not reached any chosen point just before the instant of reaching it, and is no longer moving toward that point just after.

[^V03-362]: The flowing now differs both from a single arrival and from one continuous arrival that lasts over time; both of those are temporal in different ways.

[^V03-363]: The line invites the reader to reflect inwardly. The divine reality is one and simple, though it appears in all things. Differences belong to the things in which it appears, not to God's own presence. If that presence seems to differ from one thing to another, the difference is on the side of the things, not on God's side. God remains; all else passes away.

[^V03-364]: The issue is how motion ceases after it has existed—its passing away—not the general fact that it is absent at times when it does not exist.

[^V03-365]: Each imagined part of motion is actual in relation to the part before it, which was its potential, and potential in relation to the part after it, which will become actual. Potential and actual are interwoven in motion. So just as motion comes to exist gradually, it also ceases gradually.

[^V03-366]: This also means that the natural world, whose existence is always unfolding, does not simply cease at some later time. Its nonexistence, like its coming to be, consists of successive stages. Sadra says in several books that the world's coming to be and its continued existence occupy the same stretch of time. The human soul, too, comes to be over time: its powers and habits are formed by the knowledge it gains from the beginning of life to the end, so it is not complete at a single instant. Its creation includes the whole time in which it exists. The same is true of the greater world. This does not mean that God's act is weak or slow. His command is simply “Be,” and it is. The gradual creation of heaven and earth is what is meant by their being made in six days—the span of the world's life, whose length only God knows. God's gift does not stop or weaken; the whole period unfolds within it. The six days also correspond to the call of the six messengers of resolve. The life of each, including the survival of his teachings and his twelve successors, is described as twelve thousand years: one divine day linked to the manifestation of a thousand of God's names, even if it spans thousands of ordinary years. The sixth day is the age of the Qur'an's revelation, from the first appearance of the Seal of the Prophets and his teachings to the last of his community's spiritual leaders and their rightful rule. Its universal reach and fullness do not cease. The Prophet was a prophet when Adam was still between water and clay, and Abraham was among his followers. His spiritual reality embraced all the intellects, like a universal intellect. Even if this period lasts six days or many thousands of years, to God it is like a glance or less. What is to be will be; the pen has run dry.

[^V03-367]: This may seem to contradict the earlier claim, from both Sadra and Avicenna, that motion as a whole extends across time, while motion through the middle exists in time without matching it part for part. The apparent conflict can be resolved by considering motion in two ways: its existence is all at once, while its nature is gradual; or motion exists in the world through a changing thing, while motion considered by itself is in the mind. What exists in the mind is not spread across time.

[^V03-368]: As noted earlier, motion within motion is not impossible; it occurs. What is impossible is an endless chain of changes within changes that never reaches a stable basis. The same applies when one feature belongs to another feature: the chain must end in a substance.

[^V03-369]: This follows from Sadra's view of substantial motion. Avicenna may have stated something that points toward that view, even if he did not fully adopt it.

[^V03-370]: This is itself an argument for substantial motion: a substantial form comes to be after another substantial form.

[^V03-371]: In this second sense, “measure” names a thing by what it causes: the instant makes time countable.

[^V03-372]: The shared boundary relates equally to both sides. It has no length of its own, so it does not separate them with a gap; it joins them.

[^V03-373]: This restates the point just made.

[^V03-374]: “Measure” here means something that makes another thing countable. Motion and time each make the other multiple: motion gives time its earlier and later parts, and time gives motion its count.

[^V03-375]: People, considered in themselves, have neither continuous nor separate quantity. Their bodies have continuous size, while their number is separate or discrete. The number ten is a quantity that makes them count as ten. Likewise, time is a quantity that measures motion. In this respect, time is to motion as geometrical extension is to a physical body.

[^V03-376]: Here “measure” means “make something have a certain amount.”

[^V03-377]: The copies read “by its amount”; the intended meaning is “by showing its amount.” Units of time—such as years, months, weeks, days, hours, and minutes—show how much motion has occurred.

[^V03-378]: The wording in the copies is unclear. The sense requires “by the amount,” as shown by the examples of the measuring cup and what it contains.

[^V03-379]: This refers to time.

[^V03-380]: There are not two separate existences here. The path and motion are one existence, considered in different ways. When we consider it through one aspect, it is the cause; through another, it is the effect.

[^V03-381]: The wording might suggest that motion and its continuity are two separate existences. The distinction exists only in how we think about them.

[^V03-382]: The word “in” has different meanings in different cases: something can be in a place, in time, in a material, in a subject, or in an essence or existence. So “motion in time,” “time in motion,” “a broader kind in a species,” and “a species in a broader kind” each use “in” in a different way.

[^V03-383]: The instant is not time, just as unity is not a number; the two are different kinds of things. Earlier and later occur throughout the kinds and parts of time, just as even and odd occur throughout kinds and parts of number. Hours, days, weeks, and months are kinds of time, just as two, three, and four are kinds of number.

[^V03-384]: The note proposes changing the wording from “two motions flank it” to “two periods of rest flank the motion.”

[^V03-385]: This does not fit easily with the later claim that other categories change only indirectly through the change of substance. The note leaves that tension for the reader to consider.

[^V03-386]: The reference is to motion from place to place. As explained earlier, this motion comes before changes in quality and quantity because those depend on it. The circular motion of the outermost sphere is the first and oldest motion of all.

[^V03-387]: Calling changes in other categories “indirect” conflicts with Sadra's view that they exist as modes of their subject, especially if an accident is a level of the subject's own existence. If the subject changes while its features remain fixed, those features would seem able to exist without it, which is impossible. The better view is that these categories truly change along with substance, not merely by association.

[^V03-388]: “As they exist” means “in their existence.” Earlier in the book, Sadra says that any being, even a body, belongs to metaphysics simply as something that exists; it belongs to natural philosophy as a body, and to mathematics as something measurable. Still, the timeless duration of changing things is lower than that of purely immaterial beings. The timeless realm, dahr, contains immaterial beings and changing things considered in their luminous aspect. Stable beings, insofar as they depend on the Eternal, belong to the eternal realm, sarmad. God's eternity is beyond any duration—timeless or temporal—and beyond any extension, whether across space or through a chain of things.

[^V03-389]: Most copies have this wording. It seems to be a copying error: the discussion of motion is marked as a chapter, so it would be strange for some related points to be marked as a stage.

[^V03-390]: The clearest argument here is that motion begins from pure potentiality. Some people count the actual state at which motion ends as its starting point, but motion ends in pure actuality, without the potential that it contains. Potential and actuality are opposites in this respect. Still, there is no proof that the starting point and destination of every motion are strict opposites. Where they are opposites, that is only by coincidence.

[^V03-391]: “Larger” and “smaller” here mean the larger and smaller sizes expected within a thing's own kind—not a seed's smallness compared with the size of the outermost sphere.

[^V03-392]: That is, they resemble opposites.

[^V03-393]: The two directions are the natural directions. Most motion occurs between them; in reality, there is no single natural motion from one true endpoint all the way to the other.

[^V03-394]: The beginning and end of circular motion are not points. They are positions, and the two positions are never the same at the same time.

[^V03-395]: The beginning and end may be found in different, non-overlapping parts of motion. There are also possible beginnings and ends that can coincide because they are relative to what comes before or after. Along with an actual beginning and end, these make three kinds.

[^V03-396]: This change follows the underlying thing; it is not merely something that happens to it by accident.

[^V03-397]: “In” here means “within time.” Time is one of the six things on which motion depends. If there were motion in the category of “when,” there would have to be another time in which that motion occurred.

[^V03-398]: Motion occurring within motion would only slow the first movement. In the same way, if there were motion in the category of “when,” it would slow the passage of time. There is no impossibility in that unless it leads to an endless series. When all the categories change along with a changing substance, they do not change merely in name. Each has a change suited to it and a corresponding time, so that none falls behind the substance it belongs to or runs ahead of it. Think of someone aboard a ship, who moves with the ship while also being able to move about or sit still on board.

    Neither of Avicenna's arguments settles the question. First, motion in the category of “when” would be a different individual motion from the motion through which the body comes to have a time. Nothing has shown that this is impossible. Second, another “when” would only make the substance more deeply involved in the first time, slowing its passage. There is no difficulty unless this leads to an endless regress.

[^V03-399]: Sadra reads Avicenna's words this way because “when”—existing in time—belongs to motion and to what moves. The movement and its time extend continuously together. A change from one month, hour, or minute to the next therefore proceeds gradually: there is no actual break in either time or what exists in it. Sadra takes Avicenna to be referring to the point already established: although a process unfolds gradually, the existence of that process considered as a process does not itself unfold in stages.

    I have another reading. Avicenna says “transition,” not “motion.” He may be speaking of passing from one kind of time to another, as from night to day, or from one particular hour to the next. That transition happens at the instant that separates them. Though time has no actual gap, its different kinds and individual stretches have a boundary; without that boundary, we could not distinguish them.

[^V03-400]: Avicenna means that a thing's time depends on its motion. Time is the setting in which motion occurs, and so it exists whenever the motion exists. To say that motion is “in” time does not mean that time is its subject, as a path is the subject of motion; it means that time provides the setting for motion.

[^V03-401]: This would mean that motion in the categories of acting and being acted upon is the same motion viewed from two sides: as motion of the mover and as motion of the moved thing. The question remains which category motion itself belongs to. Sadra treats it as a way that existence appears in the world of nature.

[^V03-402]: The change could also be from weak heating to stronger heating. If someone objects that change in quality passes through several shades, we reply that a quality is a stable state that can exist at an instant; it need not remain unchanged in the next instant. There need not be a pause between its degrees. Acting and being acted upon, by contrast, are gradual processes and cannot be complete in a single instant. A pause between them is no more surprising than a pause between two opposite motions.

[^V03-403]: This argument can be challenged. If a category exists only together with motion, then it must have instantaneous limits or instances where motion ends. These would be possible even if they are always potential. Just as an extended quantity can be divided again after an earlier division, a number can be divided into units that themselves contain tens. So the instant that is a boundary for one motion can be part of a time for another motion. The instant need not become time for the motion it bounds.

[^V03-404]: The more natural reading reverses this point, unless the text is deliberately reversing it or means the instant on the assumption that motion occurs within it.

[^V03-405]: All features change along with nature, but not all have the same kind of change. For some, change is part of their existence, as with the categories in which motion occurs. For others, such as acting, being acted upon, time, and motion, change belongs to the idea of the category. For still others, such as relation, change belongs indirectly to the thing from which the relation is drawn.

[^V03-406]: This reply would work only if motion had first been defined, and then used as the standard for defining rest. Why not define rest first and motion from it?

[^V03-407]: Time measures motion; the instant is a boundary of time, and before and after are temporal relations. Motion can be defined without using rest: its first completion and its gradual passage from potentiality to actuality are enough. Even if rest were defined first, motion could then be defined from it.

[^V03-408]: The note simply says that this point is disputed.

[^V03-409]: The change comes from within the body in the relevant place. So it does not follow that the change occurs without a cause.

[^V03-410]: At every instant, the moving thing is described as moving through the whole stretch of time, though its motion is not contained in one instant. What depends on a thing in its own realm cannot be separated from what it depends on in a higher realm. For example, time-bound existence depends on timeless existence, and the existence of the heavens depends on the universal intellect.

[^V03-411]: If a body's motion stops and later resumes, the new motion is not the same individual motion as before, because a different time has passed. The personal continuity that made it one motion was broken. If continuity is not broken, what occurs later is still part of the same individual motion.

[^V03-412]: The wording falls short. For a motion to remain one individual motion, five things must remain the same: its subject, time, path, starting point, and destination. Changing either endpoint changes the individual motion even when the others stay the same, just as changing the path does.

    You may object that a change of starting point or destination makes motions different in kind, as the author will say below. But a change of path can do so too. Moreover, an individual motion belongs to a kind, and that kind depends on what makes it the kind it is. A change that produces a different kind must also produce a different individual motion.

    Changing the mover alone need not produce a new motion. Two people may keep the same wheel turning, or two sources of heat may warm the same water, provided its continuous change is not interrupted. This does not mean that two independent causes each produce the very same effect. In short, the loss of any one of those five things ends the motion's individual unity, and a difference in any of them makes it another motion.

[^V03-413]: The motion's defining principles are like the essential features that make a thing a particular kind. These are its starting point, the kind of change, and its destination—not its agent, its subject, or its time. A change in kind in one of these principles gives a different kind of motion; a merely individual difference gives a different individual motion. The path can distinguish a kind as well as an individual, so there is no contradiction in mentioning it in both ways.

[^V03-414]: Speed and slowness do not even make motions different individuals, much less different kinds. The same motion becomes faster as it nears its goal.

[^V03-415]: This is a concession to the objection. In fact, motion is more unified than a straight line, which is one continuous quantity. If even ten, whose nature is to be many, has a unity and identity of its own, then motion must have them all the more, since its many parts are only potential.

[^V03-416]: This supports the earlier reply. Everything in the world combines what has passed with what is still to come, what is fading with what is renewed, and parts with a single identity. In this way, it remains one whole.

[^V03-417]: A shadow or patch of light on flowing water may look like one thing, though it is renewed at every instant. This is like the continual renewal of the world: one world passes away and another comes to be, through God's names as the One who takes away and the One who brings forth. This is the way of God, and it does not change. The world, viewed in itself, is always being renewed; viewed in relation to God, the Eternal, it is one and unchanging.

[^V03-418]: This completes the answer to the doubt. In Avicenna's view, motion through the middle of the path of a heavenly body is one, simple, and everlasting. This unity is stronger than the unity the doubters reject. Such motion depends on the one, simple, unchanging Creator, while its changing parts depend on changing events. This is how the changing is linked to the eternal.

[^V03-419]: The argument is stronger if based on this: each part of a motion is actual in relation to the part before it and potential in relation to the part after it. The same part cannot be absent between its potential and its actuality. Our senses—sight especially—often mislead us about motion and rest.

[^V03-420]: This means the resistance that opposes forced motion, unlike the resistance of the medium in natural motion. A body thrown upward through air or water also meets resistance from the medium.

[^V03-421]: You may ask: how can speed and slowness be understood independently of each other when their definitions mention less time and more time, which involve a comparison? I reply, first, that these expressions need not be accepted as definitions. Second, the discussion concerns speed and slowness in themselves; here “less” and “more” can simply mean a small or large amount. We can also speak of one motion as *faster than* or *slower than* another, but those are relative descriptions.

    The distinction is like one made earlier about length: length in itself need not be longer or shorter than anything, though comparative length is relative. Number can be many without comparison, while being more numerous than another number is a relative property.

[^V03-422]: If true opposites must differ as greatly as possible, speed and slowness do not seem to be opposites: for any fast or slow motion, we can imagine one faster or slower still. The proposed limits of moving and resisting powers do not resolve this. Opposition depends on what things are by nature, not on which examples happen to exist.

    In truth, what belongs to every motion is its speed, understood as its way of passing and coming to an end. When we compare motions, we describe one as faster or slower than another. The same motion is slower than one motion and faster than a different one. These are relations, not two qualities opposed in themselves. Just as existence can be described as stronger or weaker by comparison, speed admits similar comparisons. Speed belongs to motion itself even though we divide motions into fast and slow; likewise unity belongs to existence even though we distinguish one and many.

    The slower motion has more composition, just as multiplicity comes from a more complex existence. The simpler the motion, the faster it is; greater complexity makes it slower. I know of no leading philosopher who has put this conclusion in these words, but the arguments leave no way around it. Consider it carefully.

[^V03-423]: Time is included in the definitions of speed and slowness. This is why motion can be divided into faster and slower forms by time, as well as by the other things on which it depends.

[^V03-424]: This is like the relation between existence and what a thing is. Without a particular existence, we could not draw out what the thing is; in that sense, what it is depends on existence. In thought, we can treat what a thing is as the subject and existence as what is said of it, but in the world they are one. The commentator's own answer is that motion beyond time causes time, while motions within time depend on particular times. This fits Sadra's view that nature is always changing, and that time measures this renewal.

[^V03-425]: For example, heat and cold can each be agents in a process of becoming black.

[^V03-426]: “Beginning” and “end” here do not mean rest at the start and finish. They mean the connected states through which motion passes. Motion is a flowing state, understood by its relation to what comes before and after; as Sadra says, its nature is to leave and to aim.

[^V03-427]: A line is simple in a way a body is not. A body can keep its matter while its form changes. Straightness and curvature either define a line or belong to two kinds of line; either way, changing between them means the line itself changes.

[^V03-428]: This is another way to deny that straight and circular motions oppose each other: straight and circular paths are not opposites, as the previous chapter explained.

[^V03-429]: That is, the point a straight motion begins from would be the point a circular motion moves toward, so the two motions would run in opposite directions.

[^V03-430]: The author says “motions along them” rather than “motion along the chord,” so the point applies to every circular path compared with other circular paths.

[^V03-431]: If the arcs were all one kind, they would share one definition. But their essential features differ, so their kinds differ too.

[^V03-432]: The commentator distinguishes the celestial body's position at the end of one day's motion from its position at the start of the next. He questions the claim that these are the very same point in circular motion. The passage first denies that circular motions oppose each other, then signals a more careful account.

[^V03-433]: The reply misses its target: it assumes a shared endpoint, though none has been shown. If there were an actual shared boundary, it would be a point between lines, an instant between times, or rest between motions. In that case, the boundary would divide the lines, times, or motions into two. The critic's deeper point is sound: opposite motions are two individual motions of different kinds. If they joined without rest into one continuous motion, they would be one individual motion despite belonging to different kinds, which is impossible.

[^V03-434]: The commentator clarifies that the argument uses “becoming black” for the movement that follows reaching the darkest point and turns toward white. That movement does not begin while the thing is still white. A white thing may have a remote possibility of becoming white again, but that does not prove the same power is producing both changes at once.

[^V03-435]: The proof uses an inward tendency in the body. It can begin at an instant and can be felt as the body resists what blocks it. This avoids the earlier problem about motion having no first part: separation takes time, though it has a boundary instant.

[^V03-436]: This is not a special exception added to the proof. Turning back means leaving the destination of the first motion altogether; passing a point along the path is not the same thing.

[^V03-437]: The source word here means the felt tendency by which a body resists what blocks it. It does not mean desire or love, which the commentator says runs through all things.

[^V03-438]: The ball's motion in this example comes only from its connection to the turning wheel, not from itself. The argument concerns motion a thing has in itself; carried motion is like rest when considered on its own.

[^V03-439]: The objector is not agreeing that the stone rests. The point is that rest would not occur because the force blocking it had been removed; the force is still there, and no cause of rest has yet been shown.

[^V03-440]: Motion shows that the unusual force is present. If air resistance exists only while the stone is moving, it cannot explain how that force disappears: its supposed cause of removal depends on the very motion that reveals the force.

[^V03-441]: Once the critic has asked what causes the unusual force to disappear, he asks what causes the stone to rest above.

[^V03-442]: The question is not why the obstacle is missing after the resistance ends. The point is that Avicenna claims an extra power is needed to make the stone rest, though a balance of powers should already explain rest. The claim that this balance must last is weak: bodily powers have limited effects, especially forced powers, which do not act forever or most of the time.

[^V03-443]: “Condition” is intended here, not “preparatory cause.” A condition remains with what depends on it; a preparatory cause can act earlier. The weakening and its cause prepare for rest, while balance is a condition.

[^V03-444]: Nature resists forced movement, just as a living body resists illness and tends toward recovery and its natural activity.

[^V03-445]: The air's impacts prepare the body for rest and weaken the unusual force. A preparatory cause does not need to be present at the moment its result occurs. Nature itself is the direct cause of rest.

[^V03-446]: Someone who denies rest between motions will not accept rest at the final instant of the first motion. They accept it only after the return or turn has been completed. The proof needs rest at the upper point.

[^V03-447]: The commentator explains that an absence can still need a cause. Rest may be a possible absence, or it may follow from a positive state; either way, a cause is involved.

[^V03-448]: The eight heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere. Their motion is neither in themselves nor forced, since nothing forces the heavens.

[^V03-449]: Carried motion is still connected to one of the three main kinds. The heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere; a passenger on a ship is carried along while at rest in themselves.

[^V03-450]: The pulse should not be called voluntary, even if breathing can be controlled in some ways. The heart and arteries pulse several times during each expansion and contraction of the breathing organs, and are refreshed by what comes from the chest and lungs.

[^V03-451]: The claim that the pulse is movement from place to place is weak, since it does not change location. Unless it means a tightening motion, the pulse is better understood as a change in size: expansion and contraction, with rest between them. If it were a change of position, it would resemble a person gradually lying down and standing up, passing through countless positions with a pause between movements. The note means that “most doctors” refers to less careful medical writers, who usually classified the pulse as a change of position or size, not movement from place to place.

[^V03-452]: The passage appears to combine different views about the pulse. One holds that the heart and arteries contract and expand through their own nature. Another holds that the movement comes from the living power in the heart, as discussed earlier. A third places that power in the arteries. I have recorded other views in my poem *Gems of Insight*. Perhaps saying that the heart and arteries produce the movement simply means that they receive it. — س ره

[^V03-453]: “Air” here means smoke.

[^V03-454]: The pulse, breathing, and growth in animals are examples of motion directed by the soul through nature. This is why the author adds a fifth kind of motion, alongside the four already listed. Celestial motion is also placed in this fifth kind.

[^V03-455]: These explanations avoid two misunderstandings: that the heavens' form is a nature like the four elements, and that their motion is natural in exactly the same way as the elements' motion. Both explanations say that celestial motion is chosen, but resembles natural motion because it follows one steady pattern.

[^V03-456]: That is, “nature” is being used in one of its several meanings described earlier.

[^V03-457]: This is the view of Thābit ibn Qurra. He says the earth is not held at the center because the heavens push or pull it. Those are two other explanations. The higher does not pay attention to the lower.

[^V03-458]: We could also choose the first answer: the earth seeks the center in the sense that it seeks to have its own center coincide with the center of the world. It does not seek to occupy a point at the center. As for the earth's parts, no part exists on its own until something separates it. Until then, the earth is one continuous body. A part separated by force joins the whole again when the force is removed, so it is not an independent thing whose aim we can judge by itself. But the view that heavy bodies seek the center and light bodies seek the outer edge—even with the meaning we have given it—would mean that water and air are always being forced out of their natural places. The better answer, as the author says, is that water's natural region is around the earth, while fire's is inside the outermost sphere. Then neither needs to be constantly forced from its natural place. Someone may object that if this is so, water should not move toward the center when we dig down toward it, and air should not rise toward the outer edge if there is no fire in its way. But both move that way to prevent empty space. Their contact with air in these cases is forced, and they flee from it, as in the hanging-brick example discussed below.

[^V03-459]: Someone might say that empty space could be avoided by more air flowing in. I reply that all things naturally resist empty space. Air and oil enter the space left by a burning wick. Blood, flesh, and other matter rise into the space inside a cupping glass. This is a natural aversion to emptiness, not a choice made after thought that can be set aside when something else acts. When a flame rises from the wick, the oil follows so that no empty space forms, even if another flame or air is already there. In the same way, when a cupper draws out the air, blood and flesh rise into the space inside the glass.

[^V03-460]: You may say that a body already has a natural straight tendency. But my point is that it can also receive forced circular motion, and so it may have a natural circular motion too.

[^V03-461]: The kind of jagged form remains, but not the same individual jagged form. If the individual form lasted, the body would have to remain forced forever. Particular jagged forms, such as those of mountains, do not last through earthquakes or the breaking that comes from severe cold. They are changed and come to the “gate of gates,” since the flow of existence never stops. This is one way to understand the verse, “You see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds” (Qur'an 27:88).

[^V03-462]: Nature resists the body's forced state and keeps turning toward its natural goal. The outside condition is temporary and goes away. Natural tendency, by contrast, belongs to the body itself and is strong; impacts from the air do not remove it.

[^V03-463]: If the stone only received an upward tendency, without any change in its specific form, there would be no likeness between the effect and its source. The problem goes away if the body's substance changes continuously, in a weakened or partial way, as Sadra says.

[^V03-464]: Iron and fire each have a broad range of forms. Sadra does not mean that they are made by combining two separate forms. Rather, the iron's form lies between the two. You could call it an iron form, and you could also call it a fire form. This resembles a mixture of hot and cold, dry and moist. The form that produces the mixture remains in a middle state, not in a pure state. This all follows from the theory of substantial motion: the change here is not only in qualities, such as tendencies that come upon a body. The body's very nature also changes.

[^V03-465]: The matter has already been fully shaped and made into a stone by the stony form. The form that makes it light then belongs to a subject that already has its own form. In that way, the lightening form is an accident.

[^V03-466]: This passage can be read in two ways. First, the outside force gives the body an unusual, forced tendency that lasts until the motion ends. Avicenna is reported to hold this view. Calling an accident a “power” is not unusual, as we saw in the discussion of power and action. Second, the cause that lasts until the motion ends may be nature. The outside force gives it this role by changing nature into an unusual state or by creating a form that makes the body light. On this second reading, there are five possible views, not four. When Sadra says that one sound view remains, he means the second reading. He does not discuss the first separately because it leads back to the view he has already explained.

[^V03-467]: Sadra first mentioned number, size, and time. Here he speaks only of number and time because a power's effects are actions and motions, and a motion has no fixed spatial size. Its measure is time.

[^V03-468]: A difference in strength results from a difference in duration. There is no problem in treating the cause and its effect as two kinds of difference. In this passage, “duration” is set against an increase in duration. The author takes the rest of this explanation from al-Tusi's commentary on *The Pointers*, where he discusses whether bodily powers have limits. He uses it here to show the difference between variation in time, in number, and in strength.

[^V03-469]: This applies to effects that are motions. If an effect is not motion and its source is not bodily, it may be unlimited. For example, divine power is unlimited in strength, as God is unlimited in light. His creative act lies beyond motion and time.

[^V03-470]: This concerns bodily powers that spread through a body and qualities that exist throughout it. They can increase or decrease just as a quantity can. They are unlike powers and qualities that do not depend on bodies. A length, for example, can keep getting smaller without reaching a final smallest length; whiteness can do the same. The same applies to whether two quantities can be measured by a common unit. If one amount is greater than another, we can keep subtracting the smaller from the larger without reaching a final point. Quantity can be divided without end, unlike number, which ends at one.

[^V03-471]: This means weakness, decrease, and increase in strength. As we have already seen, a bodily power cannot be infinitely strong.

[^V03-472]: The proof can be summarized this way. If a body had no natural tendency, it would not move. We know from experience that this conclusion is false. The link in the proof is this: if the body moved without a tendency, its motion would either take time or not. If it took time, the three examples would force the time to match that of a body with a tendency. If it did not take time, it would lack one of the six things that motion must have. So motion without a natural tendency is impossible, and every body must have such a tendency.

[^V03-473]: The claim is a conditional: “If this motion occurred, it would take time.” Saying that the conditional is true does not mean that the motion actually occurs.

[^V03-474]: Someone may say that equal times do not follow from the assumptions. I reply that saying a motion without any tendency would take time is like saying, “If an immaterial being moved, its motion would take time.” This does not mean that a real motion has one amount of time for the movement itself and another for its speed, slowness, or resistance. Motion and speed exist together, just as a general kind and its specific form exist together. If two motions agree in one of the three measures discussed above but differ in another, the third must differ by the same ratio.

[^V03-475]: This is the natural tendency within the body that resists the tendency imposed by the outside force. The body's natural tendency and the outside force are held constant in the examples, while the three motions differ. So the differing motions cannot all come from the same unchanged cause; their tendencies must differ too.

[^V03-476]: On this reading, there is no need to use all three motions in the proof. A shorter argument is enough: if forced motion had no inner resistance, there would be no speed or slowness. Without speed or slowness, there would be no motion. So forced motion would not exist, which is false.

[^V03-477]: The same point applies to motion from the soul. Even if the soul's imagination and choice were at their strongest, they would not necessarily produce the same motion in all three examples. If someone says this also applies to an outside force at its strongest, “outside force” here does not mean an agent acting by choice. It means a force that acts by nature. A natural force always acts in the same way.

[^V03-478]: Al-Tusi is setting out a general point, apart from how it is used in this particular proof. His point is sound. The objector's quick response is unfair. If neither nature nor the outside force varies, but the motions do vary, then there must be some resistance that accounts for the difference. This is the result the objector wanted.

[^V03-479]: Someone may ask what sets the strength of the tendency if nature itself does not vary. The best answer is the one given by the author. A tendency is a quality that can be stronger or weaker. It lies between nature and motion: it connects the changing motion to the stable nature. It varies in itself, and outside causes help produce it.

[^V03-480]: The point is about tendency. Even when there is only one inside or outside resistance, motion can still have different degrees of speed and slowness. So the three motions in the proof cannot be set by the same resistance while their speeds differ. The same issue would arise if someone argued against empty space by using only the inside tendency, and left out resistance from the medium.

[^V03-481]: The argument can be made more briefly: if anything in the world moves by force, then nature exists. Forced motion goes against nature, so it cannot happen where there is no nature. The cause of forced motion is always a bodily power with a position. It acts by pulling or pushing, or by preparing a body to become hot, cold, or something else. A body can receive such an effect only if it already has a particular nature. Matter by itself cannot receive it until it has a definite substance and belongs to a kind. In the stages of an embryo's growth, for example, the elements prepare matter for the form of semen, and the semen prepares it for the form of the embryo. Forms do not oppose each other, and one specific form does not turn into another. Sadra points to this principle here. He could have made a shorter argument from it, though changing the proof in the middle of a reply may be poor form in a debate. If he is pointing to a different proof, however, the change is acceptable.

[^V03-482]: Sadra is answering a possible doubt: someone may be surprised that such a long argument is needed to prove both that bodies have powers and natures and that empty space is impossible. He says there are many ways to prove these claims. Some were given earlier, some here, and one short proof can be drawn from his argument: if there is forced motion in the world, there must be a natural tendency, because forced motion goes against nature. Another proof was given above: if there were no tendency, motion would have to remove itself as soon as it began.

[^V03-483]: In other words, without nature there would be no motion, since a separate, immaterial cause is too exalted to produce motion directly.

[^V03-484]: A specific form, which is called “nature” in simple bodies, makes a body the kind of thing it is. A body is a real kind in the wider order of things, but it is not a complete kind of thing among bodies until it has a specific form. Matter may already have a bodily form, but it still needs a specific form to become a particular kind of body. That form is the source of the body's different effects and the starting point of its motion and tendency. In this sense, it is called nature: the first source of a body's own motion and rest.

[^V03-485]: The phrase “within them” means that these powers are spread throughout bodies and divided with them. They do not merely sit on the surface.

[^V03-486]: This rules out the view that God directly produces these motions without powers or natures acting between Him and bodies. It also addresses the problem of how a changing effect can be connected to an unchanging cause.

[^V03-487]: The proof is clearer if we distinguish forced from natural motion. Suppose an outside force could move a large body without limit. It would move a smaller body more easily, because the smaller body offers less resistance. The larger body’s motion would therefore end before the smaller body’s. If it did not, the greater resistance would make no difference. Now consider natural motion. The power spread through a whole body is greater than the power in one of its parts. If both produced motion without limit, the part would do as much as the whole, which is impossible. If the part’s motion is finite, the ratio between the two powers is also finite, because it is the ratio of the part’s size to the whole’s. The whole body’s motion would therefore be finite too, contrary to the assumption.

    For natural motion, a large body and a small one are equally able to receive the motion from nature, since both are bodies. Their difference comes from the power that moves them: the large body contains more of that power because it is spread throughout the body, while the small body contains only part of it. In forced motion, the difference comes from the body receiving the force, since the larger body offers more resistance. These points prevent someone from saying that the greater force in the large body is cancelled out by its larger size, or that the smaller force in the small body is balanced by its smaller size. The forces differ because their bodies differ in size, and their effects must differ too.

[^V03-488]: If the sizes of two bodies have a finite ratio, then the motions of the bodies also have a finite ratio.

[^V03-489]: In natural motion, the larger body moves farther than the smaller one. In forced motion, the larger body reaches its limit sooner.

[^V03-490]: Since unity and existence do not exist as things placed inside a body, they are not divided with it. This gives us another way to answer the objection.

[^V03-491]: This objection does not apply to the proof as we have set it out. There is no need to divide the power into a part and a whole in the way the objection assumes. The effect of the small part is known, just as the effect of the whole is.

[^V03-492]: This example was discussed earlier, in the question of how a simple thing can come from a combination of things.

[^V03-493]: The objectors use a comparison between two endless series of past events. They imagine removing, for example, ten revolutions from one series and then claim that the remaining series is smaller. The philosophers reply that the events in a time sequence do not all exist together, so they cannot be compared or lined up in this way. The same applies here: the effects of bodily powers may continue one after another without limit, but they are not all actual at once and cannot be compared as a completed number.

[^V03-494]: “In potential” here means that the effect is contained in the power as strength or capacity, not merely imagined as a possibility. “Together” means held in one source, rather than separated into a sequence. This follows from the principle that whatever gives something must have it in some way. The power contains its effects in a higher, folded form; each effect then appears separately when the power acts. Since the capacity itself is real, we can compare the capacity of a part with that of the whole even before either effect has happened.

[^V03-495]: This means that a body cannot keep the same nature and identity forever, even before we consider changes in its qualities. Each power is renewed through a succession of powers. Each one has a limited existence and a limited effect, even though the succession continues without a break. This includes bodies that seem to continue on their own and bodies supported by other principles. We have already seen that everything a thing has comes to it through its existence. If a power cannot have an unlimited effect directly, it cannot have one through another cause either.

[^V03-496]: Rest still occurs in time. Avicenna's point is that we should not mistake this duration for an action produced by the earth's power.

[^V03-497]: The better word here is “contradiction,” not “opposition.” This is a detailed objection to one premise of the proof. A formal counterargument would assume the opposite conclusion and offer a separate proof for it, without attacking the original proof's premises.

[^V03-498]: The comparison concerns two powers of the same kind, where one is part of the other. It does not concern powers of different kinds, between which there is no ratio of greater and smaller. The actual effects of the moon and Saturn's movers do not exist all at once, so they cannot be compared by number. The point is the difference between what each power can do, not between effects that have already occurred.

[^V03-499]: This could also be treated as a general counterargument: if every step in the proof were accepted, the motion of the heavens would have to be finite, against the view that their revolutions continue without end. Each sphere has parts like itself. The power in a part is part of the power in the whole, so if the part's motion were finite, the whole's would be finite too. We cannot make an exception to the general rule without a reason.

[^V03-500]: A separate, immaterial power at its greatest strength could produce motion without time, even though time is one of the things motion requires. This point has been discussed above.

[^V03-501]: For example, wishes may gather in the soul's power of desire, and nature may draw closer by degrees to its final goal.

[^V03-502]: Otherwise, the agent's choice and the receiver's readiness would be fixed for no reason.

[^V03-503]: The answerer is Avicenna in *The Pointers*. He uses this argument to establish separate causes that move the heavens toward their ends. If the heavenly motion came entirely from bodily souls acting on their own, it would eventually end. Someone may ask: if a bodily power can serve as an intermediary for unlimited actions in the heavens, why can it not do so in earthly bodies? The answer is that the receiver here is either a simple element, which can be destroyed, or a compound body, which eventually breaks down. Also, in the view held by Aristotle’s followers, simple, universal intellectual causes do not act directly through lifeless, plant, and animal bodies; below animals, there are no conscious causes. The Illuminationist school holds that every body has a source of effects along with a separate intellect, but Avicenna does not accept that view.

[^V03-504]: An “intermediary of description” is something that seems to have a quality because it is joined to the thing that really has it. A passenger is said to move because the ship moves, though we can also say that the passenger is not moving in the strict sense. An “intermediary of cause” is something through which an effect truly happens. The thing that depends on it really has the effect. The intermediary may also have that quality, as fire does when it heats water, or it may not, as with the sun, which is neither hot nor cold. The same point applies to the heavens and their movers. Once we see the difference, we can see the weakness in the author's statement.

[^V03-505]: I say there is still room for an answer. Powers do have effects at their own level. Existence itself and the things that exist are not the same. Saying that only God affects existence does not mean that the heat of fire is not an effect of the nature of fire as heat and fire. Heat as something that exists comes from God. In the same way, people say that God is the giver of existence, yet still classify causes as natural, habitual, crafted, chosen, essential, or accidental. If asked what makes a chair, they answer: the carpenter. The material is wood; other things prepare the wood for the chair. But the chair's existence, simply as existence, comes from God. From the viewpoint of God's decree, only He acts. From the viewpoint of the powers He has given things, their powers act by His strength. Both ways of speaking are true. This is why philosophers still need to discuss whether the effects of bodily powers have limits. Sadra's other reply—that these powers are renewed continuously, even in the heavens—is also sound, as he has said several times.

[^V03-506]: If this reply were complete, there would be no need to discuss whether a bodily power can have an unlimited effect in the first place.

[^V03-507]: On this clear account, it is easy to show that each bodily power has a limited effect: each power that follows another exists and acts for a limited time. The succession can continue without end because it is continually renewed. If someone asks how this renewal can continue without end, the answer is that this follows from the unbroken flow of existence, which has been proved. To allow that flow to stop would go against reason and religion.

[^V03-508]: This means existence in general, not one particular kind of existence. We have already said that something is possible if it accepts existence in general—some instance of it can exist—and impossible if no instance of it can exist.

[^V03-509]: Philosophical discussions of general subjects are often built by drawing ideas from everyday speech and setting aside their incidental features through abstraction and generalisation. Examples include existence and nonexistence, mind and world, unity and multiplicity, and, among them, coming-to-be and eternity. In ordinary speech, people may choose a point in past time and compare two people by how close their existence is to that point. The one who has existed longer is called older; the one who has existed for less time is called more recent. A father, Amr, is old in relation to his son, Zayd, who is recent; Noah is old in relation to Moses, who is recent. This way of speaking means that the recent thing is preceded in existence by the older one, but not the other way around. We can take this meaning as a real feature and apply it to existence in general: existence either is preceded by something else—or, put another way, by nonexistence—and is then originated, or it is not, and is then eternal. Thinkers later found that existence can be stable or changing, and that priority and posteriority work differently in each. In changing existence, what comes before does not remain alongside what comes after. In stable existence, a cause can precede its effect while both exist, as can the essential nonexistence that is said to precede an essence. This is why they divided coming-to-be and eternity into temporal and essential kinds.

[^V03-510]: Given the definition of temporal coming-to-be as existing after a period of nonexistence, temporal eternity should be defined as not existing after any period of nonexistence. Eternity is the opposite of coming-to-be, so it is defined by negating it. If we defined it this way, time itself would be temporally eternal, as would things entirely separate from matter. The note adds an important point: coming-to-be and eternity are both based on being before or after something. That relation requires a fixed starting point from which we can judge what is before and what is after. Once such a point is set, we can speak of coming-to-be or eternity in relation to it, as when we compare the Necessary Being and possible things by existence or necessity, or compare existence and nonexistence in relation to an essence. On this account, both an eternal and an originated thing can exist in the essential sense, because we can use existence or necessity as a shared starting point. But only an originated thing can exist in the temporal sense, because only it can be related to a starting point in time. All temporal events and parts of time can be so related. A temporally eternal thing, by contrast, would have to be related to a point in time that nothing else came before. Nothing in existence fits that description. Time itself and things entirely separate from matter have no relation to a starting point in time. This also explains why the author changes the definition of temporal eternity from “a thing is not preceded by time” to “the time of its existence has no beginning,” and then denies this kind of eternity to time itself and to things wholly separate from matter.

[^V03-511]: If temporal eternity were defined as “a thing's existence has no beginning in time,” then time itself and things entirely separate from matter would count as temporally eternal. The author of *Al-Muṭāraḥāt* may have had this in mind.

[^V03-512]: Both arguments try to show that anything with an essence—in other words, anything possible or caused—has come to be essentially. This means that God, whose existence is not preceded by nonexistence, is eternal in Himself. The arguments differ in how they define essential coming-to-be. The first defines it as existence preceded by nonexistence in itself; the second, as existence preceded by something else in itself. The difference comes from looking at the matter in a broad or a precise way. On close examination, nonexistence has no standing in the world outside thought. The mind draws the nonexistence of each thing from the existence of something else. So, strictly speaking, a thing's existence is preceded by its cause's existence, rather than by nonexistence.

[^V03-513]: One could object that this makes the essence's entitlement to existence itself come after its lack of entitlement to existence, which is not the point. The point is that the essence's existence is preceded by its own nonexistence. The reply is that, in either case, we consider the essence as the subject and existence as what is said of it. What is said of a subject must come after it. So existence is preceded by a state of the essence that conflicts with existence: nonexistence.

[^V03-514]: More precisely, a possible thing, considered in itself, is entitled neither to existence nor to nonexistence. A negative statement does not require that its subject exist, while a positive statement does. The rank in question is therefore empty of existence. Avicenna's phrase “or would have no existence if it stood alone” is a negative statement that adds an alternative to “would be entitled to nonexistence if it stood alone.”

[^V03-515]: This does not mean that the essence is generally prior to existence. In reality, considering something as existing comes before every other consideration of it.

[^V03-516]: The commentator means that Avicenna's phrase “would have no existence if it stood alone” is joined to “would be entitled to nonexistence if it stood alone” as another negative statement.

[^V03-517]: This may be hard to understand because “lacking entitlement” was just described as a negative statement. A bare negative has no subject, since it can be true even when the subject does not exist. So how can nonexistence come first? Recall what we explained near the beginning about how a thing can be described. The mind strips an essence of every kind of existence and considers it on its own. In that respect, the essence has no existence; this makes it possible to call it prior by nonexistence. But in the basic way of describing it, the mind has stripped it of both existence and nonexistence. This lets us say that what comes first is nonexistence, and that coming-to-be is existence preceded by nonexistence.

[^V03-518]: The author says this because he rejects the idea that an essence comes first through its own substantial reality. Those who regard essences as real, however, say that an essence comes before its being illuminated by existence, despite having no claim to exist in itself. They call this priority by establishment or by meaning. The scholars who say that an essence comes before existence include al-Dawānī, the learned Sayyid al-Dāmād, and their followers.

[^V03-519]: This argument shows that essential coming-to-be means existence preceded by something else, just as the first argument showed that it means existence preceded by nonexistence. In both, “preceded in itself” means the shared idea behind causal priority and priority by an essence's own constitution. The first definition is broader, because “something else” includes both nonexistence and a cause.

[^V03-520]: This hints that kinds of coming-to-be differ according to the kinds of priority and posteriority. That is so, as the author indicated at the start of this discussion.

[^V03-521]: The claim that being later is an actual quality added to a thing is absurd, as the author says. Scholars generally treat it as a “second-level concept”: things truly have this feature in the world, but the mind is what applies it to them. In other words, it exists in the world only as a relation; it does not exist there as a thing in its own right. Even those who believe in such “states” nearly all agree on this point. Being later applies to things that come to be as a concept, not as an additional feature in their existence.

[^V03-522]: The main claim contains a fallacy: being preceded is a relation, not a quality.

[^V03-523]: This disproves the claim that coming-to-be comes to be through itself. That claim would mean that coming-to-be is its own essence, just as existence existing through itself would mean that existence is its own essence. If coming-to-be is its own essence, how can it also be a quality? The author gives several reasons why coming-to-be is not a quality. First, the two ideas can be understood separately: what we mean by coming-to-be is not the same as what we mean by a quality. Even someone who claims that coming-to-be is a quality must accept that distinction in thought. Second, coming-to-be applies in a way suited to each category, as existence does; it is the very existence of things that come to be. A quality, by contrast, has one meaning that does not change except through the different things it is related to. The author then adds that, although existence differs with the essences of things, it is not an extra feature added to them in the outside world. The scholar says that it is. His third reason is that the scholar's view requires an extra positive quality to be added to a newly arisen nonexistence.

[^V03-524]: The two features may be removed one at a time—as independent factors, conditions, or parts of a cause. The conclusion that a thing would be necessary and eternal if they were removed applies separately to each feature. The claim that a possible thing that is eternal would not need a cause is held by most theologians. Another reading is that the two features are a condition and a part, in which case both must be removed together. The phrase “its existence” means existence as attributed to an essence. The author clarifies this later when he says that he does not deny the role of an essence's possibility.

[^V03-525]: Put another way, the essence's possibility comes before the relational existence attributed to it: possibility comes before the possible thing exists in the sense of being described as existing. It is better to say that the philosophers mean possibility serves as a step in showing why the thing needs a cause, because it is a step in establishing that need.

[^V03-526]: This applies only to coming-to-be in time. That is clear.

[^V03-527]: The word “real” here simply stresses that this possibility is not just an abstract idea. The incidental cause is the thing's readiness or potential. Coming-to-be is the reason we recognise that readiness; it does not make the readiness exist. This is also how we explained the philosophers' statement that nonexistence is one of the causes.

[^V03-528]: That is, a substance that does not exist in something else, such as a body or prime matter. This leaves two other options: existing in a subject, as a quality does, or existing in matter, as a form does. After rejecting self-subsisting existence, the author allows that the possibility might be a form in matter. He does not separately reject that option because its weakness is already clear.

[^V03-529]: Something separate from all things would relate equally to them all. There would be no reason for one thing, rather than another, to have it.

[^V03-530]: This confirms the earlier meaning of a preparatory cause.

[^V03-531]: The first option is the subject that bears an accident; the second is matter, which bears a form; the third is the body in relation to the rational soul.

[^V03-532]: Nonexistence is one of the three first principles in a statement attributed to Aristotle by the learned Sayyid al-Dāmād. He says that the Creator brings the world into being from no existing things and does not create it from things that came before. God arranged the universal natures as He wished from the first principles of creation. The first principles and beginning of what God created are necessarily three: form, the first and noblest; matter; and nonexistence, which is not in time or place. The note then quotes the rest of that account.

[^V03-533]: This refers to accidental motion in the four familiar categories of change. That is how the earlier thinkers' view is being explained. For the author, however, changing nature is interwoven with nonexistence, so the claim that nonexistence is a direct cause extends to nature itself. He discusses this at length in *Sharḥ al-Asmāʾ*.

[^V03-534]: In a chain of causes and effects, priority by rank can reverse depending on which direction we follow; priority by causation cannot.

[^V03-535]: The point is about order in the chain. Not every endless sequence is impossible. The argument against an endless sequence applies to things that exist together in an ordered chain.

[^V03-536]: Even someone who rejects both views just mentioned must accept priority by essence, also called priority by substantial constitution. The essences of a broader kind and its defining feature come before the essence of the species in this way. An essence also comes before its essential feature, considered simply as an essence. In both cases, the priority is fixed in the order of thought, without considering existence.

[^V03-537]: Even principles that are joined to God, let alone those separate from Him, are aspects of His own being and degrees of His action. The measure of this further kind of priority is that what comes first and what comes later are treated as one thing, unlike the other kinds.

[^V03-538]: The essence of every agent comes before the essence of what it affects by causation. But the existence of an agent before the existence of what it affects is this more subtle kind of priority. True existence is not made up of different realities, individuals, or parts. It has levels in which what distinguishes one level is the same as what it shares with the others; these are the inner aspects of the One God. You might ask how the author can say there is no action and response in existence when he often writes that existence itself is made, just as the maker is a cause. The reply is that, when we consider existence as the one source preserved through all its levels, there is no separate action and response. Also, although existence itself is what is made, its being made becomes clear only through essences. An essence therefore helps us recognise that existence is made.

[^V03-539]: Both people being compared are measured against the same fixed point in time. Their existence is related to that point, and they differ in how near or far it is. The point is the same for both, and the earlier person is nearer to it. The author explains this further below.

[^V03-540]: The measure of priority in time is not time itself, but being at a time—when something exists—which cannot be divided. Another measure is the thing's relation to a fixed starting point, such as the present moment. The same applies to priority in place: it is not place itself that makes something prior, but its relation to a fixed starting point. Avicenna later says that the earlier thing has something the later lacks, and the later has nothing that the earlier does not. The commentator says Avicenna is the person being criticised, but the author does not name him out of respect. Avicenna says that the different kinds of priority nearly share one meaning by degree: the prior has something, simply as prior, that the later lacks. But he also explains the measure of time priority by a fixed point, as the author does here. The author need not repeat that qualification because the definition already refers to what comes later; definitions are also commonly understood with “in this respect” as an unstated limit.

[^V03-541]: One might ask: the phrase “because of priority” seems to say that priority causes the greater claim, while “this priority” says that priority itself is what is being compared. How do these fit together? The answer is that if priority made one thing more entitled to be prior, then priority would cause the very advantage that makes it prior. The author first rejects priority as the cause of that advantage, then rejects the idea that the prior thing is itself more entitled to priority.

[^V03-542]: This is not the same as the earlier objection that “the meaning of priority is what we want to explain.” The earlier objection was that the definition assumes what it is meant to define. Here the problem is that it explains priority through something even less clear.

[^V03-543]: In reality, all the kinds share a common meaning. But people seem to have discovered them gradually, from the clearest to the least clear, and then used *priority* for each new, less clear meaning by extending or figuratively transferring the word. Eventually, these uses became accepted as ordinary meanings in particular fields.

[^V03-544]: There are two kinds of priority here, and they do not conflict. The times of arrival are ordered in time; the two cities are ordered by place, without considering time. When the author says that Hamadan does not come before Baghdad by itself or simply by its place, the point is that priority depends on each city's relation to a fixed starting point. This is what makes priority relational, whether the order is chosen or natural. Avicenna often reduces the number of kinds of priority, as he reduces kinds of statement in logic to a single form. His deeper aim may be to show that the true coming-to-be of the whole world is essential coming-to-be: the world's true prior is its cause itself. Its temporal coming after imagined time or nonexistence that shares a rank with it is not real priority for him, because he accepts only essential priority as genuine.

[^V03-545]: Natural priority should not change according to the direction someone chooses. Here it does change when the starting point is changed. The author's point is that there is no real priority or posteriority in this case. Once someone imagines the relation, however, the order is temporal, not a separate kind of rank. The answer is the same as before.

[^V03-546]: This means being seated first at a gathering or being allowed to start an activity. The priority belongs to the seating or starting order, not to excellence itself. For example, the first and second intellects are ranked by excellence. On this account, using *priority* for excellence is simply another use of the word.

[^V03-547]: The word *priority* is used with its own meaning in some cases, figuratively in others, and as a separate word-sense in still others.

[^V03-548]: Two features account for the observed order between parts of time. First, the actual state at each point depends on the potential state of the point just before it. Potentiality and actuality, taken in their distinct forms, cannot exist together. As with a motion that grows stronger, the weaker state does not coexist with the stronger state, though the stronger depends on the weaker. Second, the two parts that contain potentiality and actuality belong to one connected, flowing existence. Because time is connected, it can be divided into parts that exist only potentially. Because time flows and never settles, no part exists separately while all the others remain; they do not coexist as separate things. And because the actual state of each part depends on the potentiality of the preceding part, the part containing potentiality comes first. It is closer to the fixed starting point in existence, which is existence in general. So priority and posteriority between parts of time concern existence, not essence. This supports the Illuminationist view that temporal priority and posteriority reduce to priority by nature. We need only divide natural priority into two kinds: one where the prior and later cannot exist together, as with time, and one where they can, as in cases that do not involve flowing existence. One might object that this should apply to motion too, since motion is also one connected flow made of potential parts, each earlier part holding the potential for the later part. The reply is that motion relates to time as a natural body relates to its measurable size. Time is motion measured at a certain speed. Motion itself is open-ended until time gives it a measure, so we cannot say what comes first or later in motion without also considering time. Time itself is the direct subject of this priority; motion is so only indirectly.

[^V03-549]: This seems to mean that time is one continuous whole, with no actual divisions between its parts, so there can be no dependence in existence between them and thus no priority by nature—only an order if we divide it in thought. But the discussion is about priority and posteriority under the assumption that time is divided. The later actual state does depend on the earlier potential state, so there is room for priority by nature.

[^V03-550]: Avicenna seems to require that the prior thing differ from what it is prior in, just as the difference between essences lies in their essences, while what they differ in is existence. The author is right: in existence, what differs and what makes the difference are one and the same. Time is one of these cases.

[^V03-551]: Change belongs to existence, not essence. Priority and posteriority are intrinsic to parts of time in the sense that the mind draws them directly from how those parts exist, not because they are parts of time's essence or necessary features of it. Since this order depends on the relation between potentiality and actuality, it returns to priority by nature. We need only divide natural priority into two kinds: one that requires the prior and later not to exist together, as in parts of time, and one that does not require this, as in parts of a cause and its effect.

[^V03-552]: In this account, “existence” is used broadly for both the essence that can either exist or not exist and existence itself, which cannot be nonexistent. The feature that makes priority by essence is the essence's own reality or established nature.

[^V03-553]: The argument as given is narrower than the claim it is meant to prove, since it does not cover one person being earlier than another—for example, Noah and the Prophet. A better reading of Bahmanyār is that temporal priority exists in thought because the earlier thing no longer exists outside the mind.
