General knowledge is still a means to this direct encounter when its meanings become firm in the soul. “Knowledge is the seed of direct vision.” May God help us join knowledge with action and protect us from error, through Muhammad and his family, the friends of God who reach the universal intellects and rise beyond them.

[^V03-725]: The argument for both claims can be summarized this way. For the first: if a cause is a cause through its full causal reality, then knowing it means knowing its necessary effect. The known cause and effect must be present together in knowledge. If the cause acts through its existence, then direct knowledge of that existence is together with the existence of its effect, since the effect’s existence depends on it. Merely knowing the cause’s essence does not reveal the effect, because causality belongs to existence, not essence. For the second claim: if the effect follows from an essence, knowing it gives knowledge of some cause, since the effect may follow from a broader essence. If it follows from existence, direct knowledge of its existence gives knowledge of an aspect of its cause, but not complete knowledge of the cause. The effect’s essence alone does not establish any cause.

[^V03-726]: This premise is the heart of the argument: the cause and effect are known together. It does not say that knowledge of the cause is a prior cause of knowledge of the effect, as al-Rāzī objects. Saying that the cause’s existence includes the relational existence of its effect does not remove the fact that they are known together. The best reading is that the author means a direct, illuminating relation between them, if this fits the philosophers’ words.

[^V03-727]: Knowledge of real existence cannot be merely a mental copy; it must be direct. Direct knowledge has three cases: an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself, its knowledge of its effect, and a thing’s knowledge of what it has become one with. The author’s claim seems to apply this rule specifically to direct knowledge of existence, as is correct in his view. Other philosophers do not limit it this way. For example, they say that knowledge of a barrier causes knowledge of a hollow, or knowledge of an opposing angle causes knowledge of a crescent shape. Those are not cases of direct knowledge. For them, God’s knowledge of Himself is direct, but His knowledge of effects is acquired through images in His being. The author does not always restrict his rule to direct knowledge; here, his wording “in its real identity” points to that restriction.

[^V03-728]: This objection also fails when a thing has no essence separate from existence.

[^V03-729]: The philosophers say both that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect and that the reverse does not follow. But if cause and effect are known together simply because they are correlatives, the same should hold in both directions. Also, their question concerns knowing a particular cause and effect, not the broad concepts of cause and effect.

[^V03-730]: The objection also reverses: knowing every aspect of an effect would include knowing that it follows from a particular cause.

[^V03-731]: This word should be read as “all the aspects,” not “if,” since it continues the reasoning and does not begin a new condition.

[^V03-732]: Someone might reply that the argument is about what we need in order to prove something, not what makes it exist. But knowing the part is also part of knowing the whole.

[^V03-733]: There is no need to answer the condition separately; this sentence explains what the philosophers mean by saying that knowing the cause means knowing the effect.

[^V03-734]: The author’s reply does not fully solve the second part of the objection: that related things are known together in thought and in the outside world, while he claims knowledge of the cause comes before knowledge of the effect. His reply also seems to accept that the category of relation is added to God’s being. A better answer is that the effect is a feature of the cause’s existence and depends on it, so the cause’s existence cannot be present in full without containing its effect. Direct knowledge of the cause therefore gives direct knowledge of the effect. The category of relation applies to the concepts of cause and effect, not to their existence.

[^V03-735]: This is like an attribute’s existence. It is one simple existence outside the mind. When related to its broad kind, such as color, it exists as a feature and depends on that kind. When related to its distinguishing feature, such as the way it separates light from the eye, it is also a cause, since the distinguishing feature gives the broad kind its specific form.

[^V03-736]: Even those who say that relations do not exist in their own separate right need not say they do not exist at all. A relation exists through the thing that gives rise to it. The argument against a separate existence for relations only rules out that first sense.

[^V03-737]: An essential property, such as evenness, differs from the essence in both its meaning and its existence in the mind. Four is a quantity; evenness is a feature of quantity. The author likely means only that the effect necessarily follows from the cause, not that it has the same kind of existence. His discussion may also apply only to causes and effects in divine philosophy.

[^V03-738]: “Full understanding” means that the mind’s account matches reality. In direct knowledge, it becomes one with that reality. The question may be intended to challenge this full union. Otherwise, there is no point in the argument: a complete cause cannot fail to produce its effect. Philosophers who discuss God’s knowledge of other things all agree that the effect is present in knowledge of the cause, though they differ on whether this is direct knowledge of existence, a mental form, luminous images, or timeless essences. A cause and effect can differ, yet the effect is present when the cause is present, just as evenness is present when four is understood. The point is not to reject full knowledge.

[^V03-739]: This point applies only to direct knowledge. The previous argument used it in that sense.

[^V03-740]: An effect cannot be particular before the cause makes it particular. Its individual identity comes from the cause. Some philosophers say that certain kinds, such as immaterial beings, cause their own individual identity. The commentator rejects this: no essence can produce individuation, because individuality belongs to existence. A particular existence gives the essence its individual identity. A particular defining feature likewise makes the broad kind into a particular species. Al-Rāzī misses this point when he assumes that a broad kind such as body already exists on its own and then asks what makes it one particular type.

[^V03-741]: This is a claim made in the logical book *The Demonstration*: certainty about something that has a cause can come only through certainty about its cause. Certainty is knowledge that something is so and cannot be otherwise. If we know that an effect exists, then we must already know that its cause exists; otherwise the effect could exist without its cause. Philosophers use this rule to set aside one kind of proof from effects: reasoning from an effect back to its own cause. They accept two kinds of proof: one that starts from a cause and establishes its effect, and one that reasons from general signs of an effect to signs of another effect. Later notes explain the limits of this claim.

[^V03-742]: Some philosophers say that all caused things can be known only through their causes. The problem is that this seems to rule out immediate knowledge, such as seeing. The commentator says the rule should not be weakened. The existence of every effect depends on its cause, and every possible thing depends on God. The mind first knows a cause’s existence and then the existence of its effect. As ʿAlī is reported to have said, “I never saw a thing without seeing God before it.”

[^V03-743]: “Matches” here means is one with. The intellectual form is the real existence itself in direct knowledge; in acquired knowledge, it is the form known directly. It may also mean that what the mind considers matches reality. In reality, each thing depends on God, so the intellect sees it that way. Being one with what is known also brings a kind of union with the known thing indirectly, since the essence appears in the mind and existence follows the same kind of existence.

[^V03-744]: This was explained earlier in the discussion of how things are brought into existence. A cause and effect share the same kind of existence: a cause of existence must itself be existence, and a cause of essence must be essence. Existence is primary in reality. If it were only an idea drawn from things, it could not belong to the highest reality. Knowing an effect that exists would then reveal its cause. If existence were only an idea, its reality would be the essence from which it is drawn.

[^V03-745]: This rule also applies to essence. We know an essence through the parts that make it what it is, such as its broad kind and distinguishing feature. These are causes that make up the essence, not causes that bring it into existence.

[^V03-746]: Particular existence is what removes nonexistence. It is the answer to both “what is it?” and “does it exist?”

[^V03-747]: Existence as existence does not change. Change belongs to the world as a set of objects, not to existence itself. God’s knowledge does not change.

[^V03-748]: Otherwise, there would be a third, independent cause that gives us knowledge of the effect apart from the cause that gives the effect its existence.

[^V03-749]: A relation is like a form, while its two sides are like the matter that receives it; both sides are needed before the relation can be known. This is still knowledge through the cause. A building displays the builder, and a book displays its author. As something received by matter, the building is an effect; as an expression of its maker, it reveals its cause first and itself second.

[^V03-750]: For example, people may be certain that everyone dies, yet their certainty can fade if someone argues that a natural compound might last forever. Those who know the causes of decay—each compound’s parts tend toward their natural places, its powers are limited, and forced states do not last—cannot lose their certainty that natural compounds will break down. Anyone who says this is only knowledge from experience, not from causes, is mistaken. Experiments help the knower see the cause’s particular features.

[^V03-751]: The first claim—that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect—is subtle; the second claim—that knowledge of an effect cannot reveal its particular cause—is even more subtle.

[^V03-752]: This is a list where one or more cases must apply, but they need not all apply. The three kinds of knowledge all occur in relation to the Necessary Being: knowing the concept, knowing the full reality, and knowing that it exists. The same three distinctions apply to existence.

[^V03-753]: God’s essence has no definition, but the meanings of His attributes can be defined and supported by proof.

[^V03-754]: This refers to the level of pure unity, to existence extended through all things, and to every essence and every limited existence. It also includes the ranks through which beings descend and rise.

[^V03-755]: The commentator says the author, who manifested God’s names of knowledge, wisdom, and power, knew that words could not express the answer. The question requires three principles. First, the existence of a cause makes up the existence of its effect: the effect’s appearance is contained in the cause’s appearance. Second, true bringing-into-existence is the real, all-pervading existence that flows from God; as explained earlier, this flow has one source. This existence, when related to God, is His act of bringing things into being; when related to created things, it is their existence. Third, God’s creative power has levels. The highest is His direct causation of the intellects; the intellects act through His power, and this power reaches down through the levels of nature. All are expressions of His power.

    With these points in view, a person’s reliable knowledge of themselves comes after reliable knowledge of their source, but only through the source’s illuminating presence and creative act. The cause’s existence makes up the effect’s existence. Knowledge works in the same way: knowledge of the source is its own existence, while knowledge of the self is the effect’s existence. Since the relation between source and effect is one of bringing into being, our knowledge of the source is its existence as it causes us. This knowledge comes before knowledge of ourselves, because the source brings us into being.

    The commentator adds a second answer: if knowing oneself is identical with one’s own existence, then God’s existence cannot remain beside it as a separate object of knowledge. Knowing God’s existence is His existence, just as knowing ourselves is our existence.

    He offers a third answer for a more ordinary reader. The claim “knowing ourselves is identical with our being” does not by itself prove that our knowledge is strong or certain; even an animal has immediate awareness of itself, and people who have forgotten God may still know themselves. Direct knowledge has levels: the soul as sensing, imagining, estimating, or thinking, and the simple intellect of a complete person. Knowledge of oneself through simple intellect is stronger than the ordinary forms of direct awareness. The author’s reply continues from the claim that God has no cause or definition to explain how a complete person can know God through the highest form of direct presence.

[^V03-756]: The main reason philosophers defend this account is to preserve the priority of knowledge: a freely chosen act must be preceded by knowledge and will. In the Illuminationist view, knowledge does not come before the act; it is the act itself. These philosophers seem to posit an intermediate realm between God’s simple, necessary existence and contingent beings: divine knowledge, containing the forms of all things, from the highest pearl to the smallest speck. These forms are grounded in God, not derived from things, so His knowledge is not passive. The Sufis describe a similar intermediate realm as the level of unity, the world of names and attributes and their fixed realities.

[^V03-757]: The author has already shown that God is necessary in every respect, including in His acts. His attributes must therefore also be necessary: He necessarily knows, has power, wills, and so on.

[^V03-758]: This raises two further problems: God would be moving toward greater perfection, and He would be affected by something outside Himself. Every accidental feature depends on a cause.

[^V03-759]: Natural kinds exist, and the universal nature exists in them, much as the continuous motion that traces a path exists through its successive parts. Creation first brings kinds into existence; they are originated directly and do not need an intermediary to connect them with the eternal.

[^V03-760]: “Eclipse” here means a lunar eclipse, as shown by the reference to the moon moving from it toward an opposite position.

[^V03-761]: Avicenna’s main concern is to show that God’s knowledge does not change with the changing existence of things, which would also make His knowledge follow rather than precede His acts. Nor does He know them through images taken from the things themselves, which would make His knowledge passive. He knows them through forms that flow from the principles and causes before the things arise. These forms are specified so that each one points to a single individual. Their role is like a mirror through which that individual is revealed. The individual is known as an individual, even though its form is intellectual. A thing may have many distinguishable features and still be one individual. The author has also said that a bodily form is known through an imagined or luminous intellectual form. These causal forms are far more complete than the things they cause and contain their perfections. Their presence in God therefore reveals the full particulars. Philosophers agree that God knows particulars, though they explain this in different ways. Avicenna’s point is not that particulars disappear from divine knowledge: intellectual knowledge does not rule out particularity. Since no concern distracts God from another, He knows each particular together with all others. The Aristotle’s followers aim to show that God’s knowledge is stable, prior, and active; they hold that this requires forms proceeding from the cause. The doctrine that the simple reality is all things in a higher way can explain this more fully, but the point remains that Avicenna did not deny any form of divine knowledge.

[^V03-762]: The passage seems to admit that the image in knowledge changes when a material particular changes, which would conflict with the claim that even sensory and imagined knowledge is immaterial. The commentator’s answer is that the images themselves do not change. What changes is their appearance to the soul, which depends on bodily acts such as seeing and hearing. When those acts stop, the image is no longer present to awareness, but the image itself remains; otherwise, we could not recall an earlier sensory image as the very one we once perceived. Knowing change, motion, or divisible quantity does not make knowledge itself change, move, or divide. A mental image must match the external thing in essence, not in its mode of existence.

[^V03-763]: The argument assumes that the direct object of knowledge is the same at both times, since the opponent treats the two acts of knowledge as one. Any difference would belong only to the indirect object—the day and night outside the mind. When night arrives, the knowledge must remain one if the claim is true. This restates the problem the argument is meant to expose.

[^V03-764]: This distinction may refer to individual motions of the outermost sphere, which mark time, and to other motions that occur in time. Strictly speaking, even the outermost sphere moves in time. The terms “in” and “with” can be used in different ways: time may be in motion as an accident is in its subject, while motion is in time as something measured is in its measure. The measured thing and its measure are linked. Something may also exist alongside time without motion, as philosophers say of bodily substances. Something “in time” is measured by the flow of the sphere’s motion. What has no motion is not in time by its nature, unless it exists only instantaneously.

[^V03-765]: The first kind is bodies; the second is bodily things or states.

[^V03-766]: “Position” here means the arrangement and relation of parts, as a category. The earlier sense is what allows something to be pointed out by the senses.

[^V03-767]: One might object that this philosopher considers space to be an immaterial dimension. If space is a surface, its material character is clear; if it is a dimension, it is material because it is the place occupied by matter. Or the point may simply be that anything tied to time and space is material.

[^V03-768]: The Illuminationists and this philosopher deny prime matter, but even those who accept it do not regard it as sheer nonexistence. The same is even clearer of bodily extension. When the author calls matter a source of absence, he means that it is not fully present to itself: each part is hidden from every other part, and the whole is not present to each part. But this is not absence in the strict sense, where a negative statement has no existing subject. Matter has an intermediate mode of existence, between nonexistence and a complete, unified existence. A bodily kind or natural form has a fuller existence than matter. Since these are all modes of existence, they are also kinds of knowledge by virtue of existence; they can be present to a knower. Existence, at every level, is light, whether dim or bright. Even a shadow is a kind of light mixed with darkness. At every level, an existent being is present to its source more fully than its existence is present to itself. That forms exist in matter does not prevent their presence to the all-encompassing source. Our knowledge, by contrast, depends on images because our relation of knowledge is not joined to the relation of bringing things into being.

[^V03-769]: The commentator asks who claims that a sensible thing itself becomes intelligible: it remains sensible, though it is known without a bodily tool. A philosopher such as Suhrawardī, who says God is seeing and hearing and that His knowledge is presence rather than a form, should not hesitate to say that these particulars are directly perceived by God.

[^V03-770]: The philosopher does not mean a categorical relation, but an illuminating relation. The great philosophers say that contingent, changing things are possible and changing in themselves, yet necessary and perfectly stable in relation to God. As existences and manifestations of God, they are necessary and stable. Ancient thinkers also held that times and places are like a single instant or point when seen from higher principles, especially from the First Principle. They illustrate this with a colored thread stretched before a person while an ant walks along it. Dāmād says that successive events in time coexist in the container of eternity, like troops passing one after another through a mountain pass as seen by a person watching from above. To grasp this, compare seeing one white thing with imagining it, then with understanding “every white thing” and making a universal judgment about all of them. The intellect encompasses them all, each according to its capacity. The author says that disappearing from or being absent to some beings does not mean being absent to others. Things with positions are so only in relation to one another, not in relation to separate intellects. Although the author does not explicitly mention existence or its primacy here, elsewhere he rejects the view that knowledge is merely a relation and speaks of the “book of existence.” This shows that he treats existence as real.

[^V03-771]: No one means that a material thing ceases to be material when considered by higher principles. Rather, relative to a separate intellect, matter is as if stripped of matter; likewise, place and time are as if stripped of place and time, because they are no longer hidden from the knower. The author elsewhere reports Dāmād’s warning not to mistake this kind of language for a denial of the material world.

[^V03-772]: The example is not literally possible, since the outermost sphere does not truly surround everything. A better example would be a sight that extends through the greatest sphere and all within it, just as existence and necessity extend through everything. From that standpoint, nothing is near or far.

[^V03-773]: This is general knowledge that includes detailed disclosure: each cause contains all the existences below it in a higher way. It is general because the higher existence is one and simple; it is detailed because that one is the very reality of the many. A thing is what it is in its full reality, not through what it lacks. Individuality and distinction belong to existence, while the essences of these existences follow from it without being later in existence. More tentatively, the Aristotle’s followers may mean by forms in causes the existences of their effects enfolded within them.

[^V03-774]: Anyone who says that all knowledge of other things is not limited to mental forms must accept that a cause knows its effect directly. How, then, can perception be limited to forms? Knowledge through a form is only needed when the knower is not the cause of what is known. Those who say all knowledge of other things is acquired knowledge through forms are the ones who must limit perception to forms.

[^V03-775]: That applies to acquired knowledge. Direct knowledge depends on the cause’s mastery and its illuminating relation to the effect, as explained in the commentary on *The Pointers*. The forms that arise from a knower are known directly and do not need further forms to reveal them. Pure existence contains all that belongs to its kind and lacks what is alien to it; nonexistence is what is alien to existence. For the Illuminationists, a thing’s being light to itself and to others is the same kind of principle.

[^V03-776]: “That exists” describes “form”; “to be” may be a complete verb or a linking verb, depending on the reading.

[^V03-777]: That is, whatever way it is taken to exist, absent or present. The point is that material existence alone would be enough for a relation of knowledge; no mental form would be needed.

[^V03-778]: If God’s relation of knowledge were not also a relation of bringing existence into being, He could not know Himself as the source of every existence. Knowing Himself would require knowing every existence before it occurs, so the relation of knowledge would be present before its object existed, while the creative relation would not yet be present. That is impossible. The divine realm of knowledge therefore includes both what already exists and what can exist.

[^V03-779]: The knowing and acting powers are inseparable for two reasons. First, one cannot be lost while the other remains, unlike perception and movement in animals: sight may fail while movement remains, or the reverse. Second, the two human powers do not have separate bodily locations, unlike animal perception, mostly in the head, and movement, in the muscles.

[^V03-780]: Some judgments need no learning, such as that justice is good and injustice bad. Others depend on custom or reasoning, such as whether killing animals is wrong. To decide to tell a particular truth, a person may reason: this is true; every truth is just; therefore this is just; every just thing is good; and every good thing should be done; so this truth should be told. The practical intellect does not directly carry out good acts. If action means ability, that is opposed to knowledge; if it means movement, it is an animal power, not an intellect. The practical intellect is a more distant source of action and a direct source of knowledge about how to act. It guides the powers of desire and movement. The Second Teacher, al-Fārābī, says that theoretical intellect lets a person know what they cannot do, while practical intellect lets them know what they can do by choice.

[^V03-781]: The three senses differ in how far they are from one another. The first concerns a power to perceive, as with the potential theoretical intellect; the second concerns actual perception, as with intellect in act; and the third concerns action.

[^V03-782]: This is a rhetorical argument: if even the lower level is called intellect, surely this higher one deserves the name.

[^V03-783]: “First principles” here means the basic starting points, as opposed to conclusions, not all self-evident truths.

[^V03-784]: Another reading, perhaps better, is that “intellect in habit” contrasts with a mere capacity or absence. The potential intellect is only a capacity; the second intellect already possesses first principles and their actuality. Avicenna discusses it in *The Origin and Return*.

[^V03-785]: This means recognizing the Active Intellect through direct encounter, not merely learning about it. Direct knowledge is the highest kind, and seeing the forms within it cannot be separated from encountering it.

[^V03-786]: “Intellect” may mean the soul itself, one of its levels, or one of its powers; in every case it is either a power or an act of knowing. The potential intellect may be understood as the first appearance of the rational soul, like embers already present in coal before it catches fire. It is then the soul at a certain level. Or it may be understood as one of the soul’s powers, just as the rational soul has theoretical and practical powers, and the animal soul has powers of perception and movement. The theoretical power itself has the four levels just listed.

[^V03-787]: The potential intellect may be understood as a readiness close to completion—the intellect in habit—or as a readiness that still needs teaching and preparation, such as intuitive or sacred insight. The wording can also be read as “prepared,” in the passive sense.

[^V03-788]: “All things” may mean everything in every realm, including the divine realm and the world of names and attributes, most of which has no matter. Or it may mean all things in the natural world.

[^V03-789]: If we consider the existence of the forms, they are one form, because all exist through the one existence of the soul. If we consider their different essences, they are many forms.

[^V03-790]: The word “intelligible” is derived from “intellect,” hinting that the knower and what is known are one. It is like calling two things “lover” and “beloved” from the same root, or calling something “ensouled” from the word “soul.”

[^V03-791]: The comparison with lines or figures pressed into wax suggests that intelligibles extend through the whole subject, not just across its surface. The Second Teacher seems to mean the other subjects in which figures are formed. In a note, the author says that the analogy may concern only shapes and arrangements on the body’s surface, since natural forms extend through the body’s depth. The point may be that the distinction between form and matter becomes less clear in intellectual things, and perhaps even in bodily things.

[^V03-792]: This differs from the earlier comparison: there the pattern spreads through the matter, while here it is treated as identical with the matter. “Figure” here may mean one of the qualities tied to quantity: straightness or curvature, evenness or oddness, shape or angle, or a shape combined with color.

[^V03-793]: The clearer reading would omit the word “not,” though it appears in the manuscripts. It can be explained by taking the sentence to mean that forms become actual only when they are present throughout the wax-like subject, not merely on its surface. Another possible reading treats the word as a passive form of “to resemble.”

[^V03-794]: The three descriptions refer to the same single meaning: the form understood may be called actual knower, actual intellect, or actual intelligible; the one who understands may likewise be called by any of these names. The same applies to the intellect itself.

[^V03-795]: The features may be separable from the form in different instances or at different levels. Some, such as place and position, can vary by subject: the outermost sphere has no place in the usual sense, but it does have an order and position. Quantity and shape, however, cannot be separated from their subject. Most features cannot be separated from one another.

[^V03-796]: “Where” has levels: being somewhere in general, being in a particular country, being in a house within that country, and being in a particular room of that house. These all count as “where” in the ordinary sense, but the general concept of “where” is distinct from any one specific place.

[^V03-797]: Read “understands” in the active sense, following the doctrine that knower and known are one in existence, not in meaning. An essence without existence cannot be established, much less be an intellect and intelligible. The existence of what is understood is the very existence of the knower. It becomes actual intellect because it is free from matter, time, and place, and has a wider, more unified existence. A particular fire known through sense or imagination is confined by time and place. Once understood intellectually, it exists in a single, encompassing way that includes every particular fire—past, future, and in the next life. To know the universal fire is to know all its fine details. This is why the universal can both bring knowledge and be known, while the particular cannot do so in the same way.

[^V03-798]: Before that, the person was “nothing worth mentioning,” as the Qur'an says: “Has there not come upon man a period of time when he was nothing worth mentioning?”

[^V03-799]: When the actual intellect, which completes other intellects, understands itself, this also points to its union with the Active Intellect. A saying attributed to the Prophet teaches: “Know God through God, and the messenger through the message.”

[^V03-800]: This means universal intellects that are separate from matter by their nature, not because someone has abstracted them from matter.

[^V03-801]: The passage can be read in two ways. It may mean that the intellect understands those forms as forms, without needing to abstract them anew; or that it understands the separate intellect itself in the way it understands itself, with the intellect as knower and the forms as what it knows. The first reading is clearer. Another grammatical reading is also possible: the separate intellect encounters forms already within itself, just as it encounters itself. In every case, the point is that forms that never existed in matter do not need to be abstracted from matter.

[^V03-802]: These forms have no material subject, but their existence in us differs in completeness from their existence in themselves. Their presence in us is limited by our capacity to receive them.

[^V03-803]: This is the actual intellect that is our own being; what is present in us as its content is the intelligibles themselves.

[^V03-804]: The Arabic can be read with either a kasra or a fatḥa on the relevant letter, giving two grammatical readings.

[^V03-805]: Philosophers disagree about whether the acquired intellect can arise while the soul is still occupied with managing the body. The commentator holds that it can. For some people who know God, the body is like a garment they can put on and take off. A simple intellect whose dominant element is itself may have no awareness except the highest kind: the simple intellect, which contains all intelligibles in one unified reality. It can know them all at once, beyond time. The commentator then cites Rumi: “The pure ones’ bodies became pure spirit; their words, their breath, their very form—all became the absolute, unmarked spirit.”

[^V03-806]: The rising and descending levels of existence form a cycle: nature rises toward intellect, and intellect descends toward nature, without losing what it has attained.

[^V03-807]: Alexander’s account leaves out the acquired intellect, just as some accounts leave out the intellect in habit. The author discusses the substance of this treatise in *Keys to the Unseen*.

[^V03-808]: “Potential” here means pure possibility without any actuality mixed into it. Prime matter is all things in pure possibility; likewise, the potential intellect is pure potential. It is a simple substance whose kind and distinguishing feature are interwoven.

[^V03-809]: The “then” marks sequence, not causation.

[^V03-810]: The Arabic construction means “so that it may become,” with a preposition omitted in a regular grammatical pattern.

[^V03-811]: The “will” is emphatic, not a reference to the future. If the intellect already had a particular intellectual form that resisted other forms, those actual forms would clash, as they would in prime matter, and it could not receive every form.

[^V03-812]: Each sense is like matter for the things it perceives, so it must be free of those particular things. Otherwise, it would perceive them mixed with its own state. The statement that the senses do not perceive their objects in themselves means that those objects are absent from the senses’ own subject. A sense must be like its object in the way matter is suited to its form, as a seed is suited to a plant, an egg to a chick, and a seed of life to an animal. Sight is suited to colors and light, hearing to sound, and so on. The potential intellect is similarly suited to universal forms. This likeness does not mean that the perceiver already contains one of the forms it perceives; that would contradict the need to be free of it.

[^V03-813]: The reference is to the “vital spirit” of the body. Each power has this spirit as its subject, like a form in matter, and the power’s subject is itself like matter for what it perceives. Taste, for example, depends on the saliva that serves as its instrument. That moisture must also be receptive, or it could not taste flavors in their pure state.

[^V03-814]: This answers an apparent objection: if touch does not sense what resembles its own heat or cold, it seems to have admitted that the sense is not free of what it perceives. A body made of elements cannot be free of all basic sensible qualities, but it is free of the particular qualities it perceives—either because they are stronger or weaker than what is in the body.

[^V03-815]: Two things prevent a power from finding its objects within itself. First, an existing form blocks another form, since what is already actual cannot receive actuality in the same respect; a receptive power must first be open, then take on a form. Second, without this openness, there can be no distinction between the power and the object. The intellect’s ability to distinguish is not like the saliva’s ability to distinguish tastes.

[^V03-816]: Every actual existent is preceded by possibility.

[^V03-817]: Perceptive powers are bodily powers spread through the vital spirits in the brain and the cavities of the nerves. They do not perceive themselves, but perceive what is absent from them; each has a limited range of objects, and so is both limited in power and actual in its own way. The potential intellect differs: because it can understand everything, it must be free of all those forms.

[^V03-818]: Just as knowledge in act is one with what is known in act, the actual knower and actual intellect are one with what is understood in act. The intelligible is therefore actual intellect and actual knower.

[^V03-819]: Having discussed the Active Intellect’s role in knowledge, Alexander turns to its role in action. It may govern the elemental world directly, returning things to their higher intellectual levels, as a steward is sometimes said to do; or it may govern through the motions of the heavens; or it may act through nature, which combines and separates the elements. These possibilities are not mutually exclusive. If we see natural powers as levels of the Active Intellect’s agency, it acts alone; if we focus on the different levels, we include the other causes as well. Some might think these lowly things and actions unworthy of the Active Intellect, but the commentator rejects that view. All its acts are wise and exact. In general, intellect and providence guide this world, as the other intellects complete the souls of the heavenly bodies. The commentator suspects that a copyist changed “intellectual levels” to “divine bodies.”

[^V03-820]: That is, through greater or lesser nearness.

[^V03-821]: This note clarifies the pronouns in Alexander’s sentence. “Whether we can understand” concerns the soul; “nor is it our work” concerns the intellect. “When we come to be” means that the Active Intellect is naturally present in us from the beginning, giving the potential intellect its foundation and the actual intellect its actuality.

[^V03-822]: This points to the union of knower and known. The knower is not a place in which the known is lodged; it changes into the intelligibles, as matter changes into forms. The sense power likewise becomes one with the forms it senses.

[^V03-823]: A natural kind is a unified whole. The difficulty is that the soul’s distinguishing feature makes it a definite form in the human being, so how can it become something indeterminate? Elsewhere, a plant becomes an animal through indeterminate matter. Also, if the soul is the body’s form, how can it become identical with what is separate from the body? And if soul and intellect are distinct kinds, how can one become the other?

[^V03-824]: Essence brings limitation and difference; existence brings breadth and identity. The essences of green, indigo, and deep black differ, but their existence is one continuous reality with degrees. Its continuous unity is the unity of one individual.

[^V03-825]: For example, a body may be potentially white and actually something else at the same time. Or a body may be actual through its bodily form and potential for motion, as philosophers argue when they establish prime matter. An intellectual being, too, may have one perfection in act and another in potentiality.

[^V03-826]: A body is actual through its form and receptive to motion through its matter, which carries potentiality. The soul is different: the very soul that is actual as a soul is also potential to receive an intellectual form. The note then offers several ways to understand this.

    The potential intellect is not prime matter in the strict sense. Strictly speaking, matter is a natural subject that carries another natural form, and both remain together in one natural level. The soul does not remain unchanged when it becomes intellect in act, just as a sensible natural form does not remain in the same way when it becomes an intelligible. The earlier form gives way to the later one, as the earthly and heavenly worlds are transformed in the next life. So the potential intellect is like matter for the intellectual world, not a material subject that remains alongside its new form. The Second Teacher likewise calls actual intellect a kind of matter for the acquired intellect.

    Potentiality in a material subject means that, at one time, the thing is without the form it is ready to receive, and later receives it. This kind of potentiality does not apply to immaterial realities: an intelligible such as universal fire has an encompassing existence beyond time and place. Thus, to say that the potential intellect becomes actual does not mean that one separate thing receives another. It means that a single, continuous reality develops through connected levels.

    If the potential intellect has learned first principles yet remains able to know other things, this does not require a second subject. The “potentiality” means that it is receptive to further knowledge. The intellect also has levels: one level may have become a particular intelligible while another has not, as portions of prime matter can become different things. Another possible answer is that the soul has real actuality and potentiality without being made of two parts: its actuality is its own, while its potentiality comes from its relation to the body, which is the soul’s matter. As it takes on intelligibles in succession, the body’s potentiality is involved in a corresponding succession.

    A further answer accepts composition, but not of prime matter and bodily form. It is a composition of potential intellect and separate intellectual form, each at its own level. This also helps explain the “Muḥammadan Reality” in the mystical tradition, said to rise in its ascent beyond the Active Intellect. The universal intellects are complete in themselves, but the prophetic spirit is joined to bodily matter, which makes further transformation possible while the body remains. There is therefore a difference between the Active Intellect considered apart from natural existence and the Active Intellect as it meets natural existence. The latter can continue to rise as far as God wills.

[^V03-827]: This means the form itself, not a mental image of it.

[^V03-828]: Something mixed with other things is not pure or unrestricted.

[^V03-829]: A wording note: the text can be read as saying that “being present to something able to understand” is part of what it means to understand, rather than being the whole meaning. The author leaves the other part of the definition open because the argument does not need it.

[^V03-830]: This argument concerns intellect in act that was once potential, not an intellect that is actual by nature from the start.

[^V03-831]: The form being discussed is the first form that makes the potential intellect actual. A natural kind becomes actual through one of its individuals.

[^V03-832]: This is the form that was first only possible. The first form is present at the level of potentiality; it cannot already be an unrelated form that is actual by nature.

[^V03-833]: A part counts as a separate part only in relation to the whole. The parts are gathered together by their shared arrangement.

[^V03-834]: This would turn potentiality into another potentiality: the part like form would become the receptive part, and the part like matter would become the form. It also leaves no role for the matter-like part, since the form-like part would already understand.

[^V03-835]: If one part can understand both parts, it is already the actual intellect; the other part does not help make the whole actual.

[^V03-836]: The reverse arrangement fails in the same way.

[^V03-837]: The author’s list may include understanding the whole through itself. If this means direct knowledge, the whole is one with what it knows, which supports the author’s point. If it means knowledge through a mental image, the same difficulty returns. The two wholes may be arranged alike or differently, but either way the argument returns to one of the failed options.

[^V03-838]: I say: Avicenna's purpose is to state what understanding means, not to give its ultimate cause. His words, "by a further form coming to exist in the potential intellect," make this clear. Nor does he reject the causal explanation merely because it would explain a thing through itself. The difficulty is that a form can exist in something receptive without being understood: this is true of a form in matter. If we add that the form must be *intelligible*, we are left asking what makes it intelligible in the first place.

[^V03-839]: The commentator offers another explanation: the potential intellect understands the form because it receives it as an immaterial reality in an immaterial being. This adds a third possibility to Avicenna’s choice.

[^V03-840]: Avicenna does not accept change from one substance into another. In particular, he does not accept that a nonmaterial substance can change its very nature.

[^V03-841]: Avicenna counts only ten separate intellects. The Illuminationists allow a complete guiding light to join the ranks of the separate lights after its bodily shell is left behind, but Avicenna does not accept separate intellects of the same level.

[^V03-842]: The soul begins through the body and continues as a spirit after death. The potential intellect is not a separate being that already knows itself as the argument requires. One possible reply is that “potential intellect” means a power to understand, or the soul after it has reached the level of intellect in habit.

[^V03-843]: Another reading is that, without the first principle, the other part would have to be both present and absent.

[^V03-844]: “Equal” here does not mean equal in size or in how many things a statement fits. It means sharing the same kind, as two people do. The rule applies to that kind of equality.

[^V03-845]: Other truths depend on the first principle through a simple argument: assume either the principle or its opposite, then rule out one side to establish the other. But the first principle does not break down into ordinary statements with a subject and a predicate. It is a basic choice between affirmation and denial.

[^V03-846]: The author points out that, before judgment, the idea of existence is the clearest starting point in thought. It also points to real existence, which comes before every particular kind of reality. Its meaning is clearer than any other basic idea; it is the end of the chain of what is self-evident, just as the Necessary Being is the end of the chain of what depends on something else.

[^V03-847]: Studying geometry, arithmetic, and logic helps in two ways: it teaches someone to check whether a proof works, and it gives practice in certainty. Many basic questions are self-evident, but people need to become used to recognizing them.

[^V03-848]: You may ask: Is the point simply that whatever is free of matter knows itself, since a body or a bodily thing does not? That conclusion does not follow merely by reversing the statement. From "everything that knows itself is nonbodily" we cannot infer that everything nonbodily knows itself; at most, an affirmative statement gives us a conclusion about some such things. I reply: The contrast with bodies may be given because we learn what things are through their opposites. It can also form a fuller argument: no body or bodily thing knows itself, and nothing wholly separate from matter is bodily. From these two premises we reach the intended result: nothing separate from matter fails to know itself. The further statement, "Every nonbodily being ...," offers another route to the conclusion. It applies to a rational soul, a separate intellect, the Necessary Being, and—if the knower truly becomes one with what it knows—to the form through which another thing is understood.

[^V03-849]: The first and second methods may be one argument stated in two ways. In any case, they strongly support the claim that separate substances know themselves. The philosophers focus on substances because an intellectual form is free of matter and potentiality. A form that exists in itself is present to itself; presence is what makes it known. The same existence that makes it present also makes it a knower.

[^V03-850]: Read “he said” as the reply to “when he had shown.”

[^V03-851]: Avicenna does not explicitly say that a form becomes one with the thing it makes actual. The commentator reads “present to it” as union, much as existence is present to existence or unity to what is one. The proof works without that reading: if a form makes another thing an actual intellect by being present to it, then a form that exists by itself is an intellect and knower in its own right.

[^V03-852]: This is the second argument. The first describes knowledge as a thing’s not being hidden from itself; the second describes it as being present to itself. “Not hidden” is more exact because “presence” sounds like a relation between two separate things.

[^V03-853]: The point is that a separate being may exist in itself without being present to something else. This is different from a thing that exists through another thing.

[^V03-854]: One might object that the author assumes the soul is separate before proving that every separate being understands itself. But he uses only the fact that we know ourselves, not that we are separate. Knowing oneself means one and the same self is both knower and known. Even an animal knows itself in a direct way because it seeks what suits it and avoids what harms it. The author’s claim about intellect is stronger: the soul understands itself as intellect, not merely through imagination or instinct.

[^V03-855]: Philosophers hold three views about how the soul knows particular things. One says the soul knows only universals; its powers know particulars, and we speak loosely when we say “the soul knows.” Another says the soul itself knows particulars through powers that are levels of the soul; this is the author’s view. A third says the soul knows particulars directly, while its powers serve as instruments. The commentator reads Suhrawardī as agreeing with the second view, not the first. The author’s criticism is that the two earlier philosophers reject the claim that the powers are levels of the soul when they explain how particulars are known. For universals, the author says the soul knows them through union with their kinds, not by looking at them from a distance.

[^V03-856]: God is the Light of lights. The only reason we cannot fully understand Him is that our limited minds cannot encompass the Necessary Being. In one sense, all things reveal Him, because each has a side turned toward the light of existence and a side marked by its own limits. Existence is light; concealment is darkness. We can know God through His attributes, which are easier to understand than His full reality. We can speak of Him through existence, light, awareness, life, unity, and love. We can also know Him directly when the self is overcome by His presence. These are ways of knowing the Necessary Being, especially when we see that our light is borrowed from Him.

[^V03-857]: The objection assumes that God has an essence that can be defined. The commentator says it is the reverse: we cannot fully grasp God’s real existence, but we can define the ordinary essence of a possible thing.

[^V03-858]: The commentator sharply criticizes al-Rāzī for confusing the shared concept of existence with real existence itself. When philosophers say God is pure existence, they mean real existence, which drives away nonexistence—not the general idea of “existence.” When they say His essence is His existence, they mean He is existence in its fullest degree, untouched by essence as a limit. This does not mean that existence in general is the Necessary Being. The levels of existence differ in completeness, and cause and effect share a connection of kind: lower levels are contained in higher ones.

[^V03-859]: This argument may be intended for philosophers in Aristotle’s school, who say that knowledge of other things comes through forms in the mind. They want to show how a separate being can know another thing. If it can be joined to another intelligible form, the image must be that form itself. But it is difficult to argue that this possibility belongs to the form’s nature. A simpler argument would be that a separate being can be present with another separate being, or that a cause and its effect are necessarily joined. Those arguments rely on direct knowledge rather than mental forms.

[^V03-860]: The main point is that separate intellects do not have knowledge through mental copies. Our own learned knowledge works differently. We directly experience immaterial forms, then, because we are also connected to matter, we compare those forms with what we see in the material world. We then form ideas and concepts such as “horse” or “tree.” This is how knowledge through mental ideas arises. Pure intellects have no such link to matter, so they do not form ideas that stand apart from existence. They know things directly, through the existence of those things themselves.

[^V03-861]: The shared kind must apply equally to every member, not by degrees. The argument does not work for a kind whose members have different levels of completeness.

[^V03-862]: This leaves open the possibility that the same kind can exist in different ways, even if its essential features remain the same.

[^V03-863]: The relation between two ideas within a mind is different from the relation between a separate being and an idea present to it. One is like two features sharing one subject; the other is like a feature and its subject. If the argument is only about images in the mind, that may avoid the problem of having a thing’s possibility depend on its already existing. The two claims concern the same moment, not one depending on the other over time.

[^V03-864]: If the argument uses a specific kind of being together, one could say it is only a feature of the mind. If it uses “being together” in the broadest sense, that broad relation does not prove that every specific kind of relation is possible. A physical form and an immaterial form, for example, cannot be together in the same way.

[^V03-865]: The first “together with” refers to what is joined; the second to what it is joined with. God cannot be joined to another thing as one item beside another. His togetherness with things means that He sustains them, not that He shares a place or relation with them.

[^V03-866]: The conclusion is even harder if applied to all separate beings, including God. If God could be together with every intelligible form at once, He would have an unlimited number of distinct aspects. The argument says such forms must be joined without order, unless another proof establishes a cause-and-effect order.

[^V03-867]: The argument may establish only that such a relation is possible. It does not, by itself, prove knowledge. To establish knowledge, one must also show that there is no barrier between two immaterial beings, such as the light-like existence of one being present to another.

[^V03-868]: This means that intellect is the union of the knower and what is known. The commentator says this is the very claim the argument was supposed to prove, so using it here assumes the conclusion.

[^V03-869]: What is understood in act is itself intellect in act, and it makes the being that receives it an actual intellect.

[^V03-870]: This refers to the first premise of the fourth argument: any separate being can be understood by another. If it can be understood in act, it must be understood by something. But in the separate world, possibility is never left waiting to become actual. Since a being understands everything it can understand, and this includes itself, it understands itself.

[^V03-871]: If “intellect in act” means an actual intelligible form, as in Farabi’s account, then there is no problem: the human soul always has at least one basic intelligible idea. But the objection means intellect in act in the stronger sense of the Active Intellect, or at least the third stage of the soul’s intellect. Avicenna’s account of separation includes freedom from time, place, direction, and potentiality, so the problem remains if the soul is separate from its first moment.

[^V03-872]: Bodily makeup may give the soul a good power of reasoning, quick insight, or sacred insight. The soul’s actions may also grow stronger through practice and good habits.

[^V03-873]: One reply is that being separate by nature does not make the soul an actual intellect from the start. In Avicenna’s view, the soul’s knowledge of particular things is a later perfection. It depends on earlier sense and imagination, which prepare the soul to form universal intellectual ideas. So the soul’s existence as a separate substance does not mean that all its intellectual powers are already actual.

[^V03-874]: Two arguments for the soul's freedom from matter have been indicated here. First, the soul must be free from matter because what it understands is free from matter. Second, it can grasp true unity and simplicity. But these arguments prove the point only for souls that have actually reached those abilities, and such souls are very few. For the author, to understand *horse* in a purely intellectual way is to become one with the intellect that governs that kind—or at least to grasp the horse as something understood in act. That is not simply the bare meaning of "horse": a nature without existence is nothing. It is one real existence that gathers many things together, even if a thousand intellects grasp it. It is the same reality present in the fully actual intellects. Each such object of understanding exists as a luminous reality free from matter, place, direction, position and time, yet includes everything belonging to its own kind. None of its intelligible features or its outward instances falls outside its knowledge. Its hearing and sight are its immediate knowledge of what is heard and seen; its hands and feet, or power of movement, are its effective knowledge and power. The senses and limbs of the natural beings belonging to that kind are lower expressions of what is present in it. The existence of an intellect is simple but embraces its many manifestations, and even their further manifestations. In that sense it is both what gives knowledge and what is known; through knowing it, we may learn about them. As for the second argument, how many people really understand a unity and simplicity in which nothing is put together out of what it has and what it lacks? Only a few who have reached the highest degrees of understanding.

[^V03-875]: It is surprising to call the acquired intellect and the Active Intellect the same kind when one is dependent and the other is what it depends on, and when one has passed through matter while the other has never been in matter. Some philosophers do not accept that members of one kind can differ in this way.

[^V03-876]: The comparison with sunlight applies to the relation between outside colors and their visible forms: colors are only visible in potentiality in the dark and become visible in light. What is directly visible is the form present to sight, not the outside color as it exists in matter. In the same way, an intelligible form receives existence from its separate source. The direct object of sight or knowledge may be called the visible or intelligible thing itself, because its image is present to the perceiver. The form is what we look through; it is not a second image inside another image. Just as light is visible by itself and makes colors visible, intellectual light is present by itself and makes intelligible forms visible. The mind should see the Active Intellect in the forms it understands, since the intellect’s existence is the shared existence of those forms.

[^V03-877]: This is the view held by Aristotle’s followers. The Illuminationists instead speak of a guiding form for each kind of thing.

[^V03-878]: This assumes that images of things exist in the Active Intellect in a cause-and-effect order.

[^V03-879]: It is strange that these forms are ordered but do not exist there as separate forms or as forms lodged in a subject. One explanation is that they are not separate from the Active Intellect: they are connected aspects of its one existence, which remain with it. The intellect contains the existence of things in a higher, simpler way; their essences follow from that existence. Their order is therefore a matter of how we understand the forms.

[^V03-880]: The point of the claim that self-awareness lasts is to distinguish this argument from the previous one and to establish the basic reality of direct awareness: the self is immediately present to itself.

[^V03-881]: This is the same kind of case: if an immaterial self knew itself through a mental image, the image and self would differ in how they exist, just as an idea in the mind differs from an outside individual. That difference is compatible with the image matching the self in nature.

[^V03-882]: In other words, self-knowledge through direct awareness can coexist with conceptual knowledge of oneself. We can also form ideas about our own thinking.

[^V03-883]: The earlier proof says that a mental image differs from the outside thing. This proof says that a universal image differs from the particular individual. It may be one argument expressed in two ways: what we know, and our knowledge of it, are both particular, so neither is simply a universal image.

[^V03-884]: “Not in a subject” is only part of the definition of a substance. A substance is a nature that exists in itself, rather than as a feature of something else.

[^V03-885]: The self’s not being hidden from itself is direct, existential awareness. That is why the speaker says that nothing remains but existence.

[^V03-886]: This is conceptual awareness, added to direct awareness. It does not make the self what it is, nor does it make awareness of anything else identical with the self’s existence.

[^V03-887]: The actual referent of “I” is the existence of the one who perceives himself. Since that existence is immaterial, it is not hidden from itself. The word “I” can be used of the Necessary Being and of other beings, but here it means any real being that is aware of itself.

[^V03-888]: If the objection is that the soul is existence and the Necessary Being is existence, so the soul must be the Necessary Being, the argument confuses a general concept with real existence. If it is framed as a formal syllogism, it is invalid. Or, if the claim is that anything whose nonexistence is impossible must be the Necessary Being, Sadra replies that the soul’s existence is limited and incomplete, while the Necessary Being is existence in its fullest perfection.

[^V03-889]: Any act of will or desire also includes awareness and love of oneself.

[^V03-890]: In every case listed, knowledge of the object includes awareness of oneself.

[^V03-891]: We cannot know a cause by way of its effect, or one effect by way of another, if doing so requires moving from the effect back to its cause and then to another effect. If we could infer our self from our own action, this would be possible. The two kinds of indirect proof under discussion do not establish knowledge in such cases. In general necessary connections that do not involve causation, indirect proof can still provide knowledge.

[^V03-892]: The argument is first stated in reverse: a material thing cannot understand an intelligible form. From this it follows that anything that does understand such a form is free of matter.

[^V03-893]: The natural universal can be said of particular individuals. When we call something by a general name, what matters is the meaning of that name. The natural universal is the nature of a thing considered just as it is, and the meaning applies to the individuals in which that nature exists.

    But the intellectual universal, considered as a separate object of thought, cannot be said of individuals in the same way. On the account used here, it has an immaterial existence of its own and is even the governing reality of the kind.

    You may ask: do we not often say that the intellectual universal gathers the existence of its individuals in a fuller way, and that it is those individuals? Yes, but that is not ordinary predication. Separate realities are not said of one another in that way. Rather, an image is in one respect the thing it images, while the original possesses what is shown in the image in a higher way. The natural universal can also be said of the intellectual universal.

[^V03-894]: The natural kind, taken simply as what it is, is not called divisible or indivisible at the level of the concept. In actual individuals it is divided. So it is not a case of something actually indivisible being one with something actually divided.

[^V03-895]: This is not a legal analogy or a formal logical example. It is only meant to suggest that something spatial could be one with something nonspatial.

[^V03-896]: There is a difference between being nonspatial without being defined by that feature, as with prime matter, and being nonspatial by nature, as with an intellectual universal.

[^V03-897]: The separate parts would have to stand apart from the whole as a condition does from what depends on it.

[^V03-898]: The second contradiction is that if the parts differed in shape or number, the whole would not be intelligible as one kind.

[^V03-899]: The object of understanding is supposed to be indivisible. If its intelligibility depends on two parts, it must be divided. The wording also allows another reading: the parts are only introduced as conditions in the argument, while the thing itself is assumed to be simple.

[^V03-900]: The first option assumes that the intellect is located at the endpoint of the thing it understands; the second assumes that the intellect and what it understands become one. In either case, the endpoint would be the boundary of the intellect’s own measurable extent.

[^V03-901]: The image is not really taken from something outside. The enormous circle could be in the sky, but the surrounding square is not an outside shape. The alternative—that it exists in brain matter—is also rejected.

[^V03-902]: The first difficulty concerns size; the second concerns shape. Shape is a way of being arranged within a size.

[^V03-903]: The point is not simply that a potential perceiver cannot cause an actual image. Rather, if the image were the form received by the faculty, it would be a material subject and the faculty would be a substance, reversing the required relationship. If the imagined shape were the agent and the faculty were affected by it, then an image, which is only a feature, would be stronger than the faculty, which is a substance.

[^V03-904]: An extended quantity cannot be directly present to itself in every part; its parts are distinct from each other and from the whole. But an efficient cause must be more fully present to its effect.

[^V03-905]: Bodily powers act gradually and need a spatial relation to the matter their effects arise from. Imagined forms arise all at once, with no matter to establish such a relation beforehand. Their making is more like creation by a simple command than a bodily action carried out over time.

[^V03-906]: “As the one perceiving” preserves the difference between the soul’s powers. The soul is one, but it understands universal ideas and perceives images through different levels or powers.

[^V03-907]: The author is right: this proof establishes that imagination—or the soul at the level of imagination—is free of ordinary matter. Here the "place" of imagined forms means what *produces* them, not a container that passively receives them. Still, the philosophers' claim can be defended in a limited sense: the proof establishes that the soul is nonmaterial in some respect, and that may be enough as a first step. Further arguments must distinguish its freedom from matter from freedom from dimensions and, beyond that, from dependence on any distinct nature or essence. That is how their interpretation can be understood.

[^V03-908]: If the soul does not take on the square’s shape, there is no specific relation by which that square exists in it.

[^V03-909]: The discussion of cause and effect can be shortened: imagined forms are present to the soul as its effects, much as bodily forms are present to the soul without making it take on their shapes.

[^V03-910]: The imagined form may come from a separate imaginal source, just as intellectual forms come from the Active Intellect. Once the soul has acquired and retained a form, it may also be attributed to the soul as its producer. The form is present to the soul as a perfection is present to something less complete, not by being lodged in it as matter.

[^V03-911]: The mirror example works whether reflected images are understood as forms in an imaginal world, as some Illuminationists say, or as reflections of natural things, as Sadra says. On Sadra’s view, the soul produces even mirror images by arranging mirrors.

[^V03-912]: This follows the theory that vision works through rays emitted from the eye.

[^V03-913]: The author gives two answers: prime matter is not actually free of size in reality, and its lack of a fixed size is not the same as the intellect’s being inherently nonspatial. The brain, by contrast, is bound to bodily extension.

[^V03-914]: The soul is not defined by being bodily, while the brain is defined by its small, measurable size.

[^V03-915]: The argument concerns blackness and whiteness being present together in the same act of judgment, not merely one after the other. “Imagination” here may refer to the shared inner sense that judges them, not only the faculty that stores images.

[^V03-916]: On the usual view, the forms exist in the mind by being received in it. On Sadra’s view, they exist by the mind’s productive act. Either way, the forms of both opposites must be present.

[^V03-917]: This is offered as a possible reply to the objection; Sadra’s stronger answer follows.

[^V03-918]: The word “or” here means “and”: the argument needs both points. Bodily things cannot produce imagined forms, because material action requires a spatial relation.

[^V03-919]: Since the questioner claims that the soul receives images as features, the reply accepts that assumption for the sake of the argument: a feature essential to the image cannot fail to be present in the image.

[^V03-920]: If forms exist in the mind through the mind’s own productive act, there is no need to treat them as features that make the mind hot, cold, black, or white.

[^V03-921]: The opposites can belong to one body at the same time, but only in different parts; they cannot be present together in one undivided subject. The argument can be set out this way: the soul or imagination cannot simultaneously know and fail to know the very same thing—for example, what is written in Zayd's book. An extended body, however, can admit opposites in distinct parts. If the soul or imagination were bodily, such a division would be possible in it; but the consequence is false. So the soul's power to imagine cannot be bodily in that way.

[^V03-922]: A point cannot itself be the subject that receives a feature. Its actual subject would be the measurable thing whose boundary it is, and that would be extended.

[^V03-923]: Earlier philosophers treated the inner powers as states of the body or its subtle life-spirit, so they would disappear when the body falls apart. On the author’s view, these inner powers are nonbodily and remain with the soul when it leaves the body, preserving its way of perceiving particulars.

[^V03-924]: Here “essential” and “necessary” have the same sense.

[^V03-925]: Even if the soul has no intellectual life before birth, it can reach this state after birth. The nature becomes actual through an individual, so the soul may acquire intellect as it develops. On this account, the soul is a lower, less complete level of intellect, while the simple intellect is its fuller inner reality.

[^V03-926]: The soul's "first source" may mean the First Cause—God—or its nearer source, the Active Intellect. Either way, describing the soul as ancient is not merely using the name of its cause for the soul, or applying a description of one thing to something connected with it. All light is one reality: its levels differ in priority, completeness and strength, from the most dazzling light to governing and guiding lights, not in the basic reality of light. In that sense the eternity of the source may be spoken of as the soul's eternity. This gives Plato's words a plausible interpretation, but it does not establish that his view is correct. The soul, properly speaking, is the stage of life connected with the body, and that stage begins in time. It begins with bodily existence and changes in its very being until it can endure as spiritual life.

[^V03-927]: The argument uses a conditional construction: if knowledge were not essential, then the soul’s lack of knowledge would be. Sadra challenges that move in the next paragraph.

[^V03-928]: The argument can also be framed by saying that a soul with no capacity for understanding would never understand. But it still overlooks the difference between lacking knowledge essentially and being able to gain it. Its answer is the one Sadra gives in the main text.

[^V03-929]: The first mistake is to assume that because the soul lacks knowledge, this lack must be essential. The second is to confuse absolute lack of knowledge with not having a particular kind of knowledge at a particular stage.

[^V03-930]: The sharper wording is that the possible thing would be impossible forever, not merely absent forever.

[^V03-931]: The claim is that being absorbed in bodily life blocks awareness of knowledge already present in the soul. Sadra replies that if an intelligible form is actually present to an immaterial soul, that very presence is awareness. Otherwise, every uneducated person would already have all knowledge in a hidden, simple form.

[^V03-932]: An uneducated soul has not yet developed the ability to recover universal ideas from such a storehouse, because it has not first understood them.

[^V03-933]: If mere potential connection to forms in the Active Intellect counted as knowing them, every soul would already know them all. This would make the claim that the soul knew them before embodiment a symbolic account, not literal knowledge.

[^V03-934]: A concept sought through thought may be unknown in its essence but known by a description or feature. Or it may be unknown in one feature and known through another. The known parts allow the search to begin, while the thing sought remains unknown in the relevant respect.

[^V03-935]: Perhaps the difficulty is this: what is already known cannot be acquired, because that would be acquiring something we already have; what is unknown cannot be acquired either, since we cannot seek what we do not know. The answer is that these are not two things, but one thing known in one respect and unknown in another. Its known and unknown aspects belong to one existence. It is like claiming that nothing can be complete in one respect and incomplete in another, because the complete aspect is wholly complete and the incomplete aspect wholly incomplete. That claim is plainly false. The objection about learning fails for the same reason.

[^V03-936]: The previous argument also dealt with this topic, but there the point was to show that the knower is immaterial; the immateriality of what is known was only part of the route to that conclusion. Here, the immateriality of what is known is itself the point.

[^V03-937]: That is, no power belonging to a body can perceive it. Here “power” first means a receptive power, and “a power in a body” means an active power.

[^V03-938]: Whether perception is passive, as most philosophers think, or active, as the author holds, it still requires a spatial relation. Otherwise matter would serve no purpose in the power's existence.

[^V03-939]: Existence comes first in the order of nature. If a material power could act without position, the argument would contradict itself: acting requires existence, and this power's existence is assumed to require matter.

[^V03-940]: Parts of a measured whole resemble the whole in kind and name. If each part can be understood like the whole, and there are infinitely many parts potentially, there would be infinitely many intelligible forms. The argument uses “potentially” to expose the conflict between divisibility and intelligibility.

[^V03-941]: This division is different from the first division into spatial parts, but the spatial division follows from the assumption that the form occupies a position.

[^V03-942]: We could never fully picture a thing through infinitely many parts. Also, if broader kinds and defining features differed in nature and were arranged in different positions, the account would imply indivisible parts of matter.

[^V03-943]: “Reality” here means the whole shared nature that is understood. Its individual examples are sensed, but not as the universal nature itself.

[^V03-944]: “Its mode of existence” means its material mode of being; existence is what a thing is, in a particular way.

[^V03-945]: The passage admits two readings. First, understanding may be a relationship to the thing's real nature, considered apart from direction, place, time, and other bodily conditions. On this account the nature exists in the material world but is not grasped by the senses, because the senses encounter it mixed with features foreign to what it is. Only the intellect grasps it. As Avicenna says in the passage quoted earlier from the *Beginning and Return*, being mixed with other things does not destroy a thing's own nature.

    Second, understanding may mean removing some features, namely those that are incidental, while keeping the essential ones and bringing them into the mind. This is not the same as the earlier account of abstraction from sensation.
