The first reading suits those who deny that things have existence in the mind; the second need not deny mental existence at first, though a closer examination makes the problem return.

    Both readings face a serious difficulty. The natures under discussion include the ability to have dimensions among their essential features, and divisibility among what follows from them. A thing's essential features cannot simply be taken away. The same difficulty troubles anyone who says the difference between universal and particular knowledge lies only in how a single object is perceived, rather than in any difference in what is known.

    The author's view offers a clearer solution. The intellectual reality exists in a new, luminous manner of being, not here in the material world stripped of a few properties. Abstraction means that this lower mode of existence is gathered into a higher one. The 'earth' of that understanding is no longer this earth, and the 'heaven' is folded away. Words such as 'substance' or 'capable of dimensions' apply to the idea in the mind as an idea, not as bodily conditions actually present there. Arguments for mental existence establish no more than this. What makes such concepts true of lower things is that the higher intellectual existence contains their reality in a more complete way.

[^V03-946]: The ascent in the argument is that this new mode of existence may not be merely another nonmaterial mode; it is specifically intellectual.

[^V03-947]: “Outside” here means the material world. This does not mean that images have no external existence in cases such as dreams, illness, or spiritual perception. A person may perceive something that exists in the soul, or at a higher level, rather than in bodily matter. Even a person of sound mind cannot always tell by sensation alone whether an image exists materially. The matter must be settled through proof or by consulting someone with knowledge of these realities.

[^V03-948]: In other words, such judgment belongs to the intellect's first principles, not to the senses.

[^V03-949]: Or through an internal imbalance, as in a fever dream.

[^V03-950]: The sensory powers are called “sensible qualities” in two respects: as representations of things, and as qualities belonging to the soul. They represent things that are sensed in themselves; in that sense they refer to the objects of perception.

[^V03-951]: As representations, these qualities have a weaker existence, mixed with nonexistence, unlike the pure existence they represent.

[^V03-952]: These forms are “human,” “horse,” and so on when considered in their own reality, not as images that represent lower things. On the view that intellects have no essences, they are even beyond being substances.

[^V03-953]: The sentence may be read as giving the reason for the divisions that follow, or as introducing a point whose conclusion is understood from the earlier discussion.

[^V03-954]: The author has already argued that sensory, imaginal, and estimative knowledge are one kind of knowing existence; there are two modes of knowing existence.

[^V03-955]: He does not separately define these kinds of existence or knowledge because he explains the corresponding kinds of knowers below.

[^V03-956]: “Animal souls” here means souls after they have left earthly bodies. Souls still joined to earthly bodies belong to the third, incomplete level.

[^V03-957]: This refers to bodies. Someone might object that, if images in knowledge exist in themselves rather than in matter, forms that stand in matter should not count as knowledge. The author includes them because they are close to the directly sensed forms that count as objects of knowledge. They depend on the positions of material objects, though only incidentally.

[^V03-958]: “Existence” here means luminous, knowing existence, not existence in every sense. This is clear from the reference to forms of knowledge.

[^V03-959]: The comparison is with mystics who include this world among the Divine Presences and as a place where the Divine appears. “Effects” means the scattered material existences.

[^V03-960]: This includes both the forms understood by us and those understood by others.

[^V03-961]: The first phrase points to the view held by Aristotle’s followers, according to which forms are imprinted in souls. The second points to the Illuminationist view, according to which these forms subsist on their own in an imaginal world.

[^V03-962]: Another possibility is that those who glide are intellects, those who race ahead are the universal souls of the heavenly spheres, and those who manage affairs are the souls within those spheres. In Illuminationist terms, the intellect is the overpowering light and the soul the governing light. Or the phrases may refer respectively to fixed realities in the realm of knowledge, the intellects, and the spheres, including both their bodies and souls.

[^V03-963]: “Mirror” here means the means by which something is revealed. If it means an instrument used to look at something else, the relation is the reverse: material and imaginal things should be mirrors for intellectual realities. Those who attend to particulars make universal and imaginal forms into mirrors of material particulars, treating them as weak even though they are strong in themselves.

[^V03-964]: The Persian verse calls even the realm of oneness something that seems not to exist: “Leave what is not but appears to be; seek what is but appears not to be.” The author's explanation is that, as beings living in nature, we do not have the kind of dependent existence that would connect us directly with that higher realm. Another reading is that this realm has no separate existence at all: its existence is wholly absorbed in God's. As the verse has it, “We were exalted letters, not yet spoken”; and another Persian line says, “When I became empty of my own existence, I knew of none but God.” As for imaginal forms, their existence is the kind of existence known to us through outward things; the word for what *is* in Plato's saying concerns the world of the senses.

[^V03-965]: Earlier arguments for Platonic forms show that the concepts “human,” “horse,” and the rest can be true of a separate intellectual being. They do not show that these concepts are its true essences, or that such a being is an intellectual individual of the natural kind.

[^V03-966]: Here 'description' includes a thing's essential qualities, not just those added to it. A definition may identify the whole nature, part of it, or something outside it. Likewise, a feature that cannot be separated from a thing may be essential or incidental. Although we can describe things through their outward parts, philosophers more often define them through the parts distinguished by the intellect.

    The mention of organs and shapes recalls the author's difficulty about understanding a whole person intellectually. We must not remove something essential and then pretend we still understand the complete person—as the saying asks, who has ever seen a lion without tail, head, or belly?

    The intellectual human being therefore has sight and eyes, but at its higher level these mean its direct knowledge of what lies beneath it, including things that are seen. It has hearing and ears in the same sense, as direct knowledge of sounds, and similarly for imagination and other powers. Its hand is its effective power to act.

    At the level where it is expressed in bodily forms, its sight and eyes appear through the many particular acts of seeing and the many eyes that perform them. The same is true of its other organs and powers. We must, however, understand these bodily powers as dependent on the intellectual reality and connected to it, not as detached pieces accidentally placed beside it.

[^V03-967]: The presence of incidental features does not prevent a universal from being understood. They can also be left out when needed.

[^V03-968]: The world of direct creation and the world in which things are brought forth are not far from you, though you see them as distant. You are nothing other than these worlds; nothing else will remain of you or be enough for you—especially the higher world of intellect, in which the knower and what is known are one. If you doubt what we have set before you, consider the reality of what is understood: the vastness of that existence, its unity despite containing many things, its light, and the way it illuminates things outside the mind. Do not stop at the meanings of things as mere concepts.

[^V03-969]: This is why I have said that the teaching that one simple reality contains all existences in a higher and simpler way is, in truth, a teaching about knowledge. To perceive something is to find and reach it; the meeting of luminous existence with luminous realities is itself knowledge. Bodily meeting is only so called by analogy, since bodies touch one another only at their edges and surfaces. That is why the mystics call the higher realm the world beyond separation. Perception through the body is not true perception in the way intellectual understanding is.

[^V03-970]: How could an image be lost and then restored if the Active Intellect were not always present? The state of one thing united with another follows the state of the other.

[^V03-971]: As when the soul's understanding of the Light of Lights, unity, simplicity, or all-encompassing existence remains as a faint image. It can then retrieve the intelligibles from its simple intellectual state and picture them in imagination and sensation.

[^V03-972]: If “particulars” means immaterial particulars, then direct recognition is a higher level than ordinary knowledge.

[^V03-973]: One may support this view with the saying, “The first duty in religion is to know God; the perfection of knowing is to affirm Him,” which treats knowing and assent as distinct.

[^V03-974]: It is easy to affirm that the things we sense exist.

[^V03-975]: The point is not that recognition means conception. Rather, we must first affirm that a thing exists before asking what its essence is.

[^V03-976]: More precisely, it is not the thing itself that is preserved, but its trace. The text may be read: “the thing disappeared and its trace remained.”

[^V03-977]: Some claim that spirits began later but preceded bodies by two thousand years, citing a report that spirits were created two thousand years before bodies. They connect this to the primordial covenant. The author notes that this view still leaves unexplained what caused each individual spirit to begin.

[^V03-978]: On this view, the spirits did not exist as separate individual essences; they existed through God and His detailed knowledge. Their acknowledgment praised God's greatness, dominion, and glory. Forgetting Him means becoming absorbed in nature and its scattered, dark forms.

[^V03-979]: They have not understood the point of the Qur'anic words, “He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity.” The gifts received depend on the capacities of the matter and natures that receive them. Nor have they understood “The likeness of His light is as a niche in which there is a lamp.” His light is the intellect fully active within the intellect that has acquired the ability to understand, which in turn is within the intellect still capable of learning; or it is the universal intellect in the universal soul, which is in universal nature. The same pattern continues through the other levels.

[^V03-980]: Earlier in this stage, “intellect” had other meanings. In *Keys to the Unseen*, it is also defined as the soul's natural ability to reach certainty about universal, true, necessary premises without proof or deliberate thought. This differs from the intellect in potential; it is a strong readiness for acquiring such knowledge.

[^V03-981]: This refers to the word “good”; the definition also explicitly mentions action.

[^V03-982]: The phrase describes doing work well, which is not itself wisdom. Wisdom is the knowledge that guides the work.

[^V03-983]: Do not assume from “mental existence” that the mind itself has a mental existence. The phrase means existence that is related to the mind.

[^V03-984]: The mind is the soul's readiness to acquire beliefs and opinions it does not yet have.

[^V03-985]: More exactly, knowledge is the beginning and end of worship, and worship follows from it.

[^V03-986]: The discussion of this point has already appeared earlier.

[^V03-987]: Knowledge has been defined as belief that excludes the opposite; opinion as belief that favors one side without excluding its opposite; and certainty as belief that something is so, together with belief that it cannot be otherwise. Earlier logicians were right to say that only certainty is knowledge in the strict sense. If the opposite remains possible, the belief is not necessary; and if the favored conclusion itself remains possible rather than necessary, it is not certain. Later logicians were mistaken to divide knowledge into certainty, compound ignorance, and other kinds.
